`MAX_TREE_DEPTH = 64`, six times the PRD's floor, enforced only as the runaway stop above. It is not a
product limit and must not be described to users as one; it exists so a corrupted parent chain fails
in milliseconds instead of consuming a connection. Serve it from `GET /config` (E-139) if any client
ever needs to know it. The ancestor chain being ≤ 64 rows is also what makes the "walk up from the
target" strategy correct to prefer over "walk down from the node", whose cost is the size of the
subtree and therefore unbounded by the PRD's own "không giới hạn node".

#### Ordering of siblings

**EXISTING REQUIREMENT, and there is no stored order.** The drive grid sorts client-side —
`sortNodes(visibleChildren, sort)` with `SortState` from the store
(`src/hooks/use-drive-location.ts:54`, `src/lib/tree.ts:255-276`): containers first by
`TYPE_WEIGHT` (project, folder, document, board, file), then by `name` / `updatedAt` / `size` /
`type`. `SortKey` and `ViewMode` are drive-listing-only and `ViewMode` is explicitly **UI, never
persisted server-side** (canon §2.6). Drag-and-drop in the tree re-parents and nothing else: the drag
payload is `{ nodeId, type, name }` (`src/lib/dnd.ts:5-9`) and the drop calls
`moveNode(dragId, parentId)` (`src/components/tree/arborist-tree.tsx:25-30`). There is no reorder
endpoint in canon §3.3 and no `position` column on `nodes`.

**RECOMMENDATION** — E-020 and E-023 return children in a deterministic order —
`(container_first, lower(name), id)` — matching `sortNodes` with the default
`{ key: "name", direction: "asc" }` (`src/store/workspace-store.ts:234`). `id` is the tiebreaker so
two siblings with the same name never swap between requests. The client re-sorts anyway; the point is
that pagination and diffing are stable. If manual sibling ordering is ever wanted it is an additive
schema change (`position NUMERIC` plus a reorder endpoint), not a change to anything documented here.

#### The `DriveNode` wire projection

```ts
/** Shared by all five variants. src/types/node.ts:48-78. */
interface DriveNodeBase {
  readonly id: string;               // nodes.id
  readonly name: string;             // nodes.name
  readonly slug: string;             // nodes.slug
  readonly parentId: string | null;  // nodes.parent_id
  readonly workspaceId: string;      // nodes.workspace_id
  readonly owner: UserSummary;       // users ⋈ nodes.owner_id
  readonly createdAt: string;        // nodes.created_at, ISO 8601
  readonly updatedAt: string;        // nodes.updated_at, ISO 8601
  readonly isFavorite: boolean;      // EXISTS(node_favorites WHERE user_id = session.user)
  readonly isTrashed: boolean;       // nodes.deleted_at IS NOT NULL
  readonly isShared: boolean;        // EXISTS(access_rules WHERE node_id = nodes.id)
  readonly isArchived?: boolean;     // nodes.archived_at IS NOT NULL; omitted when false
  readonly accessMode?: NodeAccessMode; // nodes.access_mode; omitted when 'inherit'
}
```

`isArchived?` and `accessMode?` are **optional, not nullable** (canon C-08). Omit the key; never send
`null`. `accessModeOf` reads `node.accessMode ?? "inherit"` (`visibility.ts:47-50`) and
`isArchivedNode` reads `node.isArchived === true` (`src/lib/archive.ts:13`), so an explicit `null`
would be a type error on a `readonly accessMode?: NodeAccessMode` field.

Note the one narrowing the frontend already performs: `DocumentNode.isArchived: boolean` is
**required**, not optional (`src/types/node.ts:103`), unlike the base. Emit it always for documents.

#### Access resolution — what `nodes` and `access_rules` do together

**EXISTING REQUIREMENT**, `src/lib/permissions/visibility.ts:109-174`. Access gates the **path**, not
the node. Walk root → node, carrying one boolean:

```
admits(node, inherited):
  switch node.access_mode:
    case 'workspace':  return isMember                       # opens back up, from here down
    case 'restricted': return isMember AND hasGrantOn(node)  # stops the flow
    default:           return inherited                      # 'inherit' passes it through
```

with

```
hasGrantOn(node, subject):
  if subject is the node's owner:                     return true   # the safety net
  if an access_rules row on this node names them:     return true
  if an access_rules row on this node names the workspace role they hold: return true
  return false
```

Consequences the schema has to support and a chapter must not soften:

- **A restricted node takes its whole subtree with it.** `visibleTree` prunes once from the root
  carrying the decision (`visibility.ts:197-240`), and `collectAllowed` does the same for flat reads
  (`src/lib/tree.ts:297-320`): *"a file inside a folder the viewer cannot open must not surface in
  search results just because the file itself carries no restriction of its own."* Every list
  endpoint — search, favourites, relation pickers, My Work — reads the pruned tree, not the raw one.
- **`workspace` mode widens downward and cannot punch back up** through a restriction above it
  (`visibility.ts:109-120`): a tree cannot render a child whose parent is missing, and showing one
  anyway would leak the name of the folder it sits in.
- **The refusal names nothing.** `not_found` and "you may not see it" answer identically (canon §4.2),
  and `DENIED_REASON` (`evaluate.ts:162-163`) is deliberately name-free: *"A refusal that reads
  'Finance is restricted' hands the name of a private folder to the one person who was told they may
  not have it."* `NodeVisibility.deniedAt` exists for the server's own bookkeeping and is **never**
  serialised to the refused caller (`visibility.ts:137-145`).
- **The one deliberate bypass** is E-046, gated on `workspace.permission.manage`, returning names and
  paths and no content, and audited (`visibility.ts:270-278`).

**Capability**, the second axis, then narrows (`evaluate.ts:69-87`), in this exact order:
role matrix (or owner escalation, which requires `roleRank >= member`) → **trashed** (a trashed node
accepts nothing but `node.delete`) → **frozen** (an archived ancestor refuses every write) →
**locked** (refuses the content-write key set). `READ_ONLY_KEYS = { board.export,
workspace.audit.view, secret.reveal }` pass through all three (`evaluate.ts:29-33`).

#### Relationships

| Cardinality | To | Through |
| --- | --- | --- |
| N-1 | `workspaces` | `workspace_id` |
| 1-N | `nodes` (self) | `parent_id` — the tree |
| N-1 | `users` | `owner_id`, plus five actor columns |
| 1-N | `access_rules` | `access_rules.node_id` |
| 1-N | `node_favorites` | per-user star (T-07) |
| 1-1 | `boards` | `boards.node_id UNIQUE NOT NULL`, when `kind = 'board'` |
| 1-1 | `documents` | `documents.node_id UNIQUE NOT NULL`, when `kind = 'document' AND document_kind = 'page'` |
| 1-1 | `config_documents` | `config_documents.node_id` PK, when `document_kind = 'config'` |
| 1-1 | `secret_documents` | `secret_documents.node_id` PK, when `document_kind = 'secret'` |
| 1-1 | `file_nodes` | `file_nodes.node_id` PK, when `kind = 'file'` |
| 1-N | `trash_entries` | restore metadata for a deleted subtree (T-09) |
| 1-N | `comments`, `watches`, `notifications` | via their decomposed target columns |

The five side tables are `ON DELETE CASCADE` from `nodes`, which is what makes the purge one
statement. A trash → restore round trip must **not** touch them: *"Deleting a document must not delete
its content. Trash detaches the node subtree; content stays keyed by `nodeId` and comes back intact on
restore."*

#### APIs that use it

| # | Endpoint | Behaviour | Permission |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| E-020 | `GET /workspaces/{workspaceId}/tree` | Nested `DriveNode[]`, **subtree-wide pruning** by visibility | membership |
| E-021 | `GET /workspaces/{workspaceId}/nodes/resolve?path=a/b/c` | `DriveLocation` — node + ancestors + children + `isNotFound`. Resolves slugs against the **pruned** tree, so a restricted node is *missing*, not disabled | membership |
| E-022 | `GET /nodes/{nodeId}` | `DriveNode` + `CapabilitySet` | visibility |
| E-023 | `GET /nodes/{nodeId}/children` | `DriveNode[]` | visibility |
| E-024 | `POST /workspaces/{workspaceId}/nodes` | Insert. `kind` in the body. Container check, slug minting, side-table row, all one transaction | `node.create` (+ `board.create` / `document.create` by kind) |
| E-025 | `PATCH /nodes/{nodeId}` | Rename. **The slug is not re-minted** (OQ-09) | `node.rename` |
| E-026 | `POST /nodes/{nodeId}/move` | The algorithm above | `node.move` |
| E-027 | `POST /nodes/{nodeId}/duplicate` | Recursive copy, content included, `isFavorite`/`isShared` reset (`cloneNode`, `src/lib/tree.ts:203-217`), name suffixed `" (copy)"`, slug re-uniquified (OQ-12) | `node.create` |
| E-028/E-029 | `PUT`/`DELETE /nodes/{nodeId}/favorite` | Writes `node_favorites`, **not** `nodes` | visibility |
| E-030 | `PUT /nodes/{nodeId}/archive` | Sets `archived_at`, `archived_by` | `node.archive` |
| E-031 | `DELETE /nodes/{nodeId}/archive` | Clears them. **Refused when an ancestor is archived** | `node.archive` |
| E-032 | `DELETE /nodes/{nodeId}` | Soft delete; **detaches the whole subtree**; writes the `trash_entries` row with `originalAncestorIds` and `originalPath` resolved *now, while the ancestors still exist* (`src/lib/trash.ts:49-51`) | `node.delete` |
| E-033 | `GET /workspaces/{workspaceId}/favorites` | Joins `node_favorites` | membership |
| E-034 | `GET /workspaces/{workspaceId}/archive` | Outermost archived node per subtree only | membership |
| E-035 | `GET /workspaces/{workspaceId}/nodes/search?q=` | `SearchHit[]`, name substring only, cheap | membership |
| E-037 | `POST /trash/{entryId}/restore` | Clears `deleted_at` down the subtree, re-parents to the deepest surviving ancestor, re-uniquifies the slug, reports `isRelocated` | `node.delete` |
| E-040–E-046 | access endpoints | Read `access_mode`; write it on E-041 | `node.access.manage` |
| E-047, E-091, E-099, E-101, E-113, E-114 | content entry points | *"Content is entered through its node, then addressed by its own id"* (canon P-04) | visibility |

**Transaction rules.**

- E-024, E-026, E-032, E-037 all take the per-workspace advisory lock. They are the four writes that
  change the shape of the tree.
- E-024 inserts the node **and** its side-table row in one transaction. A board node with no `boards`
  row is a 404 on a URL the sidebar is already showing.
- E-032 marks the subtree in one `UPDATE` driven by a downward recursive CTE, writes the
  `trash_entries` row, and writes the audit event — all or nothing.
- E-038 / E-039 compute reclaimed bytes from `file_assets` reachable through the subtree, decrement
  `workspaces.used_bytes` under `FOR UPDATE`, write the audit row, **then** `DELETE FROM nodes` and
  let the cascade do the rest.

**Errors** — `NODE_NOT_FOUND` (404 / `not_found`, and it is also the answer for a node the caller may
not see), `NODE_SLUG_CONFLICT` (409), `NODE_MOVE_SAME_PARENT` / `INTO_SELF` / `INTO_DESCENDANT` /
`INVALID_TARGET` (409), `NODE_NOT_CONTAINER` (409), `NODE_KIND_MISMATCH` (409 — the node exists but is
not the kind this route addresses, e.g. `GET /nodes/{id}/board` on a folder),
`NODE_ARCHIVE_INHERITED` (409), `NODE_TRASHED_READ_ONLY` (403), `NODE_FROZEN_BY_ANCESTOR` (403),
`NODE_LOCKED` (403), `PERMISSION_DENIED` (403).

**Realtime** — **RT-11 `node.changed`** `{ workspaceId, nodeId, change: "created" | "renamed" |
"moved" | "archived" | "trashed" | "restored" }` on every drive-tree write, so a second tab's sidebar
converges without polling (canon §7.2, OQ-99). **RT-05 `permission.changed`** additionally on E-041
and on E-026, because a move relocates a node under a different access chain and is *"a permission
change wearing the costume of a drag"* (`visibility.ts:293-302`). Both frames carry **ids only**; the
receiver refetches.

**Audit** — E-024, E-025, E-026, E-030/E-031, E-032, E-037, E-038 each write one `audit_events` row in
their own transaction, module `node`. Access-mode changes are module `workspace`, action
`workspace.permission.manage`, severity `warn` (`src/store/permission-store.ts:71-78`).

**OPEN QUESTION (OQ-56) — `project_status` overlaps `archived_at`, and three copies of `isArchived`.**
**What is unclear** — `ProjectStatus` has an `archived` member (`src/types/node.ts:46`) while
archiving is separately expressed by `isArchived` on the base type, and `DocumentNode.isArchived` and
`WorkspaceDocument.isArchived` are two further copies of the same fact.
**Evidence** — `ProjectStatus` is declared, seeded (`src/mock/factory.ts:35`, `src/mock/tree.ts:271`)
and **never read by any component** — `grep ProjectStatus src/` returns only the declaration, the
factory and the type import. `setNodeArchived` writes `isArchived` and never touches `status`
(`src/store/workspace-store.ts:592-611`). PRD `WS-ARC-02` lists the project lifecycle as
`Active / Archived / Restored / Moved to Trash`, which is the node lifecycle, not a fourth field.
**Recommendation** — `archived_at` is the single source of truth for the freeze, for every kind
including projects. Keep `project_status` as a **product** status (`active` / `paused`) that is
orthogonal to archiving, and have the API **reject `project_status = 'archived'` on write** with
`VALIDATION_FAILED`, returning it only if a legacy row holds it. Do not duplicate `isArchived` onto
`documents`; the document reads the node's timestamp.
**Impact if wrong** — a project can report `paused` on its own screen while being frozen by the drive,
or `archived` in one place and active in another, and the Archive listing (which reads the node,
`src/components/collections/archive-page.tsx:33`) will disagree with whatever reads `status`.

---

### Table: `access_rules`

**Purpose** — One grant, written on one node, for one subject (a person or a role), naming the role
that subject holds from that node downward. This is the entire storage behind `SY-INH-43` permission
inheritance and behind the `restricted` access mode. Nothing is copied down the tree: restricting a
folder with ten thousand descendants writes **one row**, and access is *resolved* by walking root →
node (`src/lib/permissions/visibility.ts:29-33`).

Canon names this table `access_rules` (T-08), matching the frontend's `AccessRule`
(`src/types/permission.ts:136-144`).

**Who creates a record** — E-042 (`PUT /nodes/{nodeId}/access-rules`), which is an **upsert by
`(node, subject)`: it replaces any existing rule for the same subject**. Also E-041 as a side effect:
switching a node to `restricted` **grants the actor first**, in the same transaction, because
*"Something you cannot see is something you cannot reopen"* (`src/hooks/use-node-access.ts:62-65,
118-134`). And E-024 writes none — a new node inherits.

**Lifetime** — Until E-043 (`DELETE /nodes/{nodeId}/access-rules/{ruleId}`), which is a **hard
delete**; clearing the last rule on a node makes it inherit again. Cascades away with the node
(E-038) and with the workspace (E-011). Deliberately **not** deleted when the subject leaves the
workspace — see the open question.

**Columns**

| Column | PostgreSQL Type | Nullable | Default | Unique | Description |
| ------ | --------------- | -------- | ------- | ------ | ----------- |
| `id` | `UUID` | no | `gen_random_uuid()` | PK | `AccessRule.id`. Addressed directly by E-043, so it is a wire value, not an internal key. |
| `workspace_id` | `UUID` | no | — | (composite) | Denormalised for the two-level index the resolver walks. Kept honest by a composite FK to `nodes(id, workspace_id)`. |
| `node_id` | `UUID` | no | — | (composite) | `AccessRule.nodeId`. The node the rule is **written on** — which is exactly what distinguishes `explicit` from `inherited` in the read model. |
| `subject_kind` | `access_subject_kind` | no | — | no | `user` \| `role` (`src/types/permission.ts:132-134`). |
| `subject_user_id` | `UUID` | yes | `NULL` | (partial) | Set when `subject_kind = 'user'`. |
| `subject_role` | `workspace_role` | yes | `NULL` | (partial) | Set when `subject_kind = 'role'`. *"Roles cover everyone holding them; users are exact"* (`:131`). |
| `role` | `workspace_role` | no | — | no | The role the subject holds **from this node downward**. Not the subject's workspace role — that is the floor this replaces. |
| `granted_at` | `TIMESTAMPTZ` | no | `now()` | no | `AccessRule.grantedAt`. |
| `granted_by` | `UUID` | no | — | no | `AccessRule.grantedBy` — a user id on the wire, not a `UserSummary` (`:143`). From the session (canon C-09). |

`AccessSubject` is a discriminated union on the wire and two mutually exclusive nullable columns in
the database — a shape the check constraint below makes airtight:

```ts
/** src/types/permission.ts:131-144. No `any`; exactly two branches. */
type AccessSubject =
  | { readonly kind: "user"; readonly userId: string }
  | { readonly kind: "role"; readonly role: WorkspaceRole };

interface AccessRule {
  readonly id: string;
  readonly nodeId: string;
  readonly subject: AccessSubject;
  readonly role: WorkspaceRole;
  readonly grantedAt: string;   // ISO 8601
  readonly grantedBy: string;   // users.id
}
```

```sql
-- documentation only
CREATE TYPE access_subject_kind AS ENUM ('user', 'role');
CREATE TYPE access_source       AS ENUM ('workspace', 'inherited', 'explicit', 'override');

CREATE TABLE access_rules (
  id              UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  workspace_id    UUID                NOT NULL,
  node_id         UUID                NOT NULL,
  subject_kind    access_subject_kind NOT NULL,
  subject_user_id UUID REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,
  subject_role    workspace_role,
  role            workspace_role      NOT NULL,
  granted_at      TIMESTAMPTZ         NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  granted_by      UUID                NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,

  CONSTRAINT access_rules_node_fk FOREIGN KEY (node_id, workspace_id)
    REFERENCES nodes(id, workspace_id) ON DELETE CASCADE,

  CONSTRAINT access_rules_subject_exclusive CHECK (
    (subject_kind = 'user' AND subject_user_id IS NOT NULL AND subject_role    IS NULL) OR
    (subject_kind = 'role' AND subject_role    IS NOT NULL AND subject_user_id IS NULL)
  )
);
```

`access_source` is declared here because it is the vocabulary the read model uses; it is **not** a
column. `AccessSource` is derived per request by comparing what a node's own rule says with what
would have arrived from above (`inheritance.ts:108-119`).

**Primary Key** — `id`.

**Foreign Keys**

| Column(s) | References | ON DELETE | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `(node_id, workspace_id)` | `nodes(id, workspace_id)` | `CASCADE` | A grant on a node that no longer exists grants nothing, and the composite form guarantees the rule and the node agree about which workspace they are in. The cascade also means E-038 purging a subtree cannot leave behind rules that would silently re-apply if an id were ever reused. |
| `subject_user_id` | `users(id)` | `RESTRICT` | **Deliberately not `CASCADE`.** Users are never hard-deleted, so this never fires — but declaring `CASCADE` would declare an intent the product does not have: the governance audit's own recommendation is to *keep* the rows when somebody leaves, because *"they are audit evidence and make re-invites predictable"*. A cascade would silently destroy exactly that evidence the moment anybody ran a hard delete. |
| `granted_by` | `users(id)` | `RESTRICT` | History. "Who granted this and when" is the first question asked about an unexpected grant. |

**No FK to `workspace_members`.** A `(workspace_id, subject_user_id) → workspace_members(workspace_id,
user_id)` composite FK is expressible — the unique constraint it needs already exists — and it is
still the wrong constraint. With `CASCADE` it would delete grants when somebody leaves; with
`RESTRICT` it would make removing a member fail whenever they hold a grant anywhere in the tree.
Membership is instead enforced **at the API layer** on E-042, and the frontend already says the
sentence: *"Nobody matching '{query}' is a member of this workspace. Invite them in Workspace
settings first."* (`src/components/permissions/node-access-dialog.tsx:100-115`) — *"Folder access is
downstream of workspace membership and never a way around it."*

**Unique Constraints**

| Index | Definition | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `access_rules_node_user_uniq` | `UNIQUE (node_id, subject_user_id) WHERE subject_kind = 'user'` | **At most one rule per (node, subject).** This is a correctness constraint, not hygiene: `matchIn` takes the **first** matching rule within a node (`inheritance.ts:63-76`), so a duplicate would make resolution order-dependent — the same person could resolve to `member` or `manager` depending on physical row order. The frontend's store already guarantees it by replacing on write (`src/store/permission-store.ts:86`); the database must too. |
| `access_rules_node_role_uniq` | `UNIQUE (node_id, subject_role) WHERE subject_kind = 'role'` | Same rule for the role-scoped branch. Two partial indexes rather than one, because the two subject columns are mutually exclusive and a single index over both would treat `(node, NULL)` pairs as distinct. |

These are what let E-042 be `INSERT … ON CONFLICT (node_id, subject_user_id) WHERE subject_kind =
'user' DO UPDATE SET role = EXCLUDED.role, granted_at = now(), granted_by = EXCLUDED.granted_by`. Note
this keeps the rule's `id` **stable**, where the frontend's store mints a fresh id on every write
(`permission-store.ts:63`). Stable is better: E-043 addresses a rule by id, and the frontend re-reads
the whole list after every write anyway (canon C-11), so nothing depends on the id changing.

**Indexes**

| Index | Definition | Query it serves |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `access_rules_pkey` | `(id)` | E-043. |
| `access_rules_node_user_uniq` / `_node_role_uniq` | partial uniques, above | The hot path: given the ancestor chain of a node, fetch every rule written on any node in it. `WHERE node_id = ANY(:chain)`. |
| `access_rules_workspace_node_idx` | `(workspace_id, node_id)` | Mirrors the frontend's own index shape — rules are keyed `Record<workspaceId, Record<nodeId, AccessRule[]>>` (`src/store/permission-store.ts:21-31`) — and serves the bulk load when a request resolves several nodes at once (a tree read, a search funnel). |
| `access_rules_subject_idx` | `(subject_user_id) WHERE subject_kind = 'user'` | "Which nodes is this person explicitly granted", needed to compute the `userIds` payload of **RT-05** when a node's access mode changes, and to answer OQ-02's ghost-row cleanup. |

**Check Constraints**

| Constraint | Rule | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `access_rules_subject_exclusive` | see the DDL above | The discriminated union, in the database. Without it a row can name both a person and a role, and `sameSubject` (`inheritance.ts:24-28`) would key it two ways. |

**Relationships**

| Cardinality | To | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| N-1 | `nodes` | The node the rule is written on |
| N-1 | `users` | `subject_user_id` (when user-scoped) and `granted_by` |
| N-1 | *a role* | `subject_role` is an enum value, not a row — there is no `roles` table (below) |
| derived | `nodes.isShared` | `EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM access_rules WHERE node_id = nodes.id)` |

#### How the rules are read

**EXISTING REQUIREMENT**, `src/lib/permissions/inheritance.ts:40-120`. The chain is walked
**root → node, so the last match is always the most specific one** (`:40-43`). Within one node, a rule
naming the **person** outranks one naming their **role** — *"the more specific subject wins, exactly
as the deeper node does"* (`:50-54`). The workspace role is the floor under all of it.

```
effectiveAccess(node, subject):
  base      := subject's workspace_members.role   (or 'viewer' for a role-subject)
  chain     := [root, …, parent, node]            # ordered, root first
  inherited := deepest match in chain[0 .. -2]
  own       := match on chain[-1]

  if own is null:
      return inherited ? (inherited.role, source = 'inherited', origin = inherited.node)
                       : (base,           source = 'workspace', origin = null)

  wouldHave := inherited?.role ?? base
  return (own.role,
          source = own.role == wouldHave ? 'explicit' : 'override',
          origin = own.node)
```

Canon OQ-22 position: **deepest node wins**; at one node a user-scoped rule beats a role-scoped rule;
the workspace role is the floor. The PRD's `SY-INH-43` edge case says *"Xung đột quyền giữa Group và
User: Áp dụng mức quyền cao hơn (Union of permissions)"* — union, not deepest — and the code does
deepest. Canon has decided; do not re-litigate it in a chapter.

**Resolving the chain in SQL.** The same recursive CTE as the cycle check, then one indexed fetch:

```sql
-- documentation only
WITH RECURSIVE chain(id, parent_id, depth) AS (
    SELECT id, parent_id, 0 FROM nodes WHERE id = :node_id
  UNION ALL
    SELECT n.id, n.parent_id, chain.depth + 1
      FROM nodes n JOIN chain ON n.id = chain.parent_id
     WHERE chain.depth < 64
)
SELECT r.*, c.depth
  FROM access_rules r
  JOIN chain c ON c.id = r.node_id
 WHERE r.subject_user_id = :user_id
    OR (r.subject_kind = 'role' AND r.subject_role = :caller_role)
 ORDER BY c.depth DESC;   -- depth 0 is the node itself; DESC gives node-first
```

Because the chain is depth-bounded, this is a handful of index probes, which is what makes
`SY-INH-43`'s *"Duyệt cây quyền hạn kế thừa < 50ms khi truy vấn"* achievable without a materialised
path. If profiling ever says otherwise, the alternative is an `ancestor_ids UUID[]` column on `nodes`
with a GIN index — one array containment instead of a CTE, paid for by rewriting the whole subtree on
every move. Do not add it speculatively.

#### The read model E-040 returns

`resolveAccess` (`inheritance.ts:127-167`) emits **one row per workspace member**, plus a row of its
own for every role-scoped rule anywhere on the chain — *"a grant that covers a group is never
invisible just because it names no one"* (`:136-138`) — sorted by `roleRank` **descending** (`:166`).

```ts
/** E-040 → NodeAccessResponse.entries[]. src/types/permission.ts:160-171. */
interface ResolvedAccess {
  readonly subject: AccessSubject;
  readonly role: WorkspaceRole;
  readonly source: AccessSource;              // workspace | inherited | explicit | override
  readonly origin: AccessOrigin | null;       // node the rule is written on; null = workspace default
  readonly inheritedRole: WorkspaceRole | null;
  readonly inheritedFrom: AccessOrigin | null;
}
interface AccessOrigin { readonly nodeId: string; readonly name: string; }
```

Badge copy, so a chapter does not invent its own: `workspace` → "Workspace role", `inherited` →
"Inherited", `explicit` → "Explicit", `override` → "Override" (`inheritance.ts:170-175`).

The seeded fixtures that exercise every branch are `src/mock/access.ts:24-53`: Duc is `manager` on
*Development* and taken back down to `member` on *Backend* (**override**); Lan is explicitly `member`
on *Backend* where she would have inherited `member` anyway (**explicit**); *Marketing* carries a
role-scoped grant lifting every `viewer` to `member`.

#### APIs that use it

| # | Endpoint | Behaviour | Permission |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| E-040 | `GET /nodes/{nodeId}/access` | `{ accessMode, inheritedFrom, entries: ResolvedAccess[] }`, sorted by `roleRank` desc | `node.access.manage` |
| E-041 | `PUT /nodes/{nodeId}/access-mode` | Writes `nodes.access_mode`. **When switching to `restricted`, insert a grant for the actor first, in the same transaction** | `node.access.manage` |
| E-042 | `PUT /nodes/{nodeId}/access-rules` | Upsert by `(node, subject)` | `node.access.manage` |
| E-043 | `DELETE /nodes/{nodeId}/access-rules/{ruleId}` | Hard delete; the last one removed makes the node inherit again | `node.access.manage` |
| E-044 | `GET /nodes/{nodeId}/capabilities` | `CapabilitySet`, derived from the resolved role | visibility |
| E-046 | `GET /workspaces/{workspaceId}/restricted-nodes` | The admin recovery console. Names and paths, **no content**, audited at `warn` | `workspace.permission.manage` |
| — | *every read of a node* | Gate 2 (visibility) and gate 3 (capability) both consult this table | — |

`node.access.manage` is a **Manager** key, not an Admin one (`src/lib/permissions/roles.ts:44-47`):
*"Restricting a folder is structural, not administrative: a project lead shuts their own folder
without waiting on a workspace admin. It only ever applies to a folder they can already see, so it
hands out nothing."*

**Transaction** — E-041 switching to `restricted` is two writes that must not be separable: the
actor's grant and the mode change. `useNodeAccess.setMode` does them in that order for exactly this
reason (`src/hooks/use-node-access.ts:118-140`) — *"Grant before restricting, not after: the order is
what makes it impossible to lock yourself out with one dropdown."* On a server the order matters less
than the atomicity, but do both: a crash between them must not leave a restricted node with no grants.

**Errors** — `PERMISSION_DENIED` (403, name-free copy per canon §4.4 rule 3), `NODE_NOT_FOUND` (404)
for a node the caller may not see, `MEMBER_NOT_FOUND` (404) when E-042 names a non-member,
`VALIDATION_FAILED` (400) when the subject union is malformed.

**Realtime** — every write here publishes **RT-05 `permission.changed`**
`{ workspaceId, nodeId, userIds }` (canon §7.1). `userIds` is the set of people whose resolved access
actually changed: for a user-scoped rule, that one person; for a role-scoped rule, every member
holding that role; for a mode change, the symmetric difference of the visible sets computed the way
`moveVisibilityImpact` computes it (`visibility.ts:313-333`). The frame carries **no resource
content** — *"a frame announcing a revocation must not be the thing that leaks what was revoked"*
(`src/types/realtime.ts:20-25`). The same event must invalidate any server-side authorization cache
keyed by `(workspaceId, userId)`: *revocation that takes effect on the next cache expiry is not
revocation.*

**Audit** — every write here is an `audit_events` row in the same transaction: module `workspace`,
action `workspace.permission.manage`, severity **`warn`**, `target` = the node name, `detail` = a
sentence naming the subject and the new role. The frontend already writes exactly this on both paths
(`src/store/permission-store.ts:71-78` for a grant, `:99-106` for a clear), with copy of the form
*"{subject} set to {Role} on this item."* and *"{subject} now inherits access instead of holding it
here."*

**OPEN QUESTION (OQ-02) — rules naming somebody who has left the workspace.**
**What is unclear** — whether removing a member should delete their `access_rules` rows.
**Evidence** — `withoutMember` (`src/lib/workspace-access.ts:261-263`) removes the membership and
touches no rules. `roleOf` returns `null` for a non-member (`visibility.ts:66-73`), so a **role-scoped**
rule stops matching them at once; a **user-scoped** rule still matches by id and `hasGrantOn` would
still admit them — but `VisibilityInput.isMember` is false and `nodeVisibility` refuses at
`visibility.ts:161` before that is ever reached. Net effect today: harmless, but the rows persist and
would silently re-activate on a re-invite.
**Recommendation** — keep the rows (they are audit evidence and make re-invites predictable), but
(a) filter non-members out of the `ResolvedAccess` entries E-040 returns, so the dialog does not list
ghosts, and (b) make membership authoritative in gate 1, so a rule can never be the thing that lets
somebody back in.
**Impact if wrong** — deleting them loses the record of who was granted what and when; keeping them
without gate 1 being authoritative silently restores access on re-invite to a folder nobody
re-shared.

### Table: `trash_entries`

Canon T-09.

**Purpose** — everything needed to put a deleted subtree back, recorded at the moment of
deletion rather than reconstructed at the moment of restore. The frontend's `TrashEntry`
(`src/types/system.ts:171-180`) carries the deleted node, who deleted it and when, the
ancestor chain it hung from, and `originalPath` — a human string like `Development /
Backend`, resolved at deletion **so it survives its ancestors being purged**. That last
field is the reason this is a table and not a query: by the time somebody opens the trash,
the folder the node came from may itself be gone, and a path computed on read would be a
path to nowhere.

**Who creates a record** — E-032 `DELETE /nodes/{nodeId}`, in the same transaction that sets
`nodes.deleted_at` on the subtree. Exactly one entry per delete **gesture**, written for the
subtree root only: deleting a folder of forty pages produces one trash entry, not forty,
because one gesture is what the user will want to undo.

**How long it lives** — 30 days from `deleted_at`, then the subtree is purged and the entry
goes with it. Restoring removes the entry immediately.

**How it is deleted** — three ways, all of them removing the row: restore (E-034), explicit
purge (E-035), and the retention sweep. The row is never soft-deleted; a trash entry about a
trash entry is not a thing.

**Columns**

| Column | PostgreSQL Type | Nullable | Default | Unique | Description |
| ------ | --------------- | -------- | ------- | ------ | ----------- |
| `id` | `UUID` | no | `gen_random_uuid()` | PK | |
| `workspace_id` | `UUID` | no | — | no | Denormalised from the node so the trash list is one indexed read, and so the entry is still scoped after its ancestors are purged. |
| `node_id` | `UUID` | no | — | yes | The subtree root. Unique: a node is in the trash once or not at all. |
| `deleted_by` | `UUID` | no | — | no | Projected into `TrashEntry.deletedBy` as a `UserSummary`. |
| `deleted_at` | `TIMESTAMPTZ` | no | `now()` | no | Start of the retention clock. Must equal `nodes.deleted_at` for the same node. |
| `purge_after` | `TIMESTAMPTZ` | no | `deleted_at + interval '30 days'` | no | Stored rather than computed, so changing the retention policy does not silently re-date everything already in the bin. |
| `original_parent_id` | `UUID` | yes | — | no | Where it hung. Null when it was a workspace-root node. **Not** an FK — see below. |
| `original_ancestor_ids` | `UUID[]` | no | `'{}'` | no | `TrashEntry.originalAncestorIds`, root first. Plain array, not an FK set: these ids are a *record of the past*, and half of them may no longer resolve. |
| `original_path` | `TEXT` | no | — | no | `Development / Backend`, resolved at deletion. The reason the table exists. |

**Primary Key** — `id`.

**Foreign Keys**

| Column | References | ON DELETE | Why that behaviour |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `workspace_id` | `workspaces(id)` | `CASCADE` | Deleting a workspace purges its bin with it. |
| `node_id` | `nodes(id)` | `CASCADE` | The entry describes the node; purging the node purges the entry, in one statement. |
| `deleted_by` | `users(id)` | `RESTRICT` | Users are deactivated, never hard-deleted (T-01), so this never fires — it is there to make that invariant enforceable rather than assumed. |

`original_parent_id` and `original_ancestor_ids` carry **no** foreign key, deliberately. They
are history, and a `RESTRICT` on them would make deleting an old folder impossible while
anything remembered living in it; a `CASCADE` would erase the record of where something came
from at exactly the moment that record becomes hard to reconstruct. Restore resolves them at
read time and falls back when they no longer exist — which is precisely what
`RestoreOutcome.isRelocated` reports (`src/types/system.ts:182-188`).

**Unique Constraints** — `trash_entries_node_uniq UNIQUE (node_id)`.

**Indexes**

| Index | Type | Serves |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `trash_entries_pkey` | btree, unique | |
| `trash_entries_node_uniq` | btree, unique | the restore and purge paths, which address by node |
| `trash_entries_list_idx (workspace_id, deleted_at DESC)` | btree | E-033, the trash list — the only read anyone paginates |
| `trash_entries_sweep_idx (purge_after)` | btree | the retention job, which asks one question of the whole table |

**Checks** — `CHECK (purge_after > deleted_at)`.

**Delete Behavior** — hard delete, always.

**Relationships** — 1-1 with the `nodes` row it points at, for as long as that row is
soft-deleted. N-1 to `workspaces` and to `users`.

**APIs that use it** — E-032 writes it, E-033 `GET /workspaces/{workspaceId}/trash` lists
it, E-034 `POST /nodes/{nodeId}/restore` reads and removes it, E-035 purges. `RestoreOutcome`
is assembled from this row plus a live lookup of `original_parent_id`: when that parent is
gone the node lands at the workspace root and `isRelocated` is true, which is the one case
the UI must explain rather than merely report.

---

### Roles and permissions are code, not tables

**DECIDED (canon §1.2).** There is no `roles` table and no `permission_definitions` table, and no
chapter may add one.

**`WorkspaceRole` is a Postgres enum**, `('viewer','member','manager','admin')`, and **the
declaration order is the rank**: `roleRank` is `WORKSPACE_ROLES.indexOf(role)`
(`src/types/permission.ts:10-20`). Declare the enum in that order and `roleRank` is reproducible in
SQL with `array_position(enum_range(NULL::workspace_role), role)`.

**The 39 permission keys are static service config**, not rows. `PERMISSION_KEYS`
(`src/types/permission.ts:31-78`) is a `const` array; `PermissionModule` is **derived from the key's
first segment, never declared beside it** (`src/lib/permissions/catalog.ts:8-14`) — *"a key can
therefore never be filed under a module it does not belong to."* The catalogue's labels and summaries
are UI copy in the same file. E-045 (`GET /permissions/catalog`) serves
`PermissionDefinition[]` from that config so both sides agree, and there is no write endpoint for it.

**The role matrix is cumulative and lives in one function.** `src/lib/permissions/roles.ts:84-96`
accumulates: viewer holds **zero** keys (*"the viewer column of the matrix is empty by construction
rather than by omission"*, `:11-16`), member adds 10, manager adds 21, admin adds 8 — 39 total. A
role's set is *"the one below it plus what it adds, so a permission can never be granted to Member and
withheld from Manager by accident."*

**Owner escalation is a set of five keys, not a role.** `OWNER_ESCALATIONS = { node.rename,
node.delete, node.archive, file.delete, document.lock }` (`roles.ts:102-108`), and it applies **only
from `member` upward**: `owns && OWNER_ESCALATIONS.has(key) && roleRank(role) >= roleRank("member")`
(`evaluate.ts:72-74`). A Viewer who owns a node gets no escalation. Ownership therefore needs no table
either — it is `nodes.owner_id`.

Storing any of this would create a second copy of a rule the code already owns, and the two would
drift the first time a key was added. Canon §1.2 is explicit: *"The 39-key catalogue is static config
shipped from the backend, not a table."*

---

#### Chapter notes — divergences, decisions and traps

1. **`node_access_grants` → `access_rules`.** The brief for this part asked for a table called
   `node_access_grants`. Canon §1.1 T-08 names it **`access_rules`**, matching the frontend's
   `AccessRule` interface (`src/types/permission.ts:136-144`) and the endpoint paths E-042 / E-043
   (`/nodes/{nodeId}/access-rules`). I followed canon. If the brief's name was deliberate, it needs to
   change in canon first, along with two endpoint paths and one domain-interface name.

2. **Scope boundary with the next part.** I documented `users`, `user_sessions`, `workspaces`,
   `workspace_members`, `workspace_invitations`, `nodes` and `access_rules` — every table canon
   assigns to the `identity`, `workspace` and `drive` modules except `node_favorites` (T-07) and
   `user_ui_preferences` (T-37), which the brief assigns to a later part along with recents. If
   another part also covers `user_sessions` (T-02) or `workspace_invitations` (T-05), delete one copy;
   both are canon **RECOMMENDATION** tables (OQ-01, OQ-04) and a backend developer cannot implement
   login or membership without them, so I judged a duplicate cheaper than a gap.

3. **`nodes.template_id` does not exist.** `BoardNode.templateId` is projected from
   `boards.template_id` by the 1:1 join, on the grounds that the frontend types it as a bare `string`
   *"for reference only"* (`src/types/node.ts:110-111`) and one source of truth beats two. If the
   `boards` chapter assumes a denormalised copy on `nodes`, reconcile in favour of the join — E-048
   forbids reading a board's **rows**, not its `boards` row.

4. **`locked_at` / `locked_by` live on `nodes`.** Canon OQ-30's position says the node owns
   `isLocked`, so I put the actor and timestamp beside it rather than splitting one fact across two
   tables. The `documents` chapter must project `lockedBy` from `nodes`, not store its own copy.

5. **User FKs are `ON DELETE RESTRICT` throughout**, including `access_rules.subject_user_id`, where
   `spec/audit/governance.md:1132-1170` sketches `ON DELETE CASCADE`. The cascade contradicts that
   same document's own recommendation to keep the rows as audit evidence, and users are never
   hard-deleted anyway, so `RESTRICT` states the real invariant. Flagging it because the fact sheet's
   DDL and this part's DDL differ on that one word.

6. **`nodes` has no `position` column.** No manual sibling ordering exists anywhere in the frontend:
   drag-and-drop re-parents only, and the drive grid sorts client-side. If a later part introduces one,
   it is additive and does not affect anything documented here.

7. **No new OQ ids were minted.** The two open questions raised in this part cite existing canon ids
   (OQ-56 for the archive-representation overlap, OQ-02 for orphaned grants). The `project_status`
   ambiguity is genuinely new material but sits inside OQ-56's territory rather than needing an id of
   its own; if the editor disagrees, it wants a fresh id appended to canon §8.2.

### 4.10 The board engine — what these tables are, and how they fit

Six tables carry the whole board engine: `boards` (T-10), `board_columns` (T-11), `board_rows`
(T-12), `board_row_relations` (T-13), `board_views` (T-15) and `board_templates` (T-17). Two more
tables sit beside them and belong to other chapters: `row_activity` (T-14, the `boards` module) and
`board_view_preferences` (T-16, the `views` module).

Three canon decisions shape everything below, and none of them is re-opened here:

| Decision | Where | Consequence for this chapter |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cell values live in `board_rows.cells JSONB`. There is no `cell_values` table. | canon §1.3.2 | §4.16 reproduces the trade-off analysis in full. |
| Select options live in `board_columns.config JSONB`. There is no `select_options` / `board_column_options` table. | canon §1.3.3 | §4.13 documents the option as a JSONB object with its full interface. |
| `task` / `bug` / `qa` / `apiDocs` are rows in `board_templates`. There is no `tasks`, `bugs`, `qa_cases` or `api_endpoints` table. | canon §1.3.5 | §4.20 documents the template; no chapter may add a typed table for the four. |

```mermaid
erDiagram
    nodes ||--|| boards : "node_id UNIQUE, kind='board'"
    boards ||--o{ board_columns : "board_id"
    boards ||--o{ board_rows : "board_id"
    boards ||--o{ board_views : "board_id"
    boards }o--|| board_columns : "primary_column_id (RESTRICT)"
    boards }o--o| board_templates : "template_id (SET NULL)"
    board_rows ||--o{ board_rows : "parent_row_id (SET NULL)"
    board_rows ||--o{ board_row_relations : "source_row_id"
    board_rows ||--o{ board_row_relations : "target_row_id"
    board_columns ||--o{ board_row_relations : "source_column_id"
    board_views }o--o| board_columns : "group_by / date / end_date (SET NULL)"
    board_views ||--o{ board_view_preferences : "view_id (other chapter)"
    board_rows ||--o{ row_activity : "row_id (other chapter)"
```

The shape of the aggregate is fixed by the frontend and must not be re-derived: `Board` carries
`columns` and `views` inline (`src/types/board.ts:412-427`), `BoardSnapshot` is
`{ board, rows, people, nextCursor }` (`src/types/board.ts:430-436`), and a schema response is a
complete array rather than a delta (canon C-11, `src/store/board-store.ts:698`).

### 4.11 Table: `boards`

**Purpose** — the board aggregate: one row per drive node of kind `board`. It owns the two things a
board has that a node does not — the record-id prefix and the atomic sequence counter that mints
`TASK-001` — plus the pointer to the column that titles every record. Everything a board *contains*
(columns, rows, views) hangs off this row.

**Who creates a record** — `POST /workspaces/{workspaceId}/nodes` with `kind: "board"` (E-024),
in the same transaction that inserts the `nodes` row. When the request names a `templateId`, the
same transaction also instantiates the template's columns and views (§4.20). Nothing else creates a
board: `GET /workspaces/{workspaceId}/boards` (E-048) is explicitly forbidden from seeding one
(`src/services/board-service.ts:1234-1246` — "listing them never seeds").

**Lifetime** — exactly as long as its node. Trashing the node (E-032) is a soft delete on `nodes`
and leaves this row untouched, so a restore (E-037) brings the board back whole. The row is hard
deleted only when the node is purged — `DELETE /trash/{entryId}` (E-038), `DELETE
/workspaces/{workspaceId}/trash` (E-039) or the 30-day retention sweep (canon OQ-14 position) —
through `ON DELETE CASCADE` from `nodes`.

**Columns**

| Column | PostgreSQL Type | Nullable | Default | Unique | Description |
| ------ | --------------- | -------- | ------- | ------ | ----------- |
| `id` | `uuid` | no | `gen_random_uuid()` | PK | Board identity. Wire field `board.id`. Kept alongside `node_id` on purpose (canon OQ-30). |
| `node_id` | `uuid` | no | — | yes | The drive node the board is addressed by. Wire field `board.nodeId` (`src/types/board.ts:417`). |
| `workspace_id` | `uuid` | no | — | no | Tenant key, denormalised from `nodes.workspace_id` so board-scoped reads never walk the tree. Wire field `board.workspaceId` (`src/types/board.ts:418`). |
| `row_id_prefix` | `text` | no | — | no | `TASK`, `BUG`, `QA`, `API`. Upper-case letters only, 1–6 of them (`normalizePrefix`, `src/lib/row-id.ts:18-20`). Seeded from the template. |
| `primary_column_id` | `uuid` | no | — | no | The one column that titles a record. Wire field `board.primaryColumnId`. |
| `next_sequence` | `bigint` | no | `0` | no | The atomic record-id counter. Monotonic, never decremented, never reset. See §4.11.1. |
| `template_id` | `uuid` | yes | `NULL` | no | The template this board was generated from — **for reference only** (`src/types/board.ts:414-415`). Projected onto the wire as the template's `builtin_id` when it has one, so `board.templateId === "apiDocs"` keeps working (`src/lib/api-catalog.ts:28-40`). |
| `assignee_column_id` | `uuid` | yes | `NULL` | no | **RECOMMENDATION** (OQ-48). The column that plays the assignee role. See §4.16.4. |
| `due_column_id` | `uuid` | yes | `NULL` | no | **RECOMMENDATION** (OQ-48). The column that plays the due-date role. |
| `status_column_id` | `uuid` | yes | `NULL` | no | **RECOMMENDATION** (OQ-48). The column that plays the status role. |
| `created_at` | `timestamptz` | no | `now()` | no | C-03. |
| `updated_at` | `timestamptz` | no | `now()` | no | Bumped by every column, view and board write — the frontend does exactly this (`src/services/board-service.ts:580, 657, 803`). |
| `created_by` | `uuid` | no | — | no | From the session, never the body (C-09). |

`boards` has **no `name` column.** Canon's position on OQ-30 is that the node owns `name`,
`isPinned`, `isLocked` and `isArchived`, and that they are *projected* onto the board rather than
duplicated. `board.name` on the wire is `nodes.name`. See the note at the end of this file.

**Primary Key** — `id`.

**Foreign Keys**

| Column | References | ON DELETE | Why that behaviour |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `node_id` | `nodes(id)` | `CASCADE` | A board has no life outside the tree. Purging the node must purge the board, its columns, its rows and its views in one statement — anything else leaves an unreachable aggregate holding storage and quota. |
| `workspace_id` | `workspaces(id)` | `CASCADE` | Tenant deletion (E-011) removes everything in the tenant. |
| `primary_column_id` | `board_columns(id)` `DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED` | `RESTRICT` | E-054 already refuses to delete the primary column (`COLUMN_PRIMARY_PROTECTED`, `src/services/board-service.ts:687-690`). `RESTRICT` is the database saying the same thing, so a bug in the service cannot decapitate a board. Deferred because `boards` and its first `board_columns` row are inserted in the same transaction and reference each other. |
| `template_id` | `board_templates(id)` | `SET NULL` | The template is reference data. Deleting a user-authored template (E-090) must never delete or freeze the boards made from it — a board "can add, rename, retype and delete columns and must never be constrained by the template it came from" (canon §1.3.5). |
| `created_by` | `users(id)` | `RESTRICT` | Users are soft-deactivated, never hard-deleted (T-01), so this can never fire; `RESTRICT` documents the invariant. |
| `assignee_column_id`, `due_column_id`, `status_column_id` | `board_columns(id)` | `SET NULL` | Deleting the due-date column must degrade My Work to "this board contributes nothing", exactly as the name heuristic does today (`src/lib/my-work.ts:99-110`), not fail the delete. |

**Unique Constraints**

- `UNIQUE (node_id)` — one board per node. This is what makes `GET /nodes/{nodeId}/board` (E-047) a
  single-row lookup and what canon OQ-30 requires.

**Indexes**

| Index | Serves |
| --- | --- |
| `boards_pkey (id)` | Every `/boards/{boardId}/…` route (E-049 … E-086). |
| `UNIQUE (node_id)` | E-047 `GET /nodes/{nodeId}/board`; the board-id ↔ node-id resolution the frontend does today (`src/services/board-service.ts:120-126`). |
| `(workspace_id)` | E-048 `GET /workspaces/{workspaceId}/boards`; the workspace-wide scans behind search (E-133) and My Work (E-134). |
| `(template_id) WHERE template_id IS NOT NULL` | `SearchResultKind`'s `api` / `bug` / `qa` buckets, derived from `boards.template_id` at read time (`src/services/search-service.ts:39-43`). |

**Check Constraints**

- `row_id_prefix ~ '^[A-Z]{1,6}$'` — the exact output of `normalizePrefix`
  (`src/lib/row-id.ts:9, 18-20`). Violation → `ROW_ID_PREFIX_INVALID` (400 / `validation`).
- `next_sequence >= 0`.

**Relationships**

- 1-1 with `nodes` (`node_id` unique).
- 1-N `board_columns`, `board_rows`, `board_views` — all `ON DELETE CASCADE` from here.
- N-1 `board_templates` (many boards from one template).
- N-1 `workspaces`.

**APIs that use it**

| # | Endpoint | Permission | Transaction | Realtime | Errors |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| E-024 | `POST /workspaces/{workspaceId}/nodes` (`kind: "board"`) | `node.create` + `board.create` | One: `nodes` + `boards` + template columns + template views | RT-11 `node.changed` (`created`) | `NODE_NOT_CONTAINER`, `NODE_SLUG_CONFLICT`, `ROW_ID_PREFIX_INVALID` |
| E-047 | `GET /nodes/{nodeId}/board` → `BoardSnapshot` | visibility | read-only | — | `NODE_NOT_FOUND`, `NODE_KIND_MISMATCH` |
| E-048 | `GET /workspaces/{workspaceId}/boards` → `BoardDescriptor[]` | membership | read-only, **must not read rows** | — | `WORKSPACE_NOT_FOUND` |
| E-049 | `GET /boards/{boardId}` → `Board` | visibility | read-only | — | `BOARD_NOT_FOUND` |
| E-050 | `PATCH /boards/{boardId}` → `Board` | `board.manage` (+ `node.rename` when `name` is present) | One: `boards` + `nodes.name` | RT-10 `board.schema.changed`, RT-11 `node.changed` (`renamed`) | `BOARD_NOT_FOUND`, `ROW_ID_PREFIX_INVALID` |

**Frontend callers** — `boardService.getBoard` (`src/services/board-service.ts:229-242`) behind
`useBoardStore.loadBoard`; `boardService.listBoards` (`:1238-1246`) behind
`useRelationIndex` (`src/hooks/use-relation-index.ts:35-73`) and the relation column's target
picker (`src/components/board/cells/relation-cell.tsx:104-106`).

#### 4.11.1 The record-id counter — `next_sequence`

**EXISTING REQUIREMENT.** The counter lives on `boards`, as one `bigint` column. Canon T-10 and
canon §1.4 ("Counters") both settle this: there is **no `board_row_sequences` table**, and there is
no Postgres `SEQUENCE` object per board.

Allocation, verbatim, inside the same transaction as the row insert:

```sql
-- documentation only
UPDATE boards
   SET next_sequence = next_sequence + 1
 WHERE id = $1
RETURNING next_sequence;                 -- the new row's `sequence`
```

For a batch (import E-085, bulk move E-077) the same statement adds `N` and the service hands out
the returned block, so one import lands as `TASK-042 … TASK-141` with no gaps
(`src/services/board-service.ts:1183-1214`).

Four rules, all grounded, all non-negotiable:

1. **`MAX(sequence) + 1` is forbidden.** "Two simultaneous creates must never produce `TASK-005`
   twice" — `docs/BOARD.md:266-269` names this a blocking backend requirement.
2. **The counter only increases.** Deleting `TASK-005` never hands `005` to the next record. The
   frontend service does exactly `record.sequence += 1` and never inspects the row set
   (`src/services/board-service.ts:290-293, 304`); the type comment says it outright — "Numeric part
   of the display id; monotonic per board, **never reused**" (`src/types/board.ts:242-243`). Canon
   restates it on E-062.
3. **The `UPDATE … RETURNING` takes a row lock on the board**, which is also the lock that serialises
   the batch. That lock is the reason the counter is a column here rather than a separate table:
   every row-creating write already touches this row, so a `board_row_sequences` table would add a
   join and a second lock to buy nothing.
4. **The client never invents an id.** An optimistic row carries `` `${prefix}-…` `` with
   `sequence: 0`, `revision: 0`, `isPending: true`, and is replaced in place by `replaceRow` when the
   response arrives (`src/store/board-store.ts:368-375`, `src/lib/board-records.ts:128-145`).

`displayId` is unique **per board**, not globally: two boards may both hold `TASK-001`. A cross-board
bulk move (E-077) gives the moved records **new** ids from the destination board's counter and does
not carry the source id (`src/services/board-service.ts:1133-1144`).

**OPEN QUESTION (OQ-43) — may `rowIdPrefix` change after records exist?**
**Evidence** — `normalizePrefix` is exported (`src/lib/row-id.ts:18`) but nothing in
`src/components/**` or `src/store/**` calls it; the prefix is read from the template once, at board
creation (`prefixForBoard`, `src/mock/board.ts:69-71`). `custom_id` is stored per row, so changing
`boards.row_id_prefix` would leave existing records on the old prefix. Canon lists `rowIdPrefix` as
patchable on E-050 but takes no position on the rewrite.
**Recommendation** — accept the patch only while `next_sequence = 0`. Past that, refuse with
`ROW_ID_PREFIX_INVALID` and offer an explicit rewrite job that updates every `custom_id`, writes one
`row_activity` entry per board (not per row), and re-emits RT-10.
**Impact if wrong** — one board carrying two prefixes; `extractRowReferences`
(`src/lib/row-id.ts:37-43`) silently stops linking the old ones, and every `TASK-nnn` written into a
comment body before the rename dead-ends.

---

### 4.12 Table: `board_columns`

**Purpose** — one column of one board: its name, its type, where it sits, how wide it is by default,
whether it is hidden, whether it titles the record, and the whole of its per-type configuration.
It is the board's *schema*, shared by every view — "schema lives on the column and is shared by every
view; presentation is per view" (`src/lib/board-view.ts:15-21`).

**Who creates a record** — `POST /boards/{boardId}/columns` (E-052); the board-creation transaction
when a template is instantiated (E-024, §4.20); `POST /boards/{boardId}/columns/{columnId}/duplicate`
(E-055); and `POST /boards/{boardId}/import` (E-085), which may create columns for unmatched source
columns inside the import transaction.

**Lifetime** — hard delete. `DELETE /boards/{boardId}/columns/{columnId}` (E-054) removes the row,
strips the column's key from every record's `cells`, prunes every view that referenced it, and drops
the matching `board_row_relations` edges — all in one transaction. There is no soft delete and no
trash for a column. Cascades away with its board.

**Columns**

| Column | PostgreSQL Type | Nullable | Default | Unique | Description |
| ------ | --------------- | -------- | ------- | ------ | ----------- |
| `id` | `uuid` | no | `gen_random_uuid()` | PK | Column identity. **Cells are keyed by this value** (`board_rows.cells`), as are every view's `columnOrder`, `columnWidths`, `columnDisplay`, `hiddenColumnIds`, filters and sorts. |
| `board_id` | `uuid` | no | — | no | Owning board. |
| `name` | `text` | no | — | no | Display name. Unique per board case- and punctuation-insensitively (`normalizeColumnName`, `src/lib/board-schema.ts:151-153`). |
| `type` | `column_type` | no | — | no | Enum: `text`, `longText`, `select`, `date`, `user`, `attachment`, `relation` — the frontend literals verbatim, `longText` **not** normalised to `long_text` (canon §2.0). |
| `position` | `int` | no | — | no | 0-based, densely renumbered across the whole schema on every insert, move and delete (`reposition`, `src/lib/board-schema.ts:202-206`). |
| `width` | `int` | no | `180` | no | The *schema default* width. `280` for the primary column. Clamped to `[88, 720]` (`src/lib/board-schema.ts:10-13, 70-72`). A view may override it per viewer; see §4.19. |
| `hidden` | `boolean` | no | `false` | no | The *schema* hidden flag. A view can only add hiding on top of it, never remove it (`resolveColumns`, `src/lib/board-view.ts:34`). |
| `is_primary` | `boolean` | no | `false` | no | The one column that titles a record. Never hidden, never deleted, never duplicated into a second primary (`src/services/board-service.ts:610-612`). |
| `config` | `jsonb` | no | `'{}'::jsonb` | no | `ColumnConfigByType[type]` — the discriminated branch named by `type`. Fully specified in §4.12.1. |
| `created_at` | `timestamptz` | no | `now()` | no | |
| `updated_at` | `timestamptz` | no | `now()` | no | |

**Primary Key** — `id`.

**Foreign Keys**

| Column | References | ON DELETE | Why that behaviour |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `board_id` | `boards(id)` | `CASCADE` | A column has no meaning without its board; purging the board must take the schema with it in one statement. |

**Unique Constraints**

- `UNIQUE (board_id, position) DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED` — positions are dense `0..n-1`
  (E-056 renumbers the whole list). Deferred because a reorder rewrites several rows in one
  statement and passes through transiently duplicate positions.
- `UNIQUE (board_id, lower(regexp_replace(name, '[^A-Za-z0-9]', '', 'g')))
   WHERE regexp_replace(name, '[^A-Za-z0-9]', '', 'g') <> ''` — mirrors `normalizeColumnName`
  exactly. The partial predicate matters: a name made only of punctuation normalises to the empty
  string, and `findColumnByName` returns `undefined` for an empty needle
  (`src/lib/board-schema.ts:161`), so two such columns are legal in the frontend and must stay legal
  here. Creation de-duplicates silently to `Notes`, `Notes 2`, … (`uniqueColumnName`,
  `src/lib/board-schema.ts:170-180`), so this index is a guard, not the mechanism;
  `COLUMN_NAME_CONFLICT` is raised only where the caller demanded an exact name.
- `UNIQUE (board_id) WHERE is_primary` — exactly one primary column per board.

**Indexes**

| Index | Serves |
| --- | --- |
| `board_columns_pkey (id)` | Every `/columns/{columnId}` route (E-053 … E-060). |
| `(board_id, position)` | E-051 `GET /boards/{boardId}/columns`; the ordered column list inside every `BoardSnapshot` (E-047). |
| `UNIQUE (board_id) WHERE is_primary` | Resolving `boards.primary_column_id` and the row title for E-069, E-071, E-072. |
| `(board_id, type) WHERE type = 'relation'` | The backlink and relation-index writers (§4.17) need every relation column of a board without scanning the schema. |

**Check Constraints**

- `width BETWEEN 88 AND 720` — `MIN_COLUMN_WIDTH` / `MAX_COLUMN_WIDTH`
  (`src/lib/board-schema.ts:10-11`). E-053 clamps rather than refuses, so this can only fire on a
  service bug.
- `position >= 0`.
- `NOT (is_primary AND hidden)` — `patchColumn` refuses to hide the primary
  (`src/lib/board-schema.ts:99`) and `resolveColumns` refuses to honour it if one ever got through
  (`src/lib/board-view.ts:34`). E-053 **silently ignores** `hidden` on the primary column rather
  than erroring, so this constraint also can only fire on a service bug.
- `jsonb_typeof(config) = 'object'`.

The full `config`-matches-`type` rule is **not** a check constraint. It is validated at the API
boundary against the per-type JSON schema in §4.12.1, because expressing seven mutually exclusive
object shapes with nested condition trees as a `CHECK` is unreadable and unmaintainable. Violation →
`COLUMN_TYPE_CONFIG_MISMATCH` (400 / `validation`).

**Relationships**

- N-1 `boards`.
- 1-N `board_row_relations` (as `source_column_id`) — relation columns only.
- 0-1 `boards` (as `primary_column_id`, `assignee_column_id`, `due_column_id`, `status_column_id`).
- Referenced by `board_views` through three FK columns and six JSONB payloads (§4.19).
- Referenced by `board_rows.cells` by key — **an untyped reference**. There is no FK from a JSONB
  key to `board_columns.id`, so E-054 must prune the orphaned keys in its own transaction. Canon
  §1.3.2 names this as the one real cost of the JSONB decision.

**APIs that use it**

| # | Endpoint | Permission | Transaction | Realtime | Errors |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| E-051 | `GET /boards/{boardId}/columns` → `BoardColumn[]` | visibility | read-only | — | `BOARD_NOT_FOUND` |
| E-052 | `POST /boards/{boardId}/columns` → `BoardColumn` | `board.column.create` | One: insert + renumber the rest | RT-10 | `COLUMN_TYPE_CONFIG_MISMATCH`, `COLUMN_NAME_CONFLICT` |
| E-053 | `PATCH /boards/{boardId}/columns/{columnId}` → `BoardColumn` | `board.column.update` | One row | RT-10 | `COLUMN_NOT_FOUND`, `COLUMN_TYPE_CONFIG_MISMATCH`, `CONDITION_TREE_TOO_DEEP`, `OPTION_ID_RESERVED` |
| E-054 | `DELETE /boards/{boardId}/columns/{columnId}` → `BoardColumn[]` | `board.column.delete` | One: delete + renumber + strip the key from every row's `cells` + bump each row's `revision` + prune every view + delete the relation edges | RT-10, RT-07 per touched row | `COLUMN_NOT_FOUND`, `COLUMN_PRIMARY_PROTECTED` |
| E-055 | `POST /boards/{boardId}/columns/{columnId}/duplicate` → `DuplicateColumnResponse` | `board.column.create` | One: insert at `position + 1` + copy every cell value + bump each row's `revision` | RT-10, RT-07 | `COLUMN_NOT_FOUND` |
| E-056 | `POST /boards/{boardId}/columns/reorder` → `BoardColumn[]` | `board.column.update` | One: dense renumber `0..n-1` | RT-10 | `COLUMN_NOT_FOUND` |
| E-057 | `POST /boards/{boardId}/columns/{columnId}/convert` → `ConvertColumnResponse` | `board.column.update` | One: retype + reset `config` to the type default + rewrite every cell | RT-10, RT-07 | `COLUMN_NOT_FOUND`, `COLUMN_CONVERT_UNSUPPORTED` |
| E-058 – E-060 | select-option routes | `board.column.update` | One `config` rewrite | RT-10 | see §4.13 |

**Frontend callers** — `boardService.createColumn` / `updateColumn` / `reorderColumn` /
`deleteColumn` / `duplicateColumn` / `convertColumn`
(`src/services/board-service.ts:555-756`), all behind `useBoardStore`; the Options & rules dialog
(`src/components/board/config/select-column-dialog.tsx`); the column menu in
`src/components/board/table/table-grid.tsx`.

#### 4.12.1 `board_columns.config` — the complete JSONB contract

The branch is selected by the row's `type`. This is the frontend's `ColumnConfigByType`
(`src/types/board.ts:162-170`) verbatim; no field is added and none is dropped.

```ts
/** Discriminated by `board_columns.type`. Exactly one branch is valid per row. */
interface ColumnConfigByType {
  readonly text: TextConfig;
  readonly longText: LongTextConfig;
  readonly select: SelectConfig;
  readonly date: DateConfig;
  readonly user: UserConfig;
  readonly attachment: AttachmentConfig;
  readonly relation: RelationConfig;
}

/** `{}` is the whole default. `placeholder` is declared and never written today (OQ-54). */
interface TextConfig {
  readonly placeholder?: string;
}

/** Turning a long-text column into numbered steps: `B1: …`, `T2: …`. */
interface StepNumbering {
  readonly enabled: boolean;
  /** Letters before the number — `B`, `T`, `Step `. May be empty. */
  readonly prefix: string;
  /** The number the first step takes. */
  readonly start: number;
  /** What follows the number — `:` or `.`. */
  readonly separator: string;
}

interface LongTextConfig {
  /** Preferred editor height in text rows. Default 4. */
  readonly rows: number;
  readonly stepNumbering?: StepNumbering;
}

interface SelectConfig {
  /** Ordered. The array index IS the option's position — see §4.13. */
  readonly options: readonly SelectOption[];
  readonly isMulti: boolean;
  /** What the dropdown does with an unavailable option. Default `"disabled"`. */
  readonly unavailableBehavior?: UnavailableOptionBehavior;   // "disabled" | "hidden"
  /** Option ids that mean "finished". Subtask progress counts against these. */
  readonly completedOptionIds?: readonly string[];
  readonly transitionRules?: TransitionRules;                  // §4.14
}

interface DateConfig {
  /** False → the cell is a calendar day. True → an instant. Governs C-04 vs C-03. */
  readonly includesTime: boolean;
}

interface UserConfig {
  readonly isMulti: boolean;
}

interface AttachmentConfig {
  readonly maxFiles: number;                                   // default 10
}

interface RelationConfig {
  /** Target board id. `null` means "this board" (`relation-cell.tsx:104-106`). */
  readonly boardId: string | null;
  /** Column whose value labels each chip. `null` falls back to the primary column. */
  readonly displayColumnId: string | null;
  readonly isMulti: boolean;
}
```

**Defaults minted for a new column** (`DEFAULT_CONFIG`, `src/lib/board-schema.ts:36-44`) — the
service writes these, the client never sends them:

| `type` | `config` written on create |
| --- | --- |
| `text` | `{}` |
| `longText` | `{ "rows": 4 }` |
| `select` | `{ "options": [], "isMulti": false }` |
| `date` | `{ "includesTime": false }` |
| `user` | `{ "isMulti": false }` |
| `attachment` | `{ "maxFiles": 10 }` |
| `relation` | `{ "boardId": null, "displayColumnId": null, "isMulti": true }` |

A `longText` column with no `stepNumbering` reads as
`{ enabled: false, prefix: "", start: 1, separator: ":" }` (`src/lib/step-numbering.ts:29-34`); the
default is resolved on read, not stored.

**Patch semantics.** `ColumnPatch.config` is **shallow-merged** over the stored object
(`patchColumn`, `src/lib/board-schema.ts:102`), not replaced. `PATCH …/columns/{columnId}` (E-053)
therefore accepts `{"config": {"isMulti": true}}` on a select column without resending the options
array. Two rules follow:

1. The merge is one level deep. Sending `{"config": {"options": [...]}}` replaces the **whole**
   options array — which is exactly how the Options & rules dialog commits, as one draft
   (`src/components/board/config/select-column-dialog.tsx:80-92`).
2. Unknown keys are rejected, and a key belonging to a different branch is rejected
   (`COLUMN_TYPE_CONFIG_MISMATCH`). The frontend never sends a config for a type the column is not.

**Conversion resets `config`.** `POST …/convert` (E-057) writes `defaultConfigFor(newType)` and
discards the old branch entirely (`retypeColumn`, `src/lib/board-schema.ts:209-220`;
`src/services/board-service.ts:734`). Options, transition rules and availability trees are gone the
moment a select column becomes text — which is why the endpoint offers `?dryRun=true`.

**Size ceiling — RECOMMENDATION (OQ-38).** `config` is capped at **64 KB** serialised. See §4.15 for
the condition-tree limits inside it.

---

### 4.13 Select options — stored inside `board_columns.config.options`

**There is no `board_column_options` table.** Canon §1.3.3 decides this and the decision is not
re-opened here. The reasoning, restated: options are never read without their column, and three
sibling structures inside the same `config` reference option ids by value — `completedOptionIds`,
`transitionRules.transitions` (keyed by option id, with the reserved key `"__empty__"`) and each
option's own `availability` condition tree — so splitting the options into a table would put one
atomic configuration across two tables with no foreign key able to protect any of those references.
A commit that renames an option and rewrites its transition row would become two statements that can
half-apply.

```ts
interface SelectOption {
  /** Immutable identity. Everything keys off this: cells, `completedOptionIds`,
   *  `transitionRules.transitions` (keys and targets) and condition values. */
  readonly id: string;
  /** Display only. Renaming an option changes nothing else. */
  readonly label: string;
  readonly color: SelectColor;          // gray|blue|green|amber|red|violet|cyan|pink
  /** Switched off in column settings — never selectable, whatever a record holds. */
  readonly isDisabled?: boolean;
  /** Extra gate: offered only while this holds against the record being edited.
   *  Null or absent means "always offered". §4.15. */
  readonly availability?: ConditionGroup | null;
}
```

**The option's position is its index in the `options` array.** There is no `position` field, and
adding one would be wrong: the array order is already load-bearing in three places, and a second
ordering key could disagree with it.

- `cellSortKey` sorts a select cell by the option's **index** in `config.options`, because "select
  sorts by option order, which is the meaningful one for statuses"
  (`src/lib/cell-values.ts:148-155`).
- `linearTransitions` reads the column's own order as a pipeline — each status may reach the next
  (`src/lib/transition-rules.ts:186-207`).
- Kanban builds one bucket per option, in array order, from the **schema** rather than from the
  records, so a status with no records still gets a column (`docs/BOARD.md`, "Group (`VW-GRP-17`)").

Reordering options is therefore an ordinary `config` rewrite through E-053, not a `/reorder` route.

**Option ids — the rules**

| Rule | Detail | Grounding |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Immutable once minted | Renaming an option must never re-mint its id. Everything that references it references the id. | `src/lib/board-hierarchy.ts:130-137` — "nothing here reads a label, so renaming Done to Shipped changes nothing" |
| Column-scoped by construction | UI-minted ids are `opt_<columnId>_<base36 counter>` "because two columns sharing one is a collision waiting to happen" | `src/components/board/config/select-column-dialog.tsx:70-80` |
| Server-minted ids | E-058 mints its own when the client sends none. Any collision-free string is legal; the frontend never parses an option id. | `src/services/board-service.ts:773` |
| Template ids are kept verbatim | `status_0 … status_4`, `env_0 … env_2`, `method_0 …` survive instantiation unchanged (§4.20). | `src/lib/board-templates.ts:20-22, 422-454` |
| `"__empty__"` is reserved | It is the transition table's key for the empty bucket. A user-authored option may never take it. | `EMPTY_OPTION_KEY`, `src/lib/transition-rules.ts:28` |
| Unique within the column | Enforced at the API boundary on every `config` write. | — |

Violation of the reserved id → `OPTION_ID_RESERVED` (400 / `validation`).

**Colour** is picked client-side by cycling the palette — `SELECT_COLORS[options.length % 8]`, order
`blue, green, amber, red, violet, cyan, pink, gray` (`src/lib/board-schema.ts:25-34, 225-227`) — and
sent in the request. The backend stores what it is given, validated against the eight `SelectColor`
members, and never recomputes it (canon §1.3.3).

**`isDisabled`** is the first and cheapest of the three availability gates: an option switched off in
column settings is never selectable, whatever a record already holds. The refusal string is the
constant `"Turned off in column settings"` (`src/lib/select-availability.ts:82-90`).

**Availability** is the `ConditionGroup` in §4.15. `null` and absent are the same thing, and an
*empty* group is also the same thing — "no conditions means no gate"
(`isConditionGroupEmpty`, `src/lib/conditions.ts:112-117`).

#### 4.13.1 Option lifecycle endpoints

| # | Endpoint | Behaviour | Permission |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| E-058 | `POST /boards/{boardId}/columns/{columnId}/options` → `SelectOption` | **Dedupes by trimmed, case-folded label and returns the existing option with `200`. Never `409`.** | `board.column.update` |
| E-059 | `PATCH …/options/{optionId}` → `SelectOption` | Label, colour, `isDisabled`, `availability`. The id is never re-minted. | `board.column.update` |
| E-060 | `DELETE …/options/{optionId}` → `SelectOption[]` | Removes the option and cascades inside `config`. **Cells keep the orphaned id.** | `board.column.update` |

**E-058's dedupe rule is an EXISTING REQUIREMENT**, not a nicety: "Two users typing 'Blocked' at the
same moment must end up with one option. Contract: `POST` returns the existing option when the label
already exists (200, not 409)" (`docs/BOARD.md:297-300`). The match is
`option.label.toLowerCase() === label.trim().toLowerCase()` (`findOptionByLabel`,
`src/lib/board-schema.ts:231-237`). Implement it as `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` on the column row, then
scan `config.options`, then insert — the column row lock is what makes two concurrent creates agree.

**E-060's cascade, in the same `config` rewrite** — the frontend already does all of this locally,
so the backend must match it exactly:

1. Remove the option from `options`.
2. Remove its id from `completedOptionIds`.
3. `pruneTransitionRules` — drop the option's key from `transitions` **and** drop it from every
   other key's target list (`src/lib/transition-rules.ts:256-268`).
4. Drop every `Condition` in every remaining option's `availability` whose `value` or `values` names
   the deleted id (`select-column-dialog.tsx:178-190`).
5. **Do not touch `board_rows.cells`.** Records keep the orphaned option id. `cellText` falls back to
   the cell's `text` when no id resolves (`src/lib/cell-values.ts:93-99`) and the frontend renders
   the value as unknown, not as deleted. Canon E-060 states this outright: "cells keep the orphaned
   id; the frontend renders it as unknown, not deleted."

Errors: `SELECT_COLUMN_NOT_FOUND` (404 — missing **or not of type `select`**), `OPTION_NOT_FOUND`
(404), `OPTION_ID_RESERVED` (400), `CONDITION_TREE_TOO_DEEP` (400).

---

### 4.14 Transition rules — stored inside `board_columns.config.transitionRules`

**Storage decision, per canon §1.3.3: a JSONB member of `SelectConfig`, not its own table.** The
transition table is keyed by option id and its targets are option ids, so it is part of the same
atomic configuration as the options themselves. A separate table would need every write to span two
tables with no FK protecting the option references — the exact failure canon §1.3.3 rules out.

```ts
interface TransitionRules {
  /** Off by default. With `false`, every move is permitted. */
  readonly enabled: boolean;
  /** Only value today. Left open for a future deny-list. */
  readonly mode: "allow-list";
  /** fromKey → the keys it may move to. Keys and targets are option ids,
   *  plus the sentinel "__empty__" on BOTH sides. */
  readonly transitions: Readonly<Record<string, readonly string[]>>;
}
```

Absent config reads as `{ enabled: false, mode: "allow-list", transitions: {} }`
(`NO_TRANSITION_RULES`, `src/lib/transition-rules.ts:35-39`).

**Evaluation — the backend must reproduce this exactly** (`evaluateTransition`,
`src/lib/transition-rules.ts:102-133`). The move is **allowed** when any of these hold:

1. `enabled === false`. A board behaves like a plain Kanban until someone opts in.
2. `from === to` — a move that changes nothing.
3. `!isGoverned(from) || !isGoverned(to)`, where `isGoverned(k)` is `Object.hasOwn(transitions, k)`.
   **A key the table does not mention is ungoverned and unrestricted.** This is what makes adding a
   new status safe: "an allow-list that silently strands every new status would be a trap"
   (`src/lib/transition-rules.ts:55-61`).
4. `transitions[from]` contains `to`.

Otherwise it is refused, and the refusal names both ends *and* where the record can go instead:
`` `${column.name} cannot go straight from X to Y. X can move to A, B.` `` — or
`` `… X has no permitted moves.` `` when the source's list is empty
(`src/lib/transition-rules.ts:120-132`). That sentence is the `message` on the error; the API returns
it verbatim so the UI shows it unchanged.

Two details that are easy to get wrong:

- **The source key is the record's *first* option id**, or `"__empty__"` when the cell is empty
  (`currentKey`, `src/lib/select-availability.ts:56-62`).
- **Clearing a status is always legal.** Only *arriving* somewhere is gated
  (`src/lib/board-write-rules.ts:74`).

**Where it is enforced — RECOMMENDATION (canon R-03 on the board fact sheet).** Today
`guardCellEdits` is client-side only; `board-service.updateCells` does not call it
(`src/services/board-service.ts:484-535`). The backend **must** run the same gate on:

| Endpoint | Why |
| --- | --- |
| E-066 `PATCH /boards/{boardId}/rows/cells` | The table cell editor, the drawer field, the Kanban drop and a clipboard paste are all this one call (`src/lib/board-write-rules.ts:6-13`). |
| E-074 `POST /boards/{boardId}/rows/bulk/update` | Bulk edit writes the same values across a selection. |
| E-085 `POST /boards/{boardId}/import` | An import must not be able to place a record in a status no drag could reach. |
| E-077 `POST /boards/{boardId}/rows/bulk/move` | Cross-board move re-reads values into the destination's columns. |

Without it the workflow is advisory and any direct API call bypasses it. Refusal →
`TRANSITION_NOT_ALLOWED` (409 / `conflict`).

**Validation on write** — every key and every target must be either an existing option id of the
same column or `"__empty__"`; `mode` must be `"allow-list"`. Reject anything else with
`COLUMN_TYPE_CONFIG_MISMATCH`. This is not a database constraint; it is boundary validation, because
the referenced ids live in a sibling key of the same JSONB document.

**Who may edit** — `board.column.update`, checked server-side. Rationale straight from the code: "a
member who may write a Status cell is not thereby entitled to rewrite the workflow that governs every
card on the board" (`src/services/board-service.ts:636-645`). Below that permission the editor
renders **read-only rather than hidden** — "the rule that refuses your drag is worth being able to
look up" (`src/components/board/config/transition-rules-editor.tsx:29-37`) — so `GET
/boards/{boardId}/columns` (E-051) must return `transitionRules` to any caller with visibility.

**None of this is permission.** "May this user edit Status at all" is answered separately, before any
of it, by `row.update` (`src/lib/select-availability.ts:24-29`).

---

### 4.15 Conditional select availability — the `ConditionGroup` / `Condition` JSONB schema

Stored at `board_columns.config.options[i].availability`. Fully specified, no `any`, references
option ids and never labels.

```ts
type ConditionOperator =
  | "is" | "isNot" | "contains" | "notContains"
  | "isAnyOf" | "isNoneOf"
  | "before" | "after" | "on"
  | "isEmpty" | "isNotEmpty";

/** One test against one column of the record being evaluated. */
interface Condition {
```
