### 28.5 Node access modes — INHERIT / WORKSPACE / RESTRICTED

#### 28.5.1 Three modes, on every node kind

```ts
// src/types/node.ts:3-21
export type NodeAccessMode =
  /** Whatever the nearest ancestor decided. The default. */
  | "inherit"
  /** Every member of the workspace, regardless of what an ancestor said. */
  | "workspace"
  /** Only the subjects granted here. Stops inheritance at this node. */
  | "restricted";

export const NODE_ACCESS_MODES: readonly NodeAccessMode[] = ["inherit", "workspace", "restricted"];
```

The field is **optional on the wire and absent means `inherit`** (`src/types/node.ts:61-77`,
normalised by `accessModeOf`, `src/lib/permissions/visibility.ts:47-50`). In the database it is
`nodes.access_mode node_access_mode NOT NULL DEFAULT 'inherit'` (part-03), so absence and `inherit`
are one value at rest and the API emits `inherit` explicitly.

UI copy, which the API may serve but must not paraphrase (`visibility.ts:35-45`):

| Mode | Label | Summary |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `inherit` | Inherit from parent | Whoever can see the folder this sits in. |
| `workspace` | All workspace members | Everyone in the workspace, whatever the parent says. |
| `restricted` | Restricted | Only the people listed below. |

**The mode lives on `nodes`, not on a folders table.** `src/hooks/use-node-access.ts:52-60`:
*"It works on any node, not only a folder. `accessMode` has always been on the base node type and
`visibility.ts` has always walked every node in the chain without asking whether it holds children —
the restriction was only ever in the menu that opened this. A single `.env` file being readable by
everyone who can reach its folder is exactly the case the model was built for."*

`tests/folder-access.test.ts:464-530` covers a restricted **file** end to end: invisible to an
ungranted Manager, visible to its owner, pruned out of the tree while its neighbours stay, listed in
the admin recovery path, correctly named by `deniedAt`, and covered by the lock-out guard.

#### 28.5.2 The resolution algorithm — prose

Access **gates the path, not the node**. To decide whether subject *S* may see node *N*:

1. If *S* is not a member of the workspace, the answer is **no** and there is nothing more to ask.
   *"Not a member" is not "viewer"* (`src/lib/workspace-access.ts:12-13`).
2. If *N* is `null` — the workspace root — the answer is **yes**.
3. Otherwise build the **ancestor chain root → N, inclusive**. If the chain is empty (the node is
   not in the tree at all) the answer is **visible**; the caller turns that into a *not found*. The
   access engine deliberately does not manufacture a denial for a node that does not exist
   (`visibility.ts:164-165`).
4. Walk the chain from the root, carrying a boolean `allowed`, initially `true`. At each node:
   - `workspace` → `allowed := isMember` (**re-opens**, from this node downward),
   - `restricted` → `allowed := isMember AND hasGrantOn(node, S)` (**stops inheritance**; only the
     grants written here, plus the owner, admit),
   - `inherit` → `allowed` is unchanged (**passes through**).
5. The first node that sets `allowed` to `false` **stops the walk**. Record which node it was for
   the server's own bookkeeping; never tell the caller.

The critical asymmetry: **`workspace` cannot punch back up.** Because the walk short-circuits, a
`workspace` node inside a restricted folder is still invisible to somebody not granted the parent —
*"a tree cannot render a child whose parent is missing, and showing one anyway would leak the name
of the folder it sits in"* (`visibility.ts:109-120`; `tests/folder-access.test.ts:266-301`).

Whether a grant **written on one node** admits a subject:

- the node's **owner** is always admitted, unconditionally (`visibility.ts:93`);
- a rule whose subject is exactly *S* admits;
- a rule whose subject is a **role** admits if *S* holds that **workspace** role — the workspace
  role, not their effective node role, so this is **not recursive** (`visibility.ts:66-73`).

#### 28.5.3 The resolution algorithm — pseudocode

```
# EXISTING REQUIREMENT. src/lib/permissions/visibility.ts:87-174, transcribed.

hasGrantOn(node, subject, rules, members) -> bool:
    if subject.kind == 'user' and node.owner_id == subject.userId:
        return true                              # the owner is always in
    written := rules[node.id] or []
    if any(r in written where sameSubject(r.subject, subject)):
        return true
    role := (subject.kind == 'role') ? subject.role
                                     : members[subject.userId]?.role   # NULL if not a member
    if role is NULL:
        return false
    return any(r in written where r.subject.kind == 'role' and r.subject.role == role)

admits(node, inherited, subject) -> bool:
    switch node.access_mode:
        case 'workspace':  return isMember
        case 'restricted': return isMember and hasGrantOn(node, subject, rules, members)
        default:           return inherited          # 'inherit', including an absent value

nodeVisibility(nodeId, subject) -> { isVisible, deniedAt }:
    if not isMember:        return { false, null }
    if nodeId is NULL:      return { true,  null }        # the workspace root

    chain := ancestors_inclusive(nodeId)                  # root -> node, ORDERED
    if chain is empty:      return { true,  null }        # not in the tree: a 404, not a denial

    allowed := true
    for node in chain:                                    # root first
        allowed := admits(node, allowed, subject)
        if not allowed:
            return { false, { nodeId: node.id, name: node.name } }

    return { true, null }
```

**SQL shape.** One recursive CTE for the chain and one indexed fetch for every rule written on any
node in it — the same two queries gate 3 needs, so run them once and use the result for both:

```sql
-- documentation only
WITH RECURSIVE chain(id, parent_id, access_mode, owner_id, depth) AS (
    SELECT id, parent_id, access_mode, owner_id, 0
      FROM nodes WHERE id = :node_id AND workspace_id = :workspace_id
  UNION ALL
    SELECT n.id, n.parent_id, n.access_mode, n.owner_id, chain.depth + 1
      FROM nodes n JOIN chain ON n.id = chain.parent_id
     WHERE chain.depth < 64
)
SELECT c.*, r.id AS rule_id, r.subject_kind, r.subject_user_id, r.subject_role, r.role
  FROM chain c
  LEFT JOIN access_rules r
    ON r.node_id = c.id
   AND (r.subject_user_id = :actor_id
        OR (r.subject_kind = 'role' AND r.subject_role = :actor_workspace_role))
 ORDER BY c.depth DESC;    -- depth 0 is the node itself; DESC gives root-first
```

`SY-INH-43` sets the budget at *"Duyệt cây quyền hạn kế thừa < 50ms khi truy vấn"* and `SY-RBC-42`
at *"Kiểm tra quyền hạn p99 < 10ms ở tầng Middleware/Guard"*. A depth-bounded CTE over
`nodes_parent_idx` plus one probe on `access_rules_workspace_node_idx` meets both without a
materialised path. **Do not add an `ancestor_ids UUID[]` column speculatively** — it buys one array
containment and costs a rewrite of the whole subtree on every move.

#### 28.5.4 What happens to descendants — nothing is written to them

`src/lib/permissions/visibility.ts:29-33`: *"Nothing is copied down the tree. Access is resolved by
walking from the root to the node, so restricting a folder with ten thousand descendants writes one
field, and a child's own mode is the only thing that can change what it inherited."*

`tests/folder-access.test.ts:423-442` builds a 201-deep tree, restricts the root, and asserts
`Object.keys(rules) === ["root"]` — one row, and the leaf 200 levels down is correctly invisible.

| Descendant's own `access_mode` | Effect of an ancestor's restriction |
| --- | --- |
| `inherit` (the default, and almost everything) | Follows the decision flowing in from above, unchanged. Nothing is stored on it. |
| `restricted` | Discards what flowed in **only if the chain reached it**. Its own grants (plus its owner) decide. It cannot become visible to somebody who was already refused higher up. |
| `workspace` | Re-opens to every member **from this node downwards** — and only if the chain reached it. It cannot punch back up through a restriction above. |

**A refused node takes its whole subtree with it.** `visibleTree` prunes once, root-down, carrying
the decision (`visibility.ts:184-240`) — cost is one pass, not a chain-walk per node. This is what
stops a board inside a restricted folder from surfacing in search, favourites or a relation picker
just because the board itself carries no restriction of its own
(`tests/folder-access.test.ts:182-190`).

The tree-prune function returns **the array it was given** when it removed nothing
(`visibility.ts:203-236`, `tests/folder-access.test.ts:445-450`). That is a React re-render
optimisation, not a server concern, but it tells the backend something useful: the common case is a
workspace with no restricted node at all, so the pruning path should be a cheap "are there any
restricted nodes in this workspace" check (`nodes_restricted_idx`) before any per-node work.

#### 28.5.5 On move — a move is a permission change

`src/lib/permissions/visibility.ts:293-302`:

> Moving something is a permission change wearing the costume of a drag: a board dropped into a
> restricted folder becomes invisible to everybody the folder is not shared with, and nothing about
> the board itself changed. The only honest thing to do is say so before it happens.

**What moves and what does not.**

| Thing | On `POST /nodes/{nodeId}/move` (E-026) |
| --- | --- |
| `nodes.access_mode` on the moved node | **Unchanged.** A node with its own mode carries it (`visibility.ts:318`). |
| `access_rules` rows on the moved node and its descendants | **Unchanged.** Rules are written on nodes, and the nodes still exist. |
| `nodes.owner_id` | **Unchanged.** |
| The ancestor chain | **Changed** — which is the entire effect. Everyone's visibility of the subtree is re-resolved on the next read. |
| `nodes.slug` | **Re-uniquified against the new siblings** (canon OQ-10 position). Not a permission concern, but it happens in the same transaction. |

**The pre-flight the frontend already computes.**

```ts
// src/lib/permissions/visibility.ts:304-333
export interface MoveImpact {
  /** Members who can see it now and would not afterwards. */
  readonly losing: readonly string[];
  /** Members who cannot see it now and would afterwards. */
  readonly gaining: readonly string[];
}

export function moveVisibilityImpact(input, node, targetParentId): MoveImpact {
  if (accessModeOf(node) !== "inherit") return NO_IMPACT;   // carries its own mode
  // per member: compare canSeeNode(node.id) with canSeeNode(targetParentId)
}
```

`src/store/workspace-store.ts:562-589` calls it on **every** move and folds the count into the
feedback toast: *"Moved 'Payment' to Backend — 3 people can no longer see it"*.

**EXISTING REQUIREMENT for the backend.** E-026 must compute the same impact inside its transaction
and publish **RT-05 `permission.changed`** with `userIds = losing ∪ gaining` and the moved node's
id. Without it, a user who just lost access keeps the board on screen until they reload
(`src/hooks/use-access-sync.ts:19-91`).

**RECOMMENDATION (canon has no endpoint for this).** Expose the pre-flight so the confirmation can
be honest before the write, not only after it:

```
GET /api/v1/nodes/{nodeId}/move-impact?targetParentId={uuid|null}
→ 200 { "losing": ["usr_…"], "gaining": ["usr_…"] }
```

Gated on `node.move` plus visibility of both the node and the target. It is a read; it emits no
audit row. If canon declines to register it, E-026's response should carry the same two arrays so
the toast text can be produced from the write's own result.

#### 28.5.6 On parent deletion, and the trash gap

**Soft delete (E-032).** Deleting **detaches** the subtree from the tree and parks it in the bin
with a record of where it came from (`src/lib/trash.ts:6-12`, `:29-54`). The whole subtree is
stamped `isTrashed` recursively; `access_rules` rows are **not touched** — the FK is
`ON DELETE CASCADE` against `nodes`, and a soft delete removes no `nodes` row.

**Permanent delete (E-038 / E-039 / the retention sweep).** The `nodes` rows go, and
`access_rules ON DELETE CASCADE` takes every grant on the subtree with them. That cascade is not
merely tidiness: it guarantees a purged-and-recreated id can never inherit a stale grant.

**The gap the frontend has, stated plainly, because a security reviewer will find it.**

**RECOMMENDATION — resolve gate 2 for a trashed node against its recorded ancestor chain, not
against the live tree.**

*What the frontend does today.* A trashed node is detached, so `findPathToId` returns `[]`. Two
functions then take their empty-chain branch:

- `nodeVisibility` → `if (chain.length === 0) return VISIBLE` (`visibility.ts:164-165`);
- `effectiveAccess` → `if (chain.length === 0) return { role: base, source: "workspace", origin: null }`
  (`inheritance.ts:101-102`).

*The consequence.* **Deleting a restricted folder un-restricts it.** Every workspace member can see
the entry in Trash, and their role on it is their plain workspace role — so any Manager, and any
Member who owns it, can restore it (`src/components/collections/trash-page.tsx:141-143` gates both
Restore and Delete permanently on `can("node.delete")` against the detached node). The governance
audit reaches the same conclusion from the other direction (canon OQ-10's evidence).

*Why the fix is available.* `TrashEntry` already carries the chain, resolved at deletion time
precisely because it cannot be resolved afterwards:

```ts
// src/types/system.ts:171-180
export interface TrashEntry {
  readonly id: string;
  readonly node: DriveNode;                         // the whole subtree, flagged isTrashed
  readonly deletedAt: string;
  readonly deletedBy: UserSummary;
  /** Ancestors at the moment of deletion, root first. */
  readonly originalAncestorIds: readonly string[];
  /** `Development / Backend` — resolved at deletion, so it survives a purge. */
  readonly originalPath: string;
}
```

*The rule.* For a node whose `deleted_at IS NOT NULL`, gate 2 and gate 3 walk
`trash_entries.original_ancestor_ids ++ [node]` instead of the live chain, skipping ancestors that
have themselves been purged. A skipped ancestor is treated as `inherit` — it can no longer refuse,
but the node's **own** `access_mode` and its own grants still apply, which is what preserves the
restriction on the thing that was actually restricted. E-036 (`GET /trash`) then lists only entries
the caller could have seen before the delete, and E-037 / E-038 refuse anything else with
`TRASH_ENTRY_NOT_FOUND` (404).

*Impact if this is not done.* "Restrict the folder, then delete it" is a one-click declassification
of everything inside it to every member of the workspace, followed by a one-click restore by anyone
who holds `node.delete`. It also contradicts the promise the recovery console is sold on — that a
restricted node is invisible to an admin until somebody grants it.

*Grounding note.* This is a **RECOMMENDATION**, not a transcription: the frontend's behaviour is as
described above and there is no counter-evidence. It sits between canon **OQ-14** (trash retention
and the purge sweep) and **OQ-15** (soft-delete scope); see the editor note at the end of this file.

#### 28.5.7 Switching to `restricted` — the lock-out guard

```ts
// src/hooks/use-node-access.ts:118-140
if (mode === "restricted" && !hasGrantOn(rules, node, ME, workspace.members)) {
  // Grant before restricting, not after: the order is what makes it
  // impossible to lock yourself out with one dropdown.
  setAccessRule(workspace.id, node, ME, myWorkspaceRole ?? "manager");
}
setNodeAccessMode(node.id, mode);
```

`wouldLockOut` (`visibility.ts:342-348`) is the predicate; `tests/folder-access.test.ts:310-317` and
`:524-530` assert it for a folder and for a file.

**EXISTING REQUIREMENT.** E-041 switching a node to `restricted` must insert the actor's grant and
write the mode **in one transaction**. A mode flip that commits without the grant produces a node
only its owner and the recovery console can reopen. The order matters less on a server than the
atomicity; do both.

**Revoking the last grant is allowed and announced, never blocked** (`use-node-access.ts:153-169`):
*"{name} now has nobody but its owner. An admin can reopen it from Workspace settings."*

---

### 28.6 Permission inheritance: Workspace → Project → Folder → Content

This is `SY-INH-43`, and it is the **role** axis (gate 3) — distinct from visibility (gate 2), over
the same chain.

#### 28.6.1 The hierarchy

```
Workspace          workspace_members.role                     the default, when no rule applies
   └─ Project      access_rules on the project node
        └─ Folder  access_rules on the folder node            each level may write a rule
             └─ Content (board / document / config / secret / file)
```

`SY-INH-43` states it: *"Quyền được phân bổ theo thứ bậc: Workspace → Project → Folder → Content
(Board/Doc/File). Ví dụ: User được cấp quyền Manager tại Folder 'Backend' thì tự động có quyền
Manager ở toàn bộ Board/File con bên trong."* The frontend implements exactly that, plus the
"Override Permission" the same requirement asks for.

There is nothing special about the levels. The resolver walks `parent_id` and does not ask whether a
node is a project, a folder or a leaf — which is why a **board** or a **single file** can carry a
rule of its own.

#### 28.6.2 The algorithm, verbatim

```ts
// src/lib/permissions/inheritance.ts:55-79
/**
 * The deepest rule reaching `chain` for one subject. A rule naming the person
 * outranks one naming their role at the same depth — the more specific subject
 * wins, exactly as the deeper node does.
 */
function matchIn(chain, rules, subject, memberRole): Match | null {
  let found: Match | null = null;

  for (const node of chain) {                       // root -> node
    const written = rules[node.id] ?? [];

    const direct = written.find((rule) => sameSubject(rule.subject, subject));
    const viaRole =
      subject.kind === "user" && memberRole !== null
        ? written.find((r) => r.subject.kind === "role" && r.subject.role === memberRole)
        : undefined;

    const rule = direct ?? viaRole;                 // person beats role, same node
    if (rule) found = { role: rule.role, origin: originOf(node) };   // overwrite: deepest wins
  }

  return found;
}
```

```ts
// src/lib/permissions/inheritance.ts:91-120
export function effectiveAccess({ tree, nodeId, rules, members }, subject): EffectiveAccess {
  const memberRole =
    subject.kind === "user"
      ? members.find((m) => m.id === subject.userId)?.role ?? null
      : subject.role;

  const base: WorkspaceRole = memberRole ?? "viewer";
  const chain = chainFor(tree, nodeId);                          // root -> node
  if (chain.length === 0) return { role: base, source: "workspace", origin: null };

  const self      = chain[chain.length - 1];
  const inherited = matchIn(chain.slice(0, -1), rules, subject, memberRole);
  const own       = matchIn(self ? [self] : [], rules, subject, memberRole);

  if (!own) {
    return inherited
      ? { role: inherited.role, source: "inherited", origin: inherited.origin }
      : { role: base,           source: "workspace", origin: null };
  }

  const wouldHave = inherited?.role ?? base;
  return {
    role: own.role,
    source: own.role === wouldHave ? "explicit" : "override",
    origin: own.origin,
  };
}
```

#### 28.6.3 The nine resolution rules, each with its test

| Rule | Code | Test |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No rule anywhere → the workspace role, `source: "workspace"` | `inheritance.ts:100-102` | `tests/permission-inheritance.test.ts:55-61` |
| A rule on an ancestor flows down; `source: "inherited"`, `origin` names the ancestor | `:109-111` | `:63-70` |
| **The deepest rule wins, not the strongest** — a project-level Manager is taken back down to Viewer inside one folder | `:63-77` | `:72-83` |
| A rule written here that **agrees** with what would arrive → `source: "explicit"` | `:114-118` | `:85-92` |
| A rule written here that **replaces** it → `source: "override"` | `:114-118` | `:94-103` |
| A role-scoped rule reaches everyone holding that **workspace** role | `:67-73` | `:105-111` |
| A user-scoped rule beats a role-scoped rule **at the same node** (`direct ?? viaRole`) | `:74` | `:113-120` |
| The workspace itself (`nodeId === null`) has no node to write a rule on | `:102` | `:122-127` |
| A non-member resolves to `viewer` as a **base**, never as an entitlement | `:100` | `:129-131` |

#### 28.6.4 Replacement, not maximum — the correction the prose gets wrong

`docs/GOVERNANCE.md:147` says *"the workspace role is the floor under all of it"*, and
`src/lib/permissions/inheritance.ts:14-22` repeats it. **The code does not floor.** `matchIn`
overwrites `found` unconditionally and `effectiveAccess` returns `own.role` / `inherited.role`
directly, so **a rule can take a Manager down to Viewer on a subtree**.
`tests/permission-inheritance.test.ts:72-83` asserts exactly that.

Read "floor" as *"the default when no rule applies"*, and **implement replacement, not maximum.**

The PRD disagrees. `SY-INH-43`'s edge case says *"Xung đột quyền giữa Group và User: Áp dụng mức
quyền cao hơn (Union of permissions)"* — take the higher of the two. **Canon OQ-22 has decided in
favour of the code:** deepest node wins; at one node a user-scoped rule beats a role-scoped rule;
the workspace role is the default. Do not re-litigate it. A union implementation would silently
widen every override that was written to narrow — which is the only reason anyone writes one.

#### 28.6.5 The read model E-040 returns

Documented in full in §11 (part-07) as `GET /nodes/{nodeId}/access`. Repeated here only for the
two properties a reviewer needs:

- `resolveAccess` emits a row for **every workspace member**, plus one for **every role-scoped rule
  anywhere on the chain** — *"a grant that covers a group is never invisible just because it names
  no one"* (`inheritance.ts:136-146`) — sorted by `roleRank` **descending** (`:166`).
- Badge labels (`inheritance.ts:170-175`): `workspace` → "Workspace role", `inherited` →
  "Inherited", `explicit` → "Explicit", `override` → "Override".

#### 28.6.6 The uniqueness constraint that makes resolution deterministic

`matchIn` uses `Array.find`, which takes the **first** matching rule within one node. Two rules on
the same node naming the same subject would therefore make the answer depend on physical row order —
the same person resolving to `member` or `manager` depending on which row the planner returned
first. `setAccessRule` removes any existing rule for the subject before appending
(`src/store/permission-store.ts:86`), so the frontend can never produce a duplicate.

**The database must guarantee it too** (part-03 owns the DDL; restated here because it is a
correctness constraint, not hygiene):

```sql
-- documentation only
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX access_rules_node_user_uniq
  ON access_rules (node_id, subject_user_id) WHERE subject_kind = 'user';
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX access_rules_node_role_uniq
  ON access_rules (node_id, subject_role)    WHERE subject_kind = 'role';
```

Two partial indexes rather than one, because the two subject columns are mutually exclusive and a
single index over both would treat `(node, NULL)` pairs as distinct.

### 28.7 Node ownership — a separate axis

#### 28.7.1 EXISTING REQUIREMENT — ownership is not a role

`src/types/permission.ts:3-7`: *"Ownership of a node is a separate axis — it escalates a few actions
on the things you made, it is not a role."*

```ts
// src/lib/permissions/roles.ts:98-108
/**
 * Actions a node's owner keeps even below the role that normally grants them.
 * Ownership is not a role — it escalates these few keys on your own things.
 */
export const OWNER_ESCALATIONS: PermissionSet = new Set<PermissionKey>([
  "node.rename",
  "node.delete",
  "node.archive",
  "file.delete",
  "document.lock",
]);
```

**Exactly five keys.** Applied at `evaluate.ts:72-76` with a rank floor:

```ts
const owns = Boolean(node) && node?.owner.id === user.id;
const isEscalated = owns && OWNER_ESCALATIONS.has(key) && roleRank(role) >= roleRank("member");
if (!roleHas(role, key) && !isEscalated) return false;
```

#### 28.7.2 The three properties, each with its test

| Property | Where | Test |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A **Member** who owns a node may rename, delete and archive it, delete their file and lock their page | `evaluate.ts:73-74` | `tests/rbac.test.ts:184-193`, `tests/permissions.test.ts:90-96` |
| A **Viewer** who owns a node gets **nothing** — the `roleRank >= member` floor | `evaluate.ts:74` | `tests/permissions.test.ts:98-101` |
| Owning a folder does **not** make you a manager of what is inside it | the fixed 5-key set | `tests/rbac.test.ts:190-192` — `board.column.create` and `workspace.audit.view` stay false |

**The role compared against `member` is the effective role on this node** — gate 3's output, not the
workspace role (`src/hooks/use-permissions.ts:103-117` feeds `useEffectiveRole(node)` into the
context). A Member demoted to Viewer on one subtree **loses their owner escalation inside it**. The
backend must compare the same resolved value.

#### 28.7.3 Ownership on the ACCESS axis too

Separately from escalation, `hasGrantOn` admits the owner as its first line
(`visibility.ts:87-93`): *"Somebody has to be able to get back into a folder they shut, and 'whoever
made it' is a rule a person can hold in their head — which an emergency override buried in an admin
console is not."* `tests/folder-access.test.ts:203-206` and `:487-489`.

So ownership grants **visibility unconditionally** and **five capabilities from Member upward**.
Those are two different rules with two different floors, and both must be implemented.

#### 28.7.4 In the data model

`owner` is embedded on every node as a `UserSummary` (`src/types/node.ts:53`). Stored as an id and
joined (part-03):

```sql
-- documentation only
-- nodes.owner_id UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT
CREATE INDEX nodes_owner_idx ON nodes (workspace_id, owner_id);
```

`ON DELETE RESTRICT`, not `CASCADE`: users are soft-deactivated and never hard-deleted
(`src/types/user.ts:14-17` — *"Members removed from the workspace stay resolvable so their name
still renders — flagged inactive, never dropped"*), so the restriction never fires, and declaring a
cascade would declare an intent the product does not have.

**OPEN QUESTION (OQ-02) — can ownership be transferred, and what happens when an owner leaves?**
**What is unclear** — there is no transfer path and no cleanup on member removal.
**Evidence** — no transfer exists anywhere in `src/`; `owner` is set at creation by the node
factories in `src/store/workspace-store.ts` and never written again. `withoutMember`
(`src/lib/workspace-access.ts:261-263`) removes the membership row and touches nothing else. The
directory keeps departed users resolvable, so `node.owner.id` still resolves to a name — but gate 1
refuses them, so the "owner is always in" safety net at `visibility.ts:93` silently stops protecting
the node.
**Recommendation** — add `POST /nodes/{nodeId}/owner` gated on `workspace.permission.manage` (or
`node.access.manage` plus current ownership), audited as a `node`-module event at `warn` with
`context.kind = "node"`. On member removal (E-015), either reassign owned nodes to the actor or
surface them in the recovery console.
**Impact if wrong** — a restricted node whose owner has left and whose grants have been revoked is
reachable only through the admin recovery console. Survivable, but it turns "the console must never
be removed" into an unstated invariant.

**OPEN QUESTION (OQ-60) — a Viewer-owner and `canToggleLock`.**
**What is unclear** — two functions disagree about whether a Viewer who owns a page may lock it.
**Evidence** — `can("document.lock", …)` requires `roleRank(role) >= roleRank("member")` for the
owner escalation (`evaluate.ts:74`), but `canToggleLock` (`evaluate.ts:147-153`) is
`resolve("document.lock") || document.owner.id === user.id` — an unconditional owner clause with no
rank floor. `tests/permissions.test.ts:147-154` covers only Member and Manager, so the Viewer-owner
case is untested.
**Recommendation** — make the server consistent with `can`: require the same `roleRank >= member`
floor, i.e. evaluate `can("document.lock", ctx)` with the node supplied, and treat `canToggleLock`
as a UI convenience that the API does not mirror.
**Impact if wrong** — a Viewer who owns a page could lock it and freeze editing for the whole
workspace, which no other Viewer capability allows.

### 28.8 The authorization pipeline

Every request that touches a workspace resource runs these six stages **in this order**. Each stage
can only refuse; none can restore what an earlier one took away.

#### 28.8.1 The flowchart

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    REQ["Request<br/>cookie · workspaceId · nodeId · body"] --> S1{"1 · Authentication<br/>is there a valid session?"}
    S1 -- no --> E401["401 permission_denied<br/>AUTH_REQUIRED / AUTH_SESSION_EXPIRED"]
    S1 -- "actor = sub" --> S2{"2 · Workspace membership<br/>row in workspace_members?"}

    S2 -- no --> E404W["404 not_found<br/>WORKSPACE_NOT_FOUND<br/><i>identical to 'does not exist'</i>"]
    S2 -- "R0 = membership.role" --> S3{"3 · Resource ACCESS<br/>walk root→node<br/>inherit / workspace / restricted"}

    S3 -- "refused by some node<br/>or node absent" --> E404N["404 not_found<br/>NODE_NOT_FOUND<br/><i>existence is privileged</i>"]
    S3 -- admitted --> S4["4a · Effective ROLE on node<br/>deepest rule wins<br/>user beats role · default R0"]

    S4 --> S5{"4b · CAPABILITY<br/>matrix + owner escalation"}
    S5 -- "key not held" --> E403["403 permission_denied<br/>PERMISSION_DENIED<br/>detail: Needs the {Role} role or above"]
    S5 -- "read-only key" --> OK
    S5 -- held --> S6{"4c · Lifecycle narrowing<br/>trashed → frozen → locked"}

    S6 -- trashed --> E403T["403 NODE_TRASHED_READ_ONLY<br/><i>only node.delete survives</i>"]
    S6 -- "archived ancestor" --> E403F["403 NODE_FROZEN_BY_ANCESTOR"]
    S6 -- "locked + content write" --> E403L["403 NODE_LOCKED"]
    S6 -- survives --> S7{"5 · Business validation<br/>shape · invariants · state"}

    S7 -- "malformed" --> E400["400 validation<br/>VALIDATION_FAILED"]
    S7 -- "invariant refuses" --> E409["409 conflict<br/>e.g. VIEW_LAST_REMAINING"]
    S7 -- valid --> S8["6 · Mutation<br/>+ audit row + realtime frame<br/>ONE transaction"]

    S8 --> OK["200 · the authoritative record"]

    E401 --> AUD["audit_events<br/>outcome = denied<br/>autonomous connection"]
    E404W --> AUD
    E404N --> AUD
    E403 --> AUD
    E403T --> AUD
    E403F --> AUD
    E403L --> AUD
```

#### 28.8.2 The same thing as prose, with the error each stage returns

**Stage 1 — Authentication.** Resolve the session (§8, part-01). The actor id, the client IP and
the clock all come from the session and the socket, never from the body (canon C-09;
`src/services/authz.ts:24-28`; `src/services/audit-service.ts:276-285`). No session on a protected
route → **401**, `code: "permission_denied"`, `reason: AUTH_REQUIRED`; an expired access token →
`AUTH_SESSION_EXPIRED` so the client knows to refresh. The frontend cannot distinguish 401 from 403,
which is why the refresh flow branches on `reason`.

**Stage 2 — Workspace membership.** `SELECT role FROM workspace_members WHERE workspace_id = :ws AND
user_id = :actor`. **No row is not "viewer"; it is "no".** `src/lib/workspace-access.ts:30-36`:
*"The role held, or null — never a default. A default here is a way in."* Refusal is **404**,
`WORKSPACE_NOT_FOUND` — *identical* to the answer for a workspace that does not exist, because
`workspaceAccess` returns the same shape for both *"so the URL cannot be used to learn which
workspaces exist"* (`workspace-access.ts:60-66`; `tests/workspace-access.test.ts:81-91`). The result
of this stage is `R0`, the caller's workspace role, used by gates 3 and 4.

**Stage 3 — Resource ACCESS.** §28.5. Refusal is **404**, `NODE_NOT_FOUND`, with the generic
name-free body. The node that refused is recorded in `context.gate` for the audit row and is
**never** returned (`visibility.ts:137-145`).

**Stage 4 — Permission / RBAC.** Three sub-steps that share one context:

- **4a, effective role.** §28.6. Walk the same chain and resolve `R` — replacement, not maximum,
  defaulting to `R0`.
- **4b, capability.** `roleHas(R, key) || ownerEscalation`. Refusal is **403**,
  `PERMISSION_DENIED`, `message` = `You do not have permission to {action}`, `detail` =
  `requirementFor(key)` = `Needs the {Role} role or above` (`src/services/authz.ts:67-74`;
  `evaluate.ts:169-176`). A read-only key returns ALLOW here and skips 4c.
- **4c, lifecycle narrowing.** Trashed → frozen → locked, in that order. Refusals are **403** with
  `NODE_TRASHED_READ_ONLY`, `NODE_FROZEN_BY_ANCESTOR` and `NODE_LOCKED` respectively (canon §4.3).
  These are 403 and not 404: the caller can see the thing, they simply may not do this to it.

**Stage 5 — Business validation.** Shape, enums, ranges, referential existence, and the invariants
that are not permissions: `WORKSPACE_LAST_ADMIN`, `VIEW_LAST_REMAINING`, `ROW_PARENT_CYCLE`,
`COLUMN_PRIMARY_PROTECTED`, `SECRET_KEY_DUPLICATE`, and so on. **400** for a malformed request
(`VALIDATION_FAILED`, with `fields: FieldError[]`), **409** for an invariant that refuses a
well-formed one. This stage runs **after** authorization on purpose: a validation message is a
richer oracle than a refusal, and handing one to somebody who may not touch the resource leaks the
resource's shape.

**Stage 6 — Mutation.** The write, its audit row and its realtime frame, in **one transaction**
(§29.9). The response is the authoritative record (canon C-10), never `204` where the frontend
expects an object.

#### 28.8.3 Why a denied resource answers 404 and not 403

**This is the rule, stated once, because it is the most commonly mis-implemented line in the
chapter.**

| Situation | Status | Reason | Why |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| No session | 401 | `AUTH_REQUIRED` | Nothing has been named yet. |
| Workspace does not exist | 404 | `WORKSPACE_NOT_FOUND` | — |
| Workspace exists, caller is not a member | **404** | `WORKSPACE_NOT_FOUND` | **Identical to the row above.** Otherwise the URL enumerates which workspaces are real. |
| Node does not exist | 404 | `NODE_NOT_FOUND` | — |
| Node exists, gate 3 refuses | **404** | `NODE_NOT_FOUND` | **Identical to the row above.** A 403 here confirms the existence and the id of a folder somebody was deliberately shut out of. |
| Node exists, caller can see it, lacks the key | **403** | `PERMISSION_DENIED` | The caller already knows the resource exists — they are looking at it. Telling them which role they would need is useful and leaks nothing. |
| Node exists, caller can see it, node is trashed/frozen/locked | **403** | `NODE_TRASHED_READ_ONLY` / `NODE_FROZEN_BY_ANCESTOR` / `NODE_LOCKED` | Same reasoning. The state is already visible on the surface. |

The frontend already reasons this way at the workspace level
(`src/components/workspace/workspace-guard.tsx:20-27`) and at the node level
(`visibility.ts:137-145`, `tests/permissions.test.ts:157-167` asserts the refusal text does not
contain the node name).

**The 403 body, when the caller may see the resource** (`src/services/authz.ts:73`):

```jsonc
// 403 POST /api/v1/boards/{boardId}/columns
{
  "error": {
    "code": "permission_denied",
    "message": "You do not have permission to add a column",
    "detail": "Needs the Manager role or above",
    "isRetryable": false,
    "reason": "PERMISSION_DENIED",
    "requestId": "01JB9…"
  }
}
```

**The 404 body, when existence itself is the secret.** Use the fixed `not_found` template and
nothing else (canon §4.4 rule 2):

```jsonc
// 404 GET /api/v1/nodes/{nodeId}
{
  "error": {
    "code": "not_found",
    "message": "That item could not be found",
    "isRetryable": false,
    "reason": "NODE_NOT_FOUND",
    "requestId": "01JB9…"
  }
}
```

Where a surface is *known* to be a share-request flow rather than an enumeration risk, the frontend
has a second string it renders instead — `DENIED_REASON`, *"You do not have access to this item. Ask
somebody who does to share it with you."* (`evaluate.ts:155-167`). That is a **client-side** panel
built from context the client already has; it is not what the API returns for a gate-3 refusal, and
an API that returned it would be confirming the resource exists.

**Message-writing rules the whole pipeline obeys** (canon §4.4, `evaluate.ts:155-163`):

1. `message` is rendered to the user verbatim; it is a sentence, sentence-cased.
2. `not_found` messages are always `` `${what} could not be found` `` — a fixed template.
3. **A refusal must never name something the caller was denied.** No node name, no folder name, no
   secret key, no member name, no rule id.
4. `detail` is the secondary line — what to do about it. Omitted, not `null`, when absent.
5. `isRetryable` is `false` for every refusal in this pipeline.

#### 28.8.4 Timing and side-channels

Stages 2 and 3 both answer 404 with the same body, but they do different amounts of work. A
`WORKSPACE_NOT_FOUND` returned after one index probe and a `NODE_NOT_FOUND` returned after a
recursive CTE are distinguishable by latency. **RECOMMENDATION:** this is acceptable — the
distinction leaks "you are not in this workspace" versus "you are in it and cannot see that node",
which the caller already knows from the rest of the session. Do **not** add artificial delay. Do
ensure the two bodies are byte-identical apart from `reason` and `requestId`, and that `reason` is
never used by a client to branch (it is additive; the frontend ignores it — canon §4.1).

---

### 28.9 Where enforcement belongs

#### 28.9.1 The rule

**Every rule the frontend checks must be re-checked server-side, per call, per node.** The frontend
says it in three places (quoted at the head of this chapter) and `docs/GOVERNANCE.md:326-330` lists
it as the first backend obligation: *"Enforcement of all keys, per call, per node."*

#### 28.9.2 `src/services/authz.ts` is the model to copy

The frontend already built the shape of the check. It is 75 lines and the backend's middleware
should be structurally identical:

```ts
// src/services/authz.ts:35-74 — the model, transcribed
/** The caller's effective role on a node, through the inheritance chain. */
function contextFor(nodeId: string | null) {
  const workspace = selectActiveWorkspace(useWorkspaceStore.getState());
  const tree  = getFullTree();
  const rules = usePermissionStore.getState().rulesByWorkspace[workspace.id] ?? {};

  const { role } = effectiveAccess(
    { tree, nodeId, rules, members: workspace.members },
    { kind: "user", userId: CURRENT_USER.id },       // ← resolved, never an argument
  );

  return {
    role,
    user: CURRENT_USER,
    node: nodeId ? findNodeById(tree, nodeId) : null,
    isFrozen: inheritedArchiveOf(tree, nodeId) !== null,
  };
}

/** Whether the caller holds `key` on `nodeId`. Never throws. */
export function callerCan(nodeId: string | null, key: PermissionKey): boolean {
  return can(key, contextFor(nodeId));
}

/** Refuse the call unless the caller holds `key` on `nodeId`. */
export function requirePermission(nodeId: string | null, key: PermissionKey, action: string): void {
  if (callerCan(nodeId, key)) return;
  throw permissionDenied(`You do not have permission to ${action}`, requirementFor(key));
}
```

Four properties to carry over verbatim:

1. **It resolves the caller itself rather than taking a role as an argument.**
   `src/services/authz.ts:24-28`: *"A role the client sends is a claim, not a fact, and an endpoint
   that trusts one is not enforcing anything — it is asking the caller how much access they would
   like."*
2. **It runs the same evaluator the UI runs** — one matrix, one inheritance chain, one `can` —
   *"so a control that is offered and a call that is accepted cannot drift apart the way two copies
   of a rule always eventually do"* (`authz.ts:18-22`). Ship the catalogue from E-045 and the matrix
   from one place so this stays true across a backend rewrite.
3. **It takes a `nodeId`, always.** A workspace-scoped check passes `null`; everything else names
   the node the action lands on. There is no global permission check in this system.
4. **Two entry points, not one.** `callerCan` for shaping a response (which capabilities to report,
   which rows to include); `requirePermission` for refusing a call. A handler that only ever throws
   cannot build a `CapabilitySet`.

The module also states its own honest caveat (`authz.ts:29-33`): *"there is no server here. This
module reads the same process's stores, so it is a faithful model of the check a real API must make,
not a substitute for it."*

#### 28.9.3 What the frontend actually gates today — the eleven call sites, and the gap

Every `requirePermission` / `callerCan` in `src/services/`:

| # | File:line | Key | Action string |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `src/services/board-service.ts:564` | `board.column.create` | `add a column` |
| 2 | `src/services/board-service.ts:600` | `board.column.create` | `duplicate a column` |
| 3 | `src/services/board-service.ts:653` | `board.column.update` | `change this column` |
| 4 | `src/services/board-service.ts:672` | `board.column.update` | `reorder columns` |
| 5 | `src/services/board-service.ts:687` | `board.column.delete` | `delete this column` |
| 6 | `src/services/board-service.ts:728` | `board.column.update` | `change this column's type` |
| 7 | `src/services/board-service.ts:865` | `board.view.manage` | `reorder views` |
| 8 | `src/services/board-service.ts:1189` | `board.import` | `import into this board` |
| 9 | `src/services/devtools-service.ts:148` | `document.update` | `edit this config document` |
| 10 | `src/services/devtools-service.ts:316` | `secret.reveal` (via `mayUnlock`) | reveal / copy |
| 11 | `src/services/devtools-service.ts:316` | `secret.rotate` (via `mayUnlock`) | rotate |

**Eleven checks against 140 endpoints.** That is canon **OQ-16** — *"40+ write operations carry no
permission check in the mock"* — and canon's position is unambiguous: *"Every write is gated
server-side with the catalogue key the matrix defines."* The **Perm** column of canon §3 is
normative; §28.3.3 above names the key for every one of the 39.

The five inputs the mock takes from the caller and the server must resolve instead (canon OQ-17 –
OQ-21, part-01 §8.7):

| Input | Taken from the caller today | Must come from |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `userId` | `WatchService.list/set`, `NotificationService.*`, `MyWorkInput.userId` (`src/services/my-work-service.ts:47-48`), `SearchInput.user` (`src/services/search-service.ts:45-48`) | the session (`sub`) |
| `role` | `SearchInput.role`, `RevealInput.role` (`src/services/devtools-service.ts:322-327`) | `workspace_members` + the chain; a declared role may only **narrow** (§28.11) |
| Node visibility | `ListFilesInput.canView` (`src/services/file-service.ts:96`, `:105`, `:113`) | gate 3, server-side |
| IP | never sent (correct today) | the socket / a trusted proxy header |
| The clock | `MOCK_NOW` (`src/config/app.ts:10`) | `now()` |

Two specific holes worth naming because they are cross-resource:

- **`bulkMove` (E-077) gates neither board and does not verify the target is a board** (OQ-17). It
  must require `row.delete` on the **source** node and `row.create` on the **target** node, and
  refuse `BULK_TARGET_NOT_A_BOARD` (409) when `targetNodeId` does not address a board.
- **Search (E-133) must run the permission funnel before scanning, not after** (canon §3.22). A
  ranked list truncated after filtering is a different list from one filtered after ranking, and the
  cheap version leaks the existence of matches through result counts.

#### 28.9.4 Caching, and why revocation must not wait for a TTL

`SY-RBC-42` budgets `p99 < 10ms` for the check, which invites a cache. If gate 2/3/4a results are
cached:

- key it by **`(workspaceId, userId)`**, never by `(nodeId)` alone;
- bust it on **every** `workspace_members` write (E-013 – E-016), **every** `access_rules` write
  (E-042, E-043), **every** `nodes.access_mode` write (E-041), and **every node move** (E-026);
- publish **RT-05 `permission.changed`** in the same transaction.

*"Revocation that takes effect on the next cache expiry is not revocation."* The realtime frame is
not optional either: without it a revoked user keeps a loaded board on screen until they reload
(`src/hooks/use-access-sync.ts:19-91`), and `SY-RBC-42`'s own edge case requires the opposite —
*"Người dùng bị hạ quyền khi đang mở màn hình: UI tự động vô hiệu hóa các nút chức năng bị khóa."*

The frame carries **ids only** (`src/types/realtime.ts:20-32`):

```ts
| {
    readonly type: "permission.changed";
    readonly workspaceId: string;
    /** Null when the change is workspace membership rather than one node. */
    readonly nodeId: string | null;
    readonly userIds: readonly string[];
  }
```

*"Carries no resource content on purpose — a frame announcing a revocation must not be the thing
that leaks what was revoked."*

---

### 28.10 The capability projection (`CapabilitySet`)

Six coarse flags that older surfaces branch on. They are a **projection** of the catalogue, not a
parallel rule set — *"so `capabilities.edit` and `can('row.update')` can never disagree"*
(`evaluate.ts:116-132`).

```ts
// src/types/permission.ts:109-127
export type Capability = "view" | "edit" | "upload" | "delete" | "share" | "manage";
export type CapabilitySet = Readonly<Record<Capability, boolean>>;

export const NO_CAPABILITIES: CapabilitySet = {
  view: false, edit: false, upload: false, delete: false, share: false, manage: false,
};
```

```ts
// src/lib/permissions/evaluate.ts:121-132
export function capabilitiesFor(context: PermissionContext): CapabilitySet {
  const resolve = resolverFor(context);
  return {
    view:   true,                              // ← see the warning below
    edit:   resolve(editKeyFor(context.node)),
    upload: resolve("file.upload"),
    delete: resolve("node.delete"),
    share:  resolve("node.share"),
    manage: resolve("node.archive"),
  };
}
```

`editKeyFor` (`evaluate.ts:103-114`) — one word, four permissions:

| Node kind | `edit` resolves to |
| --- | --- |
| `document` (page, config or secret) | `document.update` |
| `file` | `file.update` |
| `board` | `row.update` |
| `project` / `folder` | `node.rename` |
| no node at all | `row.update` |

**`view: true` is hard-coded, and the backend must not copy that literal.** In the frontend it is
correct because by the time `can()` runs, gate 2 has already admitted the node. On the server,
`view` **is** gate 2 — compute it. An endpoint that reports `view: true` unconditionally has
inverted the meaning of the field.

Two narrowing helpers the response shaping must mirror:

```ts
// src/lib/permissions/evaluate.ts:94-101 — a node archived in its OWN right
export function frozenResolver(resolve: PermissionResolver): PermissionResolver {
  return (key: PermissionKey) => (isWrite(key) ? false : resolve(key));
}

// src/lib/permissions/evaluate.ts:134-141
export function documentCapabilities(
  base: CapabilitySet,
  document: Pick<WorkspaceDocument, "isLocked" | "isArchived">,
): CapabilitySet {
  if (!document.isLocked && !document.isArchived) return base;
  return { ...base, edit: false, upload: false };
}

// src/lib/archive.ts:47-50 — identical shape for an inherited freeze
export function archivedCapabilities(base: CapabilitySet): CapabilitySet {
  return { ...base, edit: false, upload: false };
}
```

The distinction between `frozenResolver` and `can` is the subtle one:
`tests/rbac.test.ts:170-182` asserts that on a node archived **in its own right**, `can("node.archive")`
is **true** (so Restore can be offered) while the *surface's* wrapped resolver reports **false** for
every write — and `board.export` stays **true** through both. Reproduce this in the response, not in
the authorization decision: E-044's `manage` flag for a self-archived node should still be `true`,
and E-030/E-031 must still accept the call.

---

### 28.11 Role preview

#### 28.11.1 EXISTING REQUIREMENT — preview can only ever narrow

```ts
// src/hooks/use-permissions.ts:49-57
/**
 * Previewing narrows, never widens. A member previewing as admin still sees a
 * member's app — otherwise the preview would be a privilege escalation with a
 * dropdown in front of it.
 */
function clamp(real: WorkspaceRole, preview: WorkspaceRole | null): WorkspaceRole {
  if (preview === null) return real;
  return roleRank(preview) < roleRank(real) ? preview : real;
}
```

Effective role = **`min(real, preview)`** by rank. Applied to the workspace role
(`use-permissions.ts:67-72`) and to the resolved node role (`:83-100`).

State lives in `src/store/permission-store.ts:23-31` as `previewRole: WorkspaceRole | null`, is
initialised to `null` (`:47-51`), is **never persisted**, and is set from the dialog footer
(`src/components/permissions/permission-dialog.tsx:162-186`) with a standing banner offering an exit
(`src/components/permissions/role-preview-banner.tsx:9-15`).

`docs/GOVERNANCE.md:358-359`: *"Role preview is not a session switch. It narrows what the interface
offers; it does not re-authenticate, and a reload clears it."*

#### 28.11.2 What the backend MUST do

1. **Never accept a role as authority.** Resolve `R` from `workspace_members` and the chain, per
   request. A role in a body or a header is a claim.
2. **Where a role is declared, treat it as an additional narrowing input only.** Compute
   `effective = min(serverResolvedRole, declaredRole)`. Never `max`, never `declaredRole` alone.
   The one place the frontend passes a role across a service boundary models this as **two checks
   that must both pass** (`src/services/devtools-service.ts:302-317`):

```ts
/**
 * `role` is the role the *client* is running as, which includes the role
 * preview — a workspace admin reading the app as a member has to be refused,
 * or the preview would be a demo rather than a check. It can only ever narrow.
 *
 * `callerCan` is the real one: the signed-in user's effective role on this
 * node, resolved from the store rather than taken from the request.
 */
function mayUnlock(nodeId: string, role: WorkspaceRole, key: "secret.reveal" | "secret.rotate") {
  return roleHas(role, key) && callerCan(nodeId, key);
}
```

3. **Ignore a declared role that is higher, do not reject it.** Canon OQ-21's position: *"A declared
   role that is higher than the server's must be ignored, not rejected — rejecting would let a stale
   tab break rather than degrade."* Canon §4.3 registers `PREVIEW_ROLE_ESCALATES` (400,
   `validation`) for the strict alternative; **this specification never emits it**, and a
   deployment that turns on strict validation must do so behind a flag. See the editor note.
4. **A preview must never change what is audited.** A `secret.reveal` refused because of a preview
   is still a refusal and is still recorded, with `outcome: "denied"` and `severity: "error"`
   (`devtools-service.ts:341-348`; `tests/audit.test.ts:223-242`). The audit row records the
   **real** actor and the **server-resolved** role in `context`; the declared role goes in
   `context` too, never in `detail`.

#### 28.11.3 What the backend MUST NOT do

- **Do not build a server-side "acting as" session mode.** No impersonation state, no
  `POST /sessions/preview`, no role claim in the access token. `docs/GOVERNANCE.md:358-359` is
  explicit that preview is not a session switch, and part-01 R-4 keeps every role out of the token
  precisely so that adding a fifth role later is a matrix change and not a session change.
  *"A server that maintains 'acting as' session state is one bug away from an escalation
  primitive."*
- **Do not let preview widen anything, ever** — not a list, not a count, not a capability flag, not
  a facet.
- **Do not persist it.** It dies with the tab, by design.

**Transport, decided.** Canon does not register a preview parameter on any endpoint except the
existing `role` field on the secret reveal/copy requests. **RECOMMENDATION:** if a transport is
needed, accept an `X-Preview-Role: <WorkspaceRole>` request header, apply the `min` rule, and
document it as advisory. A header is right rather than a body field because it applies uniformly to
`GET`s and never becomes part of a resource representation. Do **not** add `previewAs` to request
bodies, where it would be indistinguishable from a real field on a create.

---

### 28.12 Endpoints

E-040 (`GET /nodes/{nodeId}/access`), E-041 (`PUT /nodes/{nodeId}/access-mode`), E-042
(`PUT /nodes/{nodeId}/access-rules`) and E-043 (`DELETE /nodes/{nodeId}/access-rules/{ruleId}`) are
specified in **§11, Folder APIs** (part-07) and are not repeated here. The three that belong to this
chapter follow.

#### 28.12.1 `GET /api/v1/nodes/{nodeId}/capabilities`

**Purpose** — The six coarse flags for one node, resolved for this caller through the full pipeline,
so a surface can decide what to render without re-deriving the rules or shipping the rule engine to
the client. It is the read that makes `usePermissions` / `useCapabilities` honest against a real
server.

**Authentication** — Required.

**Permission** — **Visibility only** (gates 1–3). No catalogue key. Reaching this endpoint means the
caller can see the node; the response then says what they may do with it. Canon E-044 lists the
permission as `visibility`.

**Path Params**

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `nodeId` | UUID | Any node of any kind. The projection's `edit` key varies by kind (§28.10). |

**Query Params** — None.

**Request Body** — None.

**Response** — `CapabilitySet`, `200`. Canon §5.2 lists `CapabilitySet` as an EXISTING domain
interface; it is returned **bare**, with no envelope (canon §6.2).

```ts
/** src/types/permission.ts:116-118 — returned verbatim. */
type Capability = "view" | "edit" | "upload" | "delete" | "share" | "manage";
type CapabilitySet = Readonly<Record<Capability, boolean>>;
```

```jsonc
// 200 GET /api/v1/nodes/{nodeId}/capabilities
// A Member who owns an unlocked, unarchived board.
{
  "view":   true,     // gate 2 said yes, which is why this response exists at all
  "edit":   true,     // row.update — the board's edit key
  "upload": true,     // file.upload
  "delete": true,     // node.delete, held here only by owner escalation
  "share":  true,     // node.share
  "manage": false     // node.archive — owner-escalated, so actually true here too
}
```

**How each flag is computed** — run the pipeline once, then evaluate six keys against the resulting
context:

| Flag | Key | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `view` | *(none)* | **Gate 2's answer.** Do not hard-code `true` — see §28.10. |
| `edit` | `editKeyFor(node.kind)` | `document.update` / `file.update` / `row.update` / `node.rename` |
| `upload` | `file.upload` | content write |
| `delete` | `node.delete` | owner-escalated |
| `share` | `node.share` | Member key |
| `manage` | `node.archive` | owner-escalated |

Then apply the narrowing the surfaces apply: if the node is **frozen by an ancestor**,
`archivedCapabilities` clears `edit` and `upload`; if it is a document that is **locked or archived
in its own right**, `documentCapabilities` clears the same two
(`src/hooks/use-permissions.ts:130-137`, `evaluate.ts:134-141`). Note the asymmetry deliberately
preserved: a node archived in its own right keeps `manage: true`, because Restore has to remain
offerable.

**Database**

| Table | Operation | Detail |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `workspace_members` | READ | Gate 1: `(workspace_id, user_id)` → `role`. Unique index `workspace_members_pkey`. One row. |
| `nodes` | READ | The recursive chain root → node: `id, parent_id, workspace_id, access_mode, owner_id, is_archived, deleted_at, kind, is_locked`. Index `nodes_parent_idx`. Depth-bounded at 64. |
| `access_rules` | READ | `WHERE node_id = ANY(:chain) AND (subject_user_id = :actor OR (subject_kind='role' AND subject_role = :R0))`. Index `access_rules_workspace_node_idx (workspace_id, node_id)`. |

Cardinality: 1 membership row, ≤ 64 chain rows, ≤ 2 rules per chain node (one user-scoped, one
role-scoped — the two partial unique indexes guarantee it). No writes.

**Transaction** — Not required. It is a read; a single `REPEATABLE READ` snapshot is enough to keep
the chain and the rules consistent with each other.

**Realtime** — None emitted. The client refetches this on **RT-05 `permission.changed`** when
`userIds` contains it and `nodeId` is null or matches.

**Possible Errors**

| HTTP | Code | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 401 | `permission_denied` | `AUTH_REQUIRED` — no session. |
| 404 | `not_found` | `WORKSPACE_NOT_FOUND` — the node's workspace, and the caller is not a member. |
| 404 | `not_found` | `NODE_NOT_FOUND` — unknown node **or** gate 3 refused it. |
| 500 | `unknown` | `INTERNAL_ERROR` |

Note what is **not** on that list: there is no 403. Every refusal at or before gate 3 is a 404, and
gates 4–6 do not run — a capability the caller lacks is reported as `false`, not as an error.

**Frontend Used By** — `src/hooks/use-permissions.ts:130-137` (`useCapabilities`), consumed by
`src/components/drive/drive-view.tsx:52`, `src/components/drive/drive-toolbar.tsx:73`,
`src/components/document/document-page.tsx:38`, `src/components/devtools/config-document-page.tsx:34`,
`src/components/files/file-preview-dialog.tsx:33`, `src/hooks/use-file-catalog.ts:40`,
`src/hooks/use-document.ts:50` and `src/components/layout/sidebar/new-item-menu.tsx:30` (with no
node, for the workspace-level Create menu).

**RECOMMENDATION — batch it.** Six flags per node, one CTE per call, and the drive grid renders a
hundred nodes. Either fold `capabilities` into the `DriveNode` payload of E-020 / E-023 (the chain
is already walked to prune the tree, so the marginal cost is the six `roleHas` lookups), or accept
`?nodeIds=` here and return `Record<nodeId, CapabilitySet>`. Canon registers neither; the first is
additive to an existing response and is the cheaper change.

#### 28.12.2 `GET /api/v1/permissions/catalog`

**Purpose** — The static 39-key catalogue, served from the backend so the matrix the UI renders and
the matrix the API enforces cannot drift apart. It is the list a reviewer checks an implementation
against.

**Authentication** — Required (any session). It is not workspace-scoped: the catalogue is identical
for every tenant.

**Permission** — None beyond a session. Canon E-045 lists the permission as `session`. The catalogue
is a description of the product's vocabulary and grants nothing; `src/components/permissions/role-matrix.tsx`
renders it to anybody who can open the dialog, including a Viewer.

**Path Params** — None.

**Query Params** — None. The response is small (39 entries, ~4 KB) and is not paginated
(canon §6.3: "bounded by construction").

**Request Body** — None.

**Response** — `readonly PermissionDefinition[]`, `200`, bare. **In `PERMISSION_KEYS` source order**
(`src/types/permission.ts:31-78`), which is also `PERMISSION_MODULES` order, which is the order the
matrix renders in.

```ts
/** src/types/permission.ts:101-107 — EXISTING. Not re-scoped. */
interface PermissionDefinition {
  readonly key: PermissionKey;          // one of the 39
  readonly module: PermissionModule;    // DERIVED from key.slice(0, key.indexOf("."))
  /** Imperative label for the matrix row: "Create columns". */
  readonly label: string;
  readonly summary: string;
}
```

```jsonc
// 200 GET /api/v1/permissions/catalog  — first three of thirty-nine
[
  { "key": "workspace.manage",
    "module": "workspace",
    "label": "Manage workspace",
    "summary": "Rename the workspace, change its plan and settings" },
  { "key": "workspace.settings.view",
    "module": "workspace",
    "label": "Open workspace settings",
    "summary": "See the workspace settings screen at all" },
  { "key": "workspace.member.manage",
    "module": "workspace",
    "label": "Manage members",
    "summary": "Invite people and change what role they hold" }
]
```

**Cacheability** — The payload changes only on deploy. Serve it with
`Cache-Control: public, max-age=3600` and a build-stamped `ETag`. It contains no tenant data and no
caller data, so a shared cache is safe. (Canon §7.5 in part-01 says the API has no `ETag` layer;
this endpoint is the one place where one is worth the exception, and it is optional.)

**Database** — **None.** The catalogue is a service constant, not a table. Canon §1.2 lists
`permission_definitions` among the tables that deliberately do not exist: *"The 39-key catalogue is
static config shipped from the backend, not a table."* A row store would be a second copy of a rule
the code already owns, and the two would drift the first time a key was added.

**Transaction** — Not required.

**Realtime** — None.

**Possible Errors**

| HTTP | Code | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 401 | `permission_denied` | `AUTH_REQUIRED` |
| 500 | `unknown` | `INTERNAL_ERROR` |

**Frontend Used By** — `src/lib/permissions/catalog.ts:70-77` (`PERMISSIONS`, `PERMISSION_BY_KEY`)
and `permissionsByModule()` (`:102-112`), rendered by
`src/components/permissions/role-matrix.tsx:57-100` and used for audit-row labels by
`src/lib/audit.ts:42-49` (`auditActionLabel`). The frontend holds it as a local constant today; the
endpoint exists so that stops being true.

**The role matrix itself is not on this endpoint.** `PermissionDefinition` carries no `heldBy`, and
canon §5.2 forbids re-scoping an existing domain interface. The four role sets therefore remain
service config on both sides, identical to `src/lib/permissions/roles.ts`.

**RECOMMENDATION — assert the two copies agree at deploy time.** Ship a startup check that the
accumulated backend sets satisfy (a) containment across the ladder, (b) `|viewer| = 0`,
`|member| = 10`, `|manager| = 31`, `|admin| = 39`, and (c) every key in `PERMISSION_KEYS` is held by
at least one role (`minimumRoleFor(key) !== null`, asserted at `tests/rbac.test.ts:119-123`). Those
three assertions catch every drift a shared endpoint would have caught. If the editor prefers to
serve the matrix, the additive shape is a sibling endpoint returning
`{ role, label, summary, rank, keys }[]` — see the editor note.

#### 28.12.3 `GET /api/v1/workspaces/{workspaceId}/restricted-nodes`

**Purpose** — The admin recovery console: every restricted node in the workspace, **whether or not
the caller can see it**. It exists so a node can never be locked beyond recovery — a folder whose
last grantee leaves and whose owner has gone would otherwise be unreachable forever.

**This is the one read in the entire system that deliberately looks past gate 3**, and the trade is
stated in the product rather than hidden (`src/lib/permissions/visibility.ts:270-278`,
`src/components/workspace/workspace-restricted-tab.tsx:15-30`):

> An admin sees **that** a restricted node exists, what it is called and where it sits — and nothing
> inside it. They still do not appear in its access list, they are still not counted as a member of
> it, and the tree, search, favourites and every other surface still hide it from them until
> somebody grants it. The alternative — an admin implicitly inside every restricted folder — makes
> "restricted" mean "restricted unless you outrank it", which is not a promise anybody can rely on.

**Authentication** — Required.

**Permission** — `workspace.permission.manage` (Admin only), plus workspace membership. There is no
node-scoped alternative: `node.access.manage` is **not** accepted here, because a Manager holding it
on one folder must not be able to enumerate every restricted node in the tenant.

**Path Params**

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `workspaceId` | UUID | The tenant. Gate 2 applies; a non-member gets `WORKSPACE_NOT_FOUND`. |

**Query Params**

| Name | Type | Required | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `limit` | integer | no | 200 | Hard server cap 500. Unpaginated by construction — canon §6.3 puts this in the "bounded" class; the partial index it reads is tiny. |

**Request Body** — None.

**Response** — `readonly RestrictedNodeEntry[]`, `200`.

Canon E-046 says the response is `DriveNode[]`. **Returning a full `DriveNode` here would violate
the endpoint's own contract**: `DriveNode` carries `excerpt`, `blockCount`, `itemCount`,
`openCount`, `previewUrl`, `thumbnailUrl` and `children` — content about a node the caller is not
allowed to see. This specification returns the narrow shape the surface actually renders and flags
the divergence for the editor.

```ts
/** RECOMMENDATION. Names and paths and nothing else. */
interface RestrictedNodeEntry {
  readonly nodeId: string;
  readonly name: string;
  /** `Development / Backend` — the ancestor path, resolved server-side.
   *  "Workspace root" when the node is top-level. `src/lib/tree.ts:74-78`. */
  readonly path: string;
  readonly kind: NodeKind;                 // project | folder | document | board | file
  /** How many subjects are granted here, owner excluded.
   *  `grantedSubjectsOn(rules, nodeId).length`, visibility.ts:104-107. */
  readonly grantedCount: number;
  /** Whether THIS caller can already see it, so the console can say so. */
  readonly isVisibleToCaller: boolean;
}
```

```jsonc
// 200 GET /api/v1/workspaces/{workspaceId}/restricted-nodes
[
  { "nodeId": "b22f…", "name": "Payroll",          "path": "Development / Backend",
    "kind": "folder", "grantedCount": 3, "isVisibleToCaller": false },
  { "nodeId": "c33a…", "name": ".env.production",  "path": "Development / Backend / Payment",
    "kind": "file",   "grantedCount": 1, "isVisibleToCaller": false }
]
```

**Explicitly absent from the payload, and it must stay absent:** children, excerpts, block counts,
row counts, file sizes, preview or thumbnail URLs, the granted subjects' identities, and the node's
own `owner`. Names, paths and a count. Nothing else.

**Database**

| Table | Operation | Detail |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `workspace_members` | READ | Gate 1 + the `workspace.permission.manage` check (`role = 'admin'`). |
| `nodes` | READ | `WHERE workspace_id = :ws AND access_mode = 'restricted' AND deleted_at IS NULL` → `id, name, kind, parent_id`. Partial index `nodes_restricted_idx (workspace_id) WHERE access_mode = 'restricted' AND deleted_at IS NULL` — most workspaces have a handful. |
| `nodes` | READ | The ancestor chain of each hit, for `path`. Batch it: one recursive CTE seeded with all hit ids, not one per row. |
| `access_rules` | READ | `SELECT node_id, count(*) FROM access_rules WHERE node_id = ANY(:hits) GROUP BY node_id` for `grantedCount`. |
| `audit_events` | **WRITE** | **One row, always.** See below. |

**Transaction** — **Required**, and this is the unusual part: a `GET` that writes. The audit row and
the read must be atomic, so a listing that reaches the caller is always accompanied by a record that
it did. Part-01 §7.8 already carves this out: *"Safe and idempotent. Never mutates, never audits —
with one deliberate exception: `GET /workspaces/{workspaceId}/restricted-nodes` (E-046) writes an
audit row at `warn`."*

**Audit** — module `workspace`, action `workspace.permission.manage`, severity **`warn`**,
`outcome: "allowed"`, `target: "Restricted items"`,
`detail: "Listed every restricted item in the workspace."`,
`context: { kind: "system", job: "restricted_nodes_listing" }`. A refusal is audited too, at
`error` / `denied`. Rationale, canon OQ-26: the console promises that *"granting yourself access is
recorded in the audit log"* (`workspace-restricted-tab.tsx:56-60`) — the grant is, and without this
row the **listing** is not, so an admin could enumerate every restricted folder and leave no trace.

**Realtime** — None.

**Possible Errors**

| HTTP | Code | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 401 | `permission_denied` | `AUTH_REQUIRED` |
| 403 | `permission_denied` | `PERMISSION_DENIED` — not `workspace.permission.manage`. `detail`: `Needs the Admin role or above`. **Audited at `error` / `denied`.** |
| 404 | `not_found` | `WORKSPACE_NOT_FOUND` — unknown workspace, or one the caller is not in. |
| 500 | `unknown` | `INTERNAL_ERROR` |

A 403 rather than a 404 on the permission failure is correct here: the caller is a member and the
workspace's existence is not the secret. The *contents* of the list are, and they are not returned.

**Frontend Used By** — `src/hooks/use-workspace-access.ts:105-117` (`useRestrictedNodes`), rendered
by `src/components/workspace/workspace-restricted-tab.tsx:36-92`, which computes `path` via
`pathLabel(tree, node.id)` (`src/lib/tree.ts:74-78`) and `granted` via
`grantedSubjectsOn(rules, node.id).length` (`src/lib/permissions/visibility.ts:104-107`) — both of
which move server-side, because the client will not have the full tree.

The tab's "Manage access" button opens `NodeAccessDialog` on a node the admin may not be able to
see, which resolves through E-040 → E-042. **E-040 and E-042 must therefore accept
`workspace.permission.manage` as an alternative to gate 3 for this one flow.** That is already the
disjunction the frontend uses (`src/hooks/use-node-access.ts:80`), and every grant it writes is an
ordinary audited rule write (§29.6).

---

### 28.13 The governance data model, recapped

The DDL is owned by §4 (part-03) for `nodes`, `workspace_members` and `access_rules`, and by §4
(part-05) for `audit_events`. Repeated here in compressed form because a reviewer reading this
chapter first should not have to page back.

```sql
-- documentation only — the four objects §28 depends on

CREATE TYPE workspace_role      AS ENUM ('viewer', 'member', 'manager', 'admin');  -- order = rank
CREATE TYPE node_access_mode    AS ENUM ('inherit', 'workspace', 'restricted');
CREATE TYPE access_subject_kind AS ENUM ('user', 'role');
CREATE TYPE access_source       AS ENUM ('workspace', 'inherited', 'explicit', 'override');
--   access_source is the vocabulary of the READ MODEL. It is NOT a column;
--   it is derived per request by inheritance.ts:108-119.

-- workspace_members  (T-04) — the outermost gate
--   PK (workspace_id, user_id); role workspace_role NOT NULL; joined_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL
--   "not a member" is the absence of a row, never role='viewer'

-- nodes  (T-06) — the two governance columns
ALTER TABLE nodes
  ADD COLUMN access_mode node_access_mode NOT NULL DEFAULT 'inherit',
  ADD COLUMN owner_id    UUID             NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT;

CREATE INDEX nodes_owner_idx      ON nodes (workspace_id, owner_id);
CREATE INDEX nodes_restricted_idx ON nodes (workspace_id)
       WHERE access_mode = 'restricted' AND deleted_at IS NULL;

-- access_rules  (T-08) — one grant, one node, one subject
CREATE TABLE access_rules (
  id              UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  workspace_id    UUID                NOT NULL,
  node_id         UUID                NOT NULL,
  subject_kind    access_subject_kind NOT NULL,
  subject_user_id UUID REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,
  subject_role    workspace_role,
  role            workspace_role      NOT NULL,
  granted_at      TIMESTAMPTZ         NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  granted_by      UUID                NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,

  CONSTRAINT access_rules_node_fk FOREIGN KEY (node_id, workspace_id)
    REFERENCES nodes(id, workspace_id) ON DELETE CASCADE,

  CONSTRAINT access_rules_subject_exclusive CHECK (
    (subject_kind = 'user' AND subject_user_id IS NOT NULL AND subject_role    IS NULL) OR
    (subject_kind = 'role' AND subject_role    IS NOT NULL AND subject_user_id IS NULL)
  )
);

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX access_rules_node_user_uniq
  ON access_rules (node_id, subject_user_id) WHERE subject_kind = 'user';
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX access_rules_node_role_uniq
  ON access_rules (node_id, subject_role)    WHERE subject_kind = 'role';
CREATE INDEX access_rules_workspace_node_idx ON access_rules (workspace_id, node_id);
CREATE INDEX access_rules_subject_idx        ON access_rules (subject_user_id)
       WHERE subject_kind = 'user';
```

The five facts a reviewer will check:

| Question | Answer |
| --- | --- |
| Cardinality, node → rules | 1 : N, at most one per `(node, subject)` — two partial unique indexes. |
| Delete behaviour | Rule cascades with the **node** (hard delete only) and with the **workspace**. It does **not** cascade with the user: `RESTRICT`, because the rows are evidence. |
| What a soft-deleted node does to its rules | Nothing. See §28.5.6 and the recommendation there. |
| Where the "restricted" bit lives | `nodes.access_mode`, on **every** node kind, not on a folders table. |
| Where ownership lives | `nodes.owner_id`. It is not a role and it is not an access rule. |

---

### 28.14 Non-functional requirements

| Budget | Source | How it is met |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Permission check `p99 < 10ms` at the guard layer | `SY-RBC-42` | One membership probe + one depth-bounded CTE + one indexed `access_rules` fetch, all on primary-key or covering indexes. Optional per-request memo so a handler that checks three keys walks the chain once. |
| Inheritance-chain walk `< 50ms` | `SY-INH-43` | Same two queries. Depth cap 64; `WS-FLD-03` only requires 10 levels. |
| Folder tree depth | `WS-FLD-03` — *"tối thiểu 10 cấp không giới hạn node"* | The CTE's 64-level bound is the safety valve against a cycle, not a product limit. |
| Restricting a folder is O(1) writes regardless of subtree size | `visibility.ts:29-33`; `tests/folder-access.test.ts:423-442` | One `nodes.access_mode` update + one `access_rules` insert. Never a subtree rewrite. |

**One memo per request, not a global cache.** Resolve `(R0, chain, rules)` once at the start of a
request and hand it to every check the handler makes. That is what makes a handler that evaluates
`row.update` and then `file.upload` cost one chain walk rather than two, and it has none of the
invalidation problems of a cross-request cache (§28.9.4).

---

### 28.15 Open questions carried by this section

| id | Question | Position taken here |
| --- | --- | --- |
| OQ-03 | Is there a fifth role, "Super Admin"? | **No.** Four roles; the PRD's "Super Admin" reads as "Admin". Canon §8.8. |
| OQ-16 | 40+ writes carry no permission check in the mock | Every write is gated with the key named in §28.3.3; canon §3's **Perm** column is normative. |
| OQ-17 | `bulkMove` gates neither board | `row.delete` on the source **and** `row.create` on the target; `BULK_TARGET_NOT_A_BOARD` (409) when the target is not a board. |
| OQ-18 | `listFiles` takes `canView` from the caller | Deleted. Gate 3 resolves visibility server-side. |
| OQ-19 / OQ-20 | `userId`, `role` and `user` are request parameters | Deleted. Resolved from the session (part-01 §8.7). |
| OQ-21 | How does role preview reach a real API? | §28.11. `min(server, declared)`; a higher declared role is **ignored**, not rejected; no server-side impersonation. |
| OQ-22 | "Deepest wins" (code) vs "union of permissions" (PRD) | **Deepest wins**, replacement not maximum. §28.6.4. |
| OQ-23 | Who may reveal a secret — Admin only, or Admin/Manager? | **Admin only**, expressed as `secret.reveal`, so moving it is one row in the matrix. |
| OQ-24 | `comment.delete` at Member — whose comments? | Own comment at `member`; anyone else's at `manager`, enforced as an ownership check on the comment row. |
| OQ-02 | Ownership transfer and departed owners | §28.7.4. `POST /nodes/{nodeId}/owner`, audited; reassign or flag on member removal. |
| OQ-60 | Viewer-owner and `canToggleLock` | §28.7.4. Apply the same `roleRank >= member` floor as `can`. |
| OQ-14 / OQ-15 | Trash retention and soft-delete scope | §28.5.6 adds a governance consequence to both: resolve gate 2/3 for a trashed node against `original_ancestor_ids`. |
