```sql
RETURNING next_sequence;                       -- this row's `sequence`
```

For a batch (E-085 import, E-077 bulk move) the same statement adds `:n` and the service hands out
the returned block `[new − n + 1 … new]`, which is why an import lands as `TASK-042 … TASK-141` with
no gaps (`src/services/board-service.ts:1196-1204`).

**Why this is correct.** `UPDATE … RETURNING` takes a row-level exclusive lock on the `boards` row
and holds it until commit. A second transaction executing the same statement blocks, then re-reads
the *committed* value — under `READ COMMITTED`, an `UPDATE` that blocks re-evaluates its predicate
against the new version of the row. Serialisation is therefore total, per board, with no advisory
lock and no retry. The `UNIQUE (board_id, sequence)` and `UNIQUE (board_id, custom_id)` constraints
remain as backstops that should never fire.

**Why the naive `MAX(sequence) + 1` is wrong — three independent reasons, any one of them fatal.**

1. **It is not atomic under `READ COMMITTED`.** Two `SELECT MAX(sequence)` calls in two concurrent
   transactions both see the last committed value, because neither has inserted yet. Both return the
   same number. This is a lost update in its textbook form, and no isolation level below
   `SERIALIZABLE` prevents it — `REPEATABLE READ` does not either, because the two transactions
   insert *different* rows and never touch a common row to conflict on.
2. **It reuses numbers.** `board_rows` soft-deletes. If `MAX` is taken over live rows, deleting
   `TASK-005` — the highest — hands `005` straight back to the next record, which the contract
   forbids outright (`src/types/board.ts:242-243`, "monotonic per board, **never reused**"; canon
   E-062, "the counter only increases"). Taking `MAX` over *all* rows including soft-deleted ones
   fixes this one symptom and leaves reason 1 untouched.
3. **It gets slower as the board grows and is wrong for batches.** `MAX` over a 50 000-row board is
   an index scan even with a good index; allocating 5 000 import ids is 5 000 of them, inside one
   transaction, each blocking the next.

**Why not a Postgres `SEQUENCE` per board.** `nextval` is non-transactional, so a rolled-back create
burns a number — acceptable, since the contract permits gaps — but the real objections are
operational: one sequence object per board is runtime DDL, thousands of catalog entries, no cascade
when the board is deleted, and no foreign key relating the sequence to anything. The counter belongs
on the row every row-creating write already locks.

**Why not an advisory lock.** `pg_advisory_xact_lock(hash(board_id))` would also work. It is rejected
because it is a *second* lock on top of the row lock the insert needs anyway, it is invisible in
`pg_locks` as anything but an integer, and it serialises row creation against every other advisory
user of the same hash. The `UPDATE … RETURNING` is one statement doing one job.

**Deadlock rule.** Always take the `boards` row lock **before** any `board_rows` lock, and for E-077
(cross-board bulk move) lock the two boards in **ascending `board_id` order**. Two simultaneous moves
in opposite directions between the same pair of boards are otherwise a textbook deadlock.

**Contract**: `POST /boards/{boardId}/rows` → `BoardRow` with the server's `id`, `displayId`,
`sequence` and `revision: 1`. `displayId` is unique **per board**, not globally (OQ-95): two boards
may both hold `TASK-001`.

### 37.2 Two users editing the same cell

**EXISTING REQUIREMENT.** Last-write-wins plus a notice, never a rejection
(`src/services/board-service.ts:484-513`; canon §6.4 and E-066).

**Failure mode being avoided.** A `409` here would be the wrong answer twice over: the user has
already seen their value on screen (the store applies optimistically before the request leaves,
`src/store/board-store.ts:340`), and a spreadsheet grid that refuses a keystroke because somebody
else typed somewhere else in the same row is unusable.

**The contract, exactly.**

```ts
// Request — PATCH /api/v1/boards/{boardId}/rows/cells
interface UpdateCellsRequest {
  readonly edits: readonly CellEdit[];                         // { rowId, columnId, value }
  /** Revision each edit was based on. Optional, per row. */
  readonly baseRevisions?: Readonly<Record<string, number>>;
}

// Response — ALWAYS 200
interface UpdateCellsResponse {
  readonly rows: readonly BoardRow[];            // authoritative, revision already bumped
  readonly conflicts: readonly ConflictNotice[];
}

interface ConflictNotice {
  readonly id: string;
  readonly rowId: string;
  readonly columnId: string;
  readonly message: string;   // `${displayId} changed elsewhere — your edit was kept`
}
```

Three properties the backend must reproduce exactly (`src/services/board-service.ts:504-512`):

1. **A missing `baseRevisions[rowId]` never conflicts.** An unqualified write is an unconditional
   write.
2. **`base < current.revision` conflicts; equal or greater does not.** Never `base !== current`.
3. **At most one notice per row per call**, raised by the **first** edit that touches that row. The
   frontend's guard is `!touched.has(edit.rowId)` — once a row is in the working set, later edits to
   it in the same batch do not raise a second notice.

The stale write is **applied**. `revision` is bumped **once** for the row, however many of its cells
the batch touched. The response carries the authoritative rows so the client reconciles rather than
guesses (`reconcileRows`, `src/lib/board-records.ts:109-116`), and the notices land in
`useBoardStore.conflicts`, dismissed individually (`src/store/board-store.ts:310-311`).

**A known and accepted false positive.** The token is per *row*, not per cell. If A edits column 1
(revision 7 → 8) and B, who loaded at revision 7, then edits column 2, B's write raises a notice even
though the two edits do not overlap. This is what the frontend implements and what the message says —
*"changed elsewhere — your edit was kept"*, not "your edit overwrote theirs". Do **not** "fix" it by
tracking per-cell revisions: `baseRevisions` is typed `Record<rowId, number>` and `BoardRow.revision`
is a single number, so per-cell granularity is not expressible in the existing contract.

**What is *not* covered by last-write-wins.** A refusal by a transition rule or a conditional option
is a `409` (`TRANSITION_NOT_ALLOWED`, `OPTION_UNAVAILABLE`) and is not a conflict at all — §37.8.

### 37.3 Optimistic concurrency: the strategy, and the 409 the frontend needs

The frontend applies mutations optimistically and rolls back on failure — `editCells` captures
`reverts` before the write and calls `revertCellEdits` in the failure branch
(`src/store/board-store.ts:335-346`); `addRow` removes the temp row; view patches carry an explicit
`rollback` function (`src/store/board-store.ts:244-257`). The backend therefore needs a token the
client can send, and a refusal the client can act on.

**The three candidates, and the choice.**

| Strategy | Verdict |
| --- | --- |
| `updated_at` timestamp | **Rejected.** Two writes in the same millisecond are indistinguishable, and `now()` in Postgres is the transaction start time — two transactions that begin in the same statement-timestamp window produce identical values. It also invites clock reasoning into a comparison that is not about time. |
| HTTP `ETag` / `If-Match` | **Rejected.** It needs a stable serialisation of the resource to hash, it puts the token in a header the frontend's service layer does not read (every service returns the bare payload, canon §6.1), and it cannot express "this row, this version" for a batch that spans many rows. |
| **A monotonic integer column on the aggregate** | **Chosen.** It already exists in three places: `board_rows.revision`, `documents.version`, `config_documents.version`, and it is already on the wire (`BoardRow.revision`, `src/types/board.ts:245`). One counter, bumped exactly once per write, whatever the write touched. |

**The rule, stated once.** Every optimistic-concurrency check in this API compares an integer the
client sends against an integer the server holds, under a row lock taken in the same transaction. The
comparison is `client < server` (stale), never `client !== server` — a client that somehow holds a
*newer* number is not stale, it is confused, and refusing it buys nothing.

**Where it refuses and where it does not:**

| Subject | Token | On stale |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Board cells (E-066) | `baseRevisions[rowId]` | **Applied**, `ConflictNotice`, `200`. Never `409`. |
| Board bulk writes (E-074…E-077) | none | Applied unconditionally; refusals surface as `BulkSkip` (OQ-55). |
| Documents (E-092) | `expectedVersion?` | `409` `DOCUMENT_VERSION_CONFLICT` when present and stale; last-write-wins when **absent** (OQ-57 position). |
| Config documents (E-100) | `expectedVersion?` | Same, plus the autosave fold. |
| Secrets (E-102) | none | Whole-list replace; an omitted `value` carries the stored ciphertext forward (`src/services/devtools-service.ts:479-560`). |
| Everything else | none | Unconditional. |

**OPEN QUESTION (OQ-57) — what does the 409 body carry so the client can reconcile?**

**What is unclear.** Canon settles that E-092 returns `409 DOCUMENT_VERSION_CONFLICT` when
`expectedVersion` is stale. It does not say what the body carries, and the frontend has no
reconciliation UI to read one: `DocumentDraft` has no version field at all
(`src/types/document.ts`), and the save path treats any thrown error as a failed save.

**Evidence.** The error envelope is `{ error: AppError }` with `code`, `message`, `detail?`,
`isRetryable` frozen by the frontend contract (`src/types/async.ts:12-20`,
`src/types/board.ts:507-509`), and canon §6.2 already adds `reason`, `requestId` and an optional
`fields` array to it — so the envelope is extensible by precedent. `SaveStatus` (`idle` / `saving` /
`saved` / `error`) is UI-only and has no `conflict` member, so the page can only show "error" today.

**Recommendation.** Add one optional field, `current`, carrying the authoritative resource — the same
shape the successful response would have returned. Nothing else changes:

```ts
interface ConcurrencyConflictError extends AppError {
  readonly code: "conflict";
  readonly reason: "DOCUMENT_VERSION_CONFLICT" | "CONCURRENCY_CONFLICT";
  readonly message: string;    // "This page changed while you were editing"
  readonly detail: string;     // "Mai Tran saved it 2 minutes ago. Reload to see their version."
  readonly isRetryable: false;
  /** RECOMMENDATION (OQ-57). The authoritative resource, so the client can diff without a second round trip. */
  readonly current: WorkspaceDocument | ConfigDocument;
}
```

Body: `{ "error": { …, "current": { … } } }`. The frontend ignores unknown keys today, so this ships
without a client release and becomes useful the moment a reconcile dialog exists.

**Impact if wrong.** Without `current`, a conflicted save costs a second `GET` before the user can be
shown what changed, and the window between the `409` and that `GET` is another chance to be stale.
With it and no client support, the cost is a slightly larger error body — the response is already
being serialised.

### 37.4 Moving a folder while another user is inside it

**Three distinct races, one lock.**

**(a) Two concurrent moves producing a cycle.** A is moved under B and B under A, simultaneously.
Each transaction's recursive descendant check passes against a tree the other has not yet committed;
both commit; the two nodes are now unreachable from the root and every ancestor walk over them does
not terminate. **No constraint can express this** — a cycle is a property of a set of rows, and
Postgres has no `EXCLUDE` or check that spans them. **Mitigation:
`pg_advisory_xact_lock(hash(workspace_id))` held for the whole move transaction.** Moves are rare and
human-paced; the lock is free in practice and is the only correct answer short of `SERIALIZABLE`.
E-024, E-026, E-032 and E-037 all take it, because those four are the writes that change the shape of
the tree.

**(b) Someone has the moved node — or a descendant — open, and loses access.** The move relocates the
node under a different access chain. `moveVisibilityImpact` computes `losing` and `gaining` **before**
the update (§36.11), and RT-05 `permission.changed` carries the union as `userIds`, with `nodeId` set
and **no resource content**. The receiving tab re-resolves its own access and drops what it may no
longer hold — the tree repaints for free because it is derived, but a *loaded board's records* are a
copy and have to be thrown away explicitly (`src/hooks/use-access-sync.ts:19-37`). This is the
mechanism, and it is why RT-05 fires on a move at all.

**(c) Someone is mid-write on a descendant.** B's `PATCH …/rows/cells` resolved permission at the
start of its transaction, against the old chain. The move commits a millisecond later. B's write
lands under permission the move has just revoked.

**This window is real, is one transaction wide, and is accepted.** The alternative — making every
row write take a shared advisory lock on the workspace so it cannot interleave with a move — would put
a workspace-wide lock on the hottest path in the product to close a window measured in milliseconds,
for a permission change that RT-05 closes on the very next request. Document it, do not engineer it.
What the API *must* do is resolve permission **inside** the write transaction from the live ancestor
chain, never from a cached decision taken in middleware (§38.2), so the window is one transaction and
not one cache TTL.

**(d) The stale URL.** The drive addresses nodes by path, and `resolvePath` walks slugs
(`src/lib/tree.ts:48-57`). A move re-uniquifies the slug against the new siblings (OQ-10), so B's open
URL may no longer resolve. `GET /workspaces/{workspaceId}/nodes/resolve?path=` returns a
`DriveLocation` with `isNotFound` rather than a 404, which is exactly the shape a "this moved" screen
needs. RT-11 `node.changed` (`moved`) lets a second tab converge without waiting for the user to
click.

**Errors**: `NODE_MOVE_INTO_DESCENDANT`, `NODE_MOVE_INTO_SELF`, `NODE_MOVE_SAME_PARENT`,
`NODE_MOVE_INVALID_TARGET`, `NODE_SLUG_CONFLICT`.

### 37.5 Deleting a resource while someone is editing it

Four subjects, four different correct answers. The difference is whether the delete is soft.

| Deleted | Concurrent write | Answer | Grounding |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Node** (E-032, soft) | any write on it or a descendant | `403` `NODE_TRASHED_READ_ONLY`. A trashed node accepts nothing but `node.delete`. The check is `if (node?.isTrashed) return key === "node.delete"` — it runs **before** the frozen and locked narrowings. | `src/lib/permissions/evaluate.ts:79-81` |
| **Row** (E-065, hard) | `PATCH …/rows/cells` naming it | **Silently skipped.** The edit loop does `const current = …; if (!current) continue` — the row simply does not appear in `UpdateCellsResponse.rows`, and the call is still `200`. Not a `404`: a batch of 30 edits must not fail because one row was deleted under it. | `src/services/board-service.ts:498-502` |
| **Column** (E-054) | a cell write naming it | `404` `COLUMN_NOT_FOUND`, for the whole batch. E-054 takes the board's schema lock (§37.9), so the two are serialised: the edit commits first and E-054 then prunes the orphan key from `cells`, or E-054 commits first and the edit is refused. | canon E-054 — "prunes every view of references in the same transaction" |
| **Comment** (E-122, soft) | a reply to it | **Succeeds.** Delete is a tombstone precisely so replies do not orphan; the row is still present, so `rootIdFor` resolves. The reply hangs under a tombstone, which is what the thread renderer expects. | canon E-122; `src/lib/comments.ts:72-84` |

**The row case deserves the extra sentence.** Because the write is silently skipped, B's screen keeps
showing a record that no longer exists until something tells it otherwise. That something is **RT-09
`row.deleted` `{ boardId, rowIds }`** — and it is the reason RT-09 is on the recommended list rather
than optional. `reconcileRows` only overwrites by id and never removes
(`src/lib/board-records.ts:109-116`), so nothing else in the client can drop the row.

**Deleting a node while an upload into it is in flight.** The `uploads` row records its destination;
E-111 `complete` re-checks `file.upload` **against the destination recorded on the upload row**, and a
destination that is now trashed refuses with `NODE_TRASHED_READ_ONLY`. The object is already in the
bucket; the reaper collects it because no `file_assets` row was ever written (T-03).

### 37.6 Concurrent role or access change while a request is in flight

**Failure mode.** A revocation commits between the moment a request's permission check passed and the
moment its write commits. The write lands under permission that no longer exists.

**Three mitigations, in the order they matter.**

1. **Resolve permission inside the write transaction, from the live chain.** Gate 1 (membership) may
   be answered from cache; **gates 2 and 3 — visibility and the `PermissionKey` — must be a read in
   the same transaction as the write**, against `nodes` + `access_rules` + `workspace_members`. This
   is what bounds the window to one transaction. A middleware that decides and hands a boolean to a
   handler that then opens a transaction has a window as wide as the handler.
2. **A cache epoch, not a TTL.** Effective access is expensive enough to cache
   (`access:{workspaceId}:{epoch}:{userId}:{nodeId}`), and a TTL alone means a revocation is honoured
   *up to* the TTL late. Instead, every access-affecting write — E-013, E-014, E-015, E-016, E-041,
   E-042, E-043, E-026 — does `INCR access-epoch:{workspaceId}` after commit. The epoch is part of
   the cache key, so one `INCR` invalidates the whole workspace's cached decisions with no scan and
   no delete. Keep a short TTL (≤60 s) as well, purely so abandoned epochs expire.
3. **The last-admin invariant needs a set lock, not a row lock.** `SELECT user_id FROM
   workspace_members WHERE workspace_id = :ws AND role = 'admin' FOR UPDATE` locks every admin row.
   Without it, two concurrent demotions of the last two admins each see one other admin, both pass
   `isLastAdmin`, and the workspace ends with zero admins — unrecoverable, because
   `workspace.member.manage` is an admin key. The three guards that read `isLastAdmin`
   (`src/lib/workspace-access.ts:84-157`) all sit behind this lock: E-014 role change, E-015 removal,
   E-016 leave.

**What the client sees.** RT-05 `permission.changed` `{ workspaceId, nodeId | null, userIds }`, ids
only. `useAccessSync` drops the loaded board, the open drawer and the row cache for anything the
caller may no longer open (`src/hooks/use-access-sync.ts:38-60`). A request already in flight
completes and its response is applied; the *next* request is refused with `PERMISSION_DENIED` (403) or
`NODE_NOT_FOUND` (404), whichever the visibility rule dictates (§38.2).

**Preview mode is not a race and must not become one.** `previewAs` may only **narrow** the caller's
real role; a preview that outranks it is `PREVIEW_ROLE_ESCALATES` (400). The real role always comes
from the session (C-09) — the preview is a display filter applied on top, never a substitute
(`src/store/permission-store.ts:29,115`, OQ-21).

### 37.7 Import creating duplicate rows on a retry — idempotency

**Failure mode.** E-085 commits, the response is lost to a timeout, the client retries. Nothing in the
request distinguishes the retry from a second deliberate import of the same file, so 5 000 records
land twice, each with its own block of `TASK-` ids, and there is no way to undo it: E-076
`bulk/delete` needs the ids, and the operator does not have them.

**Mitigation — an idempotency key on `import_jobs` (T-38).** **RECOMMENDATION**, OQ-41.

- The client sends `Idempotency-Key: <uuid v4>` as a header on `POST /boards/{boardId}/import`,
  generated once when the wizard reaches the confirm step and **kept across retries of that step**.
- Step 0 of §36.7 is `INSERT INTO import_jobs (…, idempotency_key, …) ON CONFLICT (board_id,
  idempotency_key) DO NOTHING RETURNING id`.
- Zero rows returned means the key is already committed: read `import_jobs.outcome` and return the
  stored `ImportOutcome` with `200`. The body is byte-identical to the first response, which is what
  makes the retry safe rather than merely harmless.
- A row inserted but with `completed_at IS NULL` and `created_at` inside the last few minutes means a
  first attempt is still running: refuse with `409` `CONCURRENCY_CONFLICT`, `isRetryable: true`,
  `retryAfterSeconds`. This is one of the very few legitimate uses of that reason.
- Keys are scoped to the board and swept with the job rows.

**What else needs it, and what does not.**

| Endpoint | Idempotent today? | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| E-111 `POST /uploads/{uploadId}/complete` | **Yes, already.** | The `uploads` row is read `FOR UPDATE` and its `state` is the guard; `file_assets_storage_uniq (storage_key)` is the second one. A replay finds `state = 'completed'` and returns the existing `FileAsset`. |
| E-085 import | With the key above. | |
| E-062 create row, E-120 create comment | **No.** | A retry creates a second record or a second comment. This is *why* the frontend's optimistic create keys on a client temp id and replaces it with the response (`replaceRow`, `src/lib/board-records.ts:128-145`) rather than de-duplicating by content. |
| E-074…E-077 bulk | **No.** | Bulk writes carry no concurrency token and the client has no conflict UI for them — **OQ-55**. `bulk/archive` and `bulk/delete` are naturally idempotent (setting `archived_at` twice is the same state); `bulk/update` and `bulk/move` are not. |

**OPEN QUESTION (OQ-55) — should the idempotency key generalise to every write?**
**What is unclear.** Whether `Idempotency-Key` becomes a service-wide convention.
**Evidence.** No frontend call site sends one; the retry story is entirely optimistic-UI rollback
(`src/store/board-store.ts:335-346`), and the only retry the user can trigger is the "Try again"
button driven by `AppError.isRetryable` (`src/services/errors.ts:31`).
**Recommendation.** Require it on the three endpoints where a duplicate is expensive and
irreversible — E-085 import, E-086 export with `board` scope, E-110 create upload — and accept
at-most-once-in-practice elsewhere. A general key needs a store, and a general store is a 40th table
canon does not have.
**Impact if wrong.** A duplicated `POST /comments` on a flaky connection posts the same comment
twice, which is visible, embarrassing and manually fixable. A duplicated import is none of those.

### 37.8 Transition rules changed while a Kanban card is mid-drag

**Failure mode.** B has the Kanban open. The select column's `transitionRules` were loaded with the
board. A edits them (E-053) — turning them on, or removing a transition. B drops a card. B's
client-side guard evaluates against the **stale** configuration and lets the write leave.

**What the server does.** Re-evaluates against the current configuration, inside the write
transaction, having read the schema at step 2 of §36.4. If the rules now refuse:

```jsonc
// 409 PATCH /api/v1/boards/{boardId}/rows/cells
{
  "error": {
    "code": "conflict",
    "message": "In Progress cannot move to Done",
    "detail": "The board's status rules changed. Reload to see the current workflow.",
    "isRetryable": false,
    "reason": "TRANSITION_NOT_ALLOWED",
    "requestId": "01JB9…"
  }
}
```

**This does not contradict "E-066 is always 200".** The distinction is exact and load-bearing:

- **A stale *revision* is a conflict between two writers.** Last-write-wins plus a `ConflictNotice`,
  `200`. Nobody's write was wrong; they were merely ordered.
- **A refusal by a transition rule or a conditional option is an invalid write.** It is not a
  disagreement between two writers, it is a value the board does not accept. `409`
  `TRANSITION_NOT_ALLOWED` / `OPTION_UNAVAILABLE`. Canon lists both among E-066's errors.

The frontend already models these as two different things: `guardCellEdits` splits a batch into
`allowed` and `rejected` **before** anything optimistic happens — *"an edit a transition rule or a
conditional option refuses never becomes an optimistic write, so nothing has to be rolled back and no
request leaves the client"* (`src/store/board-store.ts:317-330`) — and the rejection is surfaced as
`feedback(rejection.message)`, not as a conflict banner. And the guard is deliberately not permission:
*"Permission answers 'may this person edit Status at all'; a transition rule answers 'may Status go
from here to there'. Both are checked, separately, before a drop is written."*
(`src/lib/transition-rules.ts:21-24`).

**Batch semantics: the whole batch is refused.** `UpdateCellsResponse` has `rows` and `conflicts` and
no `skipped` channel — unlike `BulkResult`, which does. There is nowhere to report "27 of 30 applied",
so a rule refusal aborts the transaction and nothing is written. The client's own pre-split means this
is rare by construction.

**What closes the window.** RT-10 `board.schema.changed` `{ boardId }` fires on every column write
(E-052…E-060) and the client refetches the **whole** schema, matching C-11. B's next drag is evaluated
against the current rules on both sides.

**Two related rules the server owns.** `"__empty__"` is a reserved option id and must be rejected as
user-authored (`OPTION_ID_RESERVED`, `src/lib/transition-rules.ts:28`); and **a status the rule table
does not mention is ungoverned** — moves in and out of it are allowed even while rules are on, which
is what makes adding a status safe (`src/lib/transition-rules.ts:56-60`). A backend that treats an
allow-list as "everything not listed is forbidden" freezes every newly added status, which is exactly
the trap the comment warns about.

### 37.9 Concurrent position updates — columns, rows, views

Three orderings, two mechanisms.

**(a) Column reorder (E-056) and view reorder (E-082) — dense integers.** `reposition` renumbers the
whole list `0..n-1` (`src/lib/board-schema.ts:163-167`), and both endpoints return the **complete
array** (C-11).

*Failure mode.* A reorder and a concurrent create/delete interleave: `createColumn` appends at
`MAX(position) + 1` computed against the pre-reorder list, and the new column lands on a position the
reorder has just given to somebody else. Two columns share a slot; the order becomes whatever the
index returns.

*Mitigation.* **Every board schema write takes `SELECT … FROM boards WHERE id = :boardId FOR UPDATE`
first** (RECOMMENDATION, §36.12). One serialisation point per board for E-052, E-054, E-055, E-056,
E-057, E-058, E-059, E-060, E-079…E-082 and E-085. Boards are edited by people, not by loops; the lock
costs nothing and removes the entire class. Second line of defence: `UNIQUE (board_id, position)
DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED` on both `board_columns` and `board_views`, so a lost update becomes a
constraint error rather than silent duplication, and the deferral lets the dense renumber collide
transiently inside its own statement.

*Contract.* Last writer wins **wholesale** — a reorder replaces the entire ordering, so there is no
partial merge to get wrong. Views are shared state: *"the order is the board's, not the reader's"*, so
a lost update is visible to everybody, which is why the unique constraint is worth having here and not
merely tidy.

**(b) Row reorder (E-073) and insert-after (E-062) — a fractional index.** `board_rows.position` is
`NUMERIC` (OQ-34 position). Append is `COALESCE(MAX(position), 0) + 1`; insert after *R* is the
midpoint of *R* and its successor.

*Failure mode.* Two concurrent inserts after the same row compute the **same** midpoint and both write
it. This is not corruption: the cursor's sort key is `(position, id)` (canon §6.3), which stays total,
so pagination is still correct and no row is skipped or repeated. What is lost is only the relative
order of those two rows, which was never determined anyway.

*Mitigation.* Accept it. `NUMERIC` is arbitrary precision, so midpoints never run out; renormalise the
board to dense integers when any denominator exceeds ~40 digits, in a single ordered `UPDATE` under
the board's `FOR UPDATE`, emitting one RT-10. Do **not** put a unique constraint on `(board_id,
position)` — it would turn a harmless tie into a failed record creation, and the subtask rule ("a new
child files directly after its parent's last descendant", `lastDescendantOf`,
`src/services/board-service.ts:342-356`) makes ties genuinely common.

**(c) Deadlock avoidance, everywhere.** Lock in a fixed order: `boards` before `board_columns` before
`board_rows`; within a set, ascending `id`; across two boards (E-077), ascending `board_id`. Every
multi-row `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` in this specification carries an explicit `ORDER BY id`.

### 37.10 Summary

| # | Race | Failure mode | Mechanism | Client contract |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Custom row id | Two `TASK-005`, or a 500 on an ordinary create | `UPDATE boards SET next_sequence = next_sequence + 1 … RETURNING`, in the insert's transaction | `BoardRow` with the server's `displayId`; optimistic row replaced by id |
| 2 | Same cell, two users | A refused keystroke in a grid | Per-row `revision`; stale write applied | `200` + `ConflictNotice[]`, never `409` |
| 3 | Optimistic rollback | No token to send, no refusal to act on | Integer `revision` / `version` on the aggregate; `client < server` is stale | `409` + `reason` + (RECO) `current` |
| 4 | Move under an open node | Cycle; a loaded board outliving its access | Per-workspace advisory lock; `moveVisibilityImpact` before the update | RT-11 `node.changed`, RT-05 `permission.changed` |
| 5 | Delete under an editor | Orphaned writes; a ghost record on screen | Soft delete + `NODE_TRASHED_READ_ONLY`; skip-not-404 for rows | RT-09 `row.deleted` is what removes it |
| 6 | Role/access change in flight | A write under revoked permission | Permission resolved **inside** the write transaction; Redis access epoch; `FOR UPDATE` over the admin set | RT-05, then `403`/`404` on the next call |
| 7 | Import retry | 5 000 duplicate records | `Idempotency-Key` → `UNIQUE (board_id, idempotency_key)` on `import_jobs` | Replay returns the stored `ImportOutcome`, `200` |
| 8 | Rules changed mid-drag | A write the current workflow forbids | Re-evaluate server-side inside the transaction; whole batch refused | `409 TRANSITION_NOT_ALLOWED`; RT-10 to resync |
| 9 | Concurrent reorder | Two columns in one slot; a lost ordering | Board-level `FOR UPDATE` for schema; deferrable unique on `position`; fractional index for rows | Complete array returned (C-11) |

---

## 38. Security Requirements

The frontend is unusually explicit that its own checks are not security. `src/services/authz.ts:24-32`
says it in the file that performs them: *"a role the client sends is a claim, not a fact, and an
endpoint that trusts one is not enforcing anything — it is asking the caller how much access they
would like"*, and *"there is no server here… it is a faithful model of the check a real API must
make, not a substitute for it."* `src/lib/permissions/evaluate.ts:24-25` repeats it. Everything in
this section is the server half of that sentence.

### 38.1 Workspace isolation — enforced centrally, never per handler

**The requirement.** Every query that touches a workspace-scoped table is scoped by
`workspace_id`, and the scope comes from the request context, never from the request body.

**Where the scope comes from.** One middleware, once per request:

1. Resolve the session → `userId`. Never from a header, a query parameter or a body field (C-09).
2. Resolve the `workspaceId` from the **path** (`/workspaces/{workspaceId}/…`) or, for a
   resource-rooted route (`/nodes/{nodeId}`, `/boards/{boardId}`, `/comments/{commentId}`), from the
   resource's own `workspace_id` column in the same query that loads it.
3. Gate 1: `workspace_members_pair_uniq` probe. **Not a member → `WORKSPACE_NOT_FOUND` (404), never
   403.** "Not a member" is not "viewer" (`src/lib/workspace-access.ts:4-14`), and answering 403
   would confirm the workspace exists.
4. Bind `WorkspaceContext { workspaceId, userId, role, ip, requestId }` to the request. It is
   immutable and is the only source of these five values for the rest of the request.

**How "centrally, not per handler" is achieved.** Three mechanisms, in the order they should be
built:

- **A repository layer that cannot be called without a context.** Every read and write method takes
  `WorkspaceContext` as its first parameter and injects `workspace_id = :ctx.workspaceId` into the
  predicate itself. A handler never writes SQL. This is the primary control, because it is the only
  one that a code reviewer can verify by looking at a type signature.
- **Tables without a `workspace_id` reach it through a mandatory join, declared once.** `board_columns`
  and `board_rows` → `boards`; `secrets`, `secret_rotations`, `secret_access_events` →
  `secret_documents`; `document_versions` → `documents`; `config_versions` → `config_documents`;
  `cell_attachments` → `board_rows`; `comment_attachments` → `comments`; `board_view_preferences` →
  `board_views` → `boards`; `node_favorites` and `trash_entries` → `nodes`. The repository for each of
  these carries the join; there is no method that fetches one by id alone.
- **A test that fails the build.** One integration test per workspace-scoped endpoint: create the
  same-shaped resource in workspace A and workspace B, then call every endpoint as a member of A with
  B's id. Every one must answer `404`. This catches the handler somebody wrote by hand at 6pm.

**Postgres row-level security is defence in depth, not the primary control.** `ALTER TABLE … ENABLE
ROW LEVEL SECURITY` with a policy on `current_setting('app.workspace_id')`, set with `SET LOCAL` at
the start of every transaction, is worth adding: it turns a missed scope from a data leak into an
empty result set. It is not the primary control because it is invisible at the call site, it needs a
bypass role for the sweeps and the reconciliation jobs (which legitimately cross workspaces), and a
connection pooler that reuses a connection without resetting `app.workspace_id` fails open.

**The one deliberate exception.** `users` has no `workspace_id` and is intentionally global — a person
is a member of several workspaces, and E-006's directory is built from `workspace_members`, not from
a scan of `users`. `users` is never queried by anything but an id or an email that came from a
workspace-scoped row.

### 38.2 Node access isolation

Three gates, in this order, on every request that names a node. They are cumulative and they are not
interchangeable.

| Gate | Question | Failure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Is the caller a member of this workspace? | `WORKSPACE_NOT_FOUND` (404) |
| 2 | May the caller **see** this node? `canSeeNode` over the ancestor chain. | `NODE_NOT_FOUND` (404) |
| 3 | Does the caller hold the endpoint's `PermissionKey` on this node? `can(key, context)`. | `PERMISSION_DENIED` (403) |

**Gate 2 answers 404, not 403.** Canon §4.2 is explicit: `not_found` means "the resource does not
exist, **or the caller may not see it** — the two answer identically". Distinguishing them would let
an outsider enumerate the tree by watching status codes.

**Pruning is subtree-wide.** `collectAllowed` drops a node **together with its whole subtree**: *"a
file inside a folder the viewer cannot open must not surface in search results just because the file
itself carries no restriction of its own"* (`src/lib/tree.ts:297-320`). Every list endpoint that
returns nodes — E-020 tree, E-023 children, E-033 favourites, E-034 archive, E-035 quick-find, E-113
folder files, E-133 search — prunes this way. Filtering leaf-by-leaf is a bug, not a shortcut.

**The three narrowing layers only ever take away** (`src/lib/permissions/evaluate.ts:69-88`):
trashed → only `node.delete`; frozen by an archived ancestor → no writes at all; locked → no content
writes. `READ_ONLY_KEYS = { board.export, workspace.audit.view, secret.reveal }` pass through all
three. Owner escalation (`node.rename`, `node.delete`, `node.archive`, `file.delete`,
`document.lock`) applies only from `member` upward, and is a widening that happens *before* the
narrowings, never after.

**A refusal must not name what was refused.** `DENIED_REASON` is *"You do not have access to this
item. Ask somebody who does to share it with you."* — deliberately name-free, because *"a refusal
that reads 'Finance is restricted' hands the name of a private folder to the one person who was told
they may not have it"* (`src/lib/permissions/evaluate.ts:154-163`). Applies to `message`, to
`detail`, and to every log line (§38.12).

**The one place that deliberately looks past access** is E-046 `GET /workspaces/{workspaceId}/restricted-nodes`, the admin recovery console. It is gated on `workspace.permission.manage`, it
exposes **names and paths and no content**, and — per canon OQ-26 — **the read itself is audited at
`warn`**. It exists because *"a workspace admin can already grant themselves any folder, so
withholding the name of one would buy nothing but a folder nobody can ever unlock"*
(`src/lib/permissions/visibility.ts:270-278`).

### 38.3 Secret encryption

**Envelope encryption** (canon OQ-65 position):

- A per-workspace **data key (DEK)**, generated on first use, wrapped by a **KMS master key (CMK)**
  and stored wrapped. The plaintext DEK lives only in process memory, cached briefly.
- `AES-256-GCM`. `secrets.value_encrypted BYTEA` holds `IV (12 bytes) ‖ ciphertext ‖ tag (16 bytes)`,
  with `dek_version` beside it so a rotation of the DEK does not require rewriting every row at once.
- **AAD = `secret_id ‖ node_id ‖ workspace_id`.** Without it, a ciphertext copied from one row into
  another decrypts happily; with it, a moved ciphertext fails authentication. This is cheap and it
  closes the one attack a database-level adversary can mount without the key.

**Handling rules, all grounded:**

- **`value_encrypted` is never selected on a list read.** Canon T-23 says so; the enforcement is that
  the `secrets` repository has two methods — a list method whose `SELECT` names
  `id, key, environment_id, note, position, rotated_by, updated_at` and nothing else, and a
  single-secret method used only by E-103/E-104. **`SELECT *` on `secrets` is a review-blocking
  defect.**
- **`maskedValue` is a constant 12 `U+2022` bullets, never derived from the real length**
  (`src/services/devtools-service.ts:35`; `src/types/devtools.ts:76-77` — *"Fixed-width mask; never
  derived from the real value's length"*). A length-preserving mask leaks the length of every
  credential in the workspace to every viewer.
- **`SecretEntry` has no `value` field, by design** — *"plaintext only ever arrives from an explicit,
  permission-checked reveal, and it is never written back into this shape"*
  (`src/types/devtools.ts:69-72`).
- **An omitted `value` on E-102 means "leave the stored value untouched"** — that is what lets the
  editor rename a key, reorder the list or delete a neighbour without the client ever holding the
  plaintext of the rows it is not changing (`SecretDraftEntry`, `src/services/devtools-service.ts:458-470`).
- **`secret_rotations` has no value column, ever** (canon T-24). Version history for a secret records
  *that* it rotated, by whom, when — and projects into `VersionEntry` with `hasSnapshot: false`, so
  E-096 and E-098 refuse a secret version with `VERSION_NOT_RESTORABLE`.
- **Reveal returns plaintext once**, in the response body, and is rate-limited (§38.7). The response
  is `Cache-Control: no-store`.
- `copy` has **no permission key of its own** — it is gated by `secret.reveal` and audited as a reveal
  (`src/services/devtools-service.ts:384-386`).

### 38.4 Audit coverage

**The log is append-only by construction.** No write endpoint exists and no chapter may add one
(canon §3.23). Enforce it in the database too: `GRANT SELECT, INSERT ON audit_events` to the
application role and **no `UPDATE`, no `DELETE`**. The retention sweep runs as a separate role whose
grant is scoped by the `audit_events_retention_idx` predicate — it can never reach a denial or an
error (§35.4).

**What is audited** (canon OQ-25 position: every action whose key is held only from `manager` or
`admin`, plus `node.share`, plus **every denial of any key**):

| Class | Actions | Severity | Outcome |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Membership and roles | E-013, E-014, E-015, E-016, E-011 | `warn` | `allowed` |
| Access rules and mode | E-041, E-042, E-043 | `warn` | `allowed` |
| Node lifecycle | E-026 move, E-030/E-031 archive, E-032 delete, E-038/E-039 purge | `info`, or `warn` when a move takes access away | `allowed` |
| Board governance | E-050, E-054, E-057, E-085 import, E-086 export, E-090 | `info` | `allowed` |
| Documents | E-094 lock/unlock, E-097 version restore, E-100 on a Production config (OQ-62) | `info` / `warn` | `allowed` |
| Secrets | E-102 rotate, E-103 reveal, E-104 copy | `warn` | both |
| **Privileged reads** (OQ-26) | E-136 audit list, E-137 audit export, E-046 restricted nodes, E-040 node access list | `warn` | `allowed` |
| **Every denial** | any endpoint, any key | `error` | `denied` |

The severity default reproduces the frontend: `severity ?? (outcome === "denied" ? "error" : "info")`
(`src/services/audit-service.ts:296`).

**What is not audited.** Ordinary `row.update` and `comment.create` traffic at `info`. The activity
stream (`row_activity`, T-14) already covers it, and mixing them buries the nine error rows in
eighty-eight thousand info rows — at which point the severity filter stops being useful and so does
the log.

**Five rules about the row itself:**

1. **The IP is stamped by the server from the socket.** *"A real backend reads it off the socket — the
   client must never send one, which is why this lives here and not in any hook"*
   (`src/services/audit-service.ts:280-285`). Behind a proxy, take the last hop from a trusted
   `X-Forwarded-For` chain, never the first.
2. **`target` is a human label, never an id and never a payload** (`src/types/audit.ts:35-36`).
3. **`detail` is one sentence** the UI renders verbatim (`src/types/audit.ts:37-38`). It never
   contains a secret value, a cell value, a comment body or a token. §38.12.
4. **The structured payload goes in `context`**, an internal JSONB column that is **never returned by
   E-136** (`AuditContext`, canon §5.3, OQ-25).
5. **The row is written inside the action's transaction** (T-01), including on the denied path — for a
   secret reveal, *before* the refusal is returned (canon E-103).

### 38.5 Signed, expiring file URLs and private-by-default storage

**The bucket is private.** Block-all-public-access on, no object ACLs, no public bucket policy, no
CDN origin that bypasses signing. Nothing in this product is served by an unauthenticated URL.

**Persist only `assetId`** (canon OQ-75). `url` and `thumbnailUrl` are **minted per response** as
short-lived signed URLs and are **never accepted on write**. The frontend already says why: the URLs
it holds are `URL.createObjectURL` handles — *"Session object URL; null once the session that produced
it ends"* (`src/types/collab.ts:35-36`, `src/types/board.ts:206-207`). Persisting one stores a string
that is dead the moment the tab closes.

| Direction | Endpoint | TTL | Conditions on the signature |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Upload | E-110 presigned `PUT` | **15 minutes**; the `uploads` row expires at 30 | Exact `storage_key`; `content-length-range` bounded by the declared size; `Content-Type` pinned to the declared type. No `x-amz-meta-*` accepted from the client. |
| Download | E-116 file, E-117 asset | **5 minutes** (RECOMMENDATION) | Exact key, `GET` only, `response-content-disposition: attachment; filename*=UTF-8''…`, `response-content-type` forced to the sniffed type. |
| Export | E-086 `board` scope | Job's `expires_at`, then the reaper deletes the object | Same as download. |

**A signed URL is a bearer token.** For its lifetime, anybody holding it can read the object with no
session and no permission check. Three consequences, all mandatory: the TTL is minutes, not hours; the
URL is **never logged and never written into an audit `detail`** (§38.12); and permission is checked
when the URL is *minted*, not when it is used — so `GET /assets/{assetId}/url` (E-117) must verify
that the caller may see **at least one owner** of the asset (`file_nodes`, `cell_attachments`,
`comment_attachments`, `document_asset_refs`) before signing. That check is the reason the four
`*_asset_idx` indexes exist (§35.2.7).

**Serve user content from a different origin.** Signed object URLs point at the storage host, not at
the API host, so a stored file can never execute against the application's origin. Add
`X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` and `Content-Disposition: attachment` on every object response;
never `Content-Type: text/html` for user content.

### 38.6 Upload validation: MIME sniffing, size, and why the extension is not trusted

**What the frontend does, and why it is not enough.** `validateUpload` checks three things — non-empty,
`≤ MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES`, and extension on `ALL_ACCEPTED_EXTENSIONS` (`src/lib/file-validation.ts:28-57`).
The extension comes from the file name. Nothing sniffs content. This is **OQ-70**, marked
**security** in canon, and the server owns it.

**The four checks, and where each one runs:**

| # | Check | Where | Error |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Non-empty | E-110, before signing | `FILE_EMPTY` (400) |
| 2 | Size ≤ limit | E-110 against the declared size; **E-111 against the object's real size from the store's `HEAD`**; and in the presigned policy's `content-length-range` | `FILE_TOO_LARGE` (400), `UPLOAD_INCOMPLETE` (422) |
| 3 | Extension on the allow-list | E-110 | `FILE_TYPE_REJECTED` (400) |
| 4 | **Sniffed content matches the extension** | **E-111, after the object lands, before `file_assets` is written** | `FILE_CONTENT_TYPE_MISMATCH` (400) |

Check 2 is done **three times on purpose**. The declared size is a claim; the policy condition is what
the storage service enforces; the `HEAD` is what the database records. A client that declares 1 MB and
uploads 90 MB is stopped by the policy; one that declares 90 MB and uploads 1 MB is caught by the
`HEAD` and refused with `UPLOAD_INCOMPLETE`.

**Check 4, precisely.** Read the first 4 096 bytes of the landed object, detect the type by magic
bytes, and compare against the set the extension permits. Refuse on mismatch, delete the object, mark
the `uploads` row `aborted`. Two clarifications: text and source-code extensions (`txt`, `md`, `ts`,
`json`, `sql`, `sh`, `yml`, …) have no magic bytes, so the check for those is a **UTF-8 validity and
control-character** check, not a signature match; and `xlsx`/`docx` are ZIP containers, so the
signature is `PK\x03\x04` and the discriminator is the archive's content-type part.

**The size limit is server-owned.** The frontend says 25 MB (`MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES`,
`src/lib/file-validation.ts:4`; `ACCEPTED_HINT`, `:22`); the PRD `WS-FIL-06` says 100 MB. **OQ-69**,
and canon's position is that **100 MB is the API and storage contract, and the client pre-check is
served from `GET /config` (E-139) so the two cannot disagree**. The extension allow-list ships from
the same endpoint for the same reason. Neither number is duplicated in the client.

**Two things the allow-list is doing quietly and must keep doing.** `svg` is **not** on it
(`images: ["png", "jpg", "jpeg"]`), which is what stops a stored SVG carrying script; and `html`,
`htm` and `xhtml` are not on it either. Any proposal to add them is a security change, not a
convenience change, and it needs §38.5's separate-origin rule to already be in place.

**Storage keys are server-generated.** `workspaces/{workspaceId}/assets/{uuid}` plus the extension.
The user's file name is stored in `file_assets.name` for display and **never** used to build a path —
path traversal in an object key is the same bug it is on a filesystem.

### 38.7 Rate limiting, per endpoint class

Redis token buckets. The key is `rl:{class}:{subject}`, where `subject` is the user id for an
authenticated call and the client IP for an unauthenticated one. Every refusal is `429` with
`retryAfterSeconds` and **`isRetryable: true` set explicitly** (canon §4.2 — `validation` defaults to
`false`, and this is the documented exception).

| Class | Endpoints | Limit (RECOMMENDATION) | Key | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `auth` | E-001, E-003, E-019 | 10 / 15 min per IP **and** per email | IP + email | `AUTH_RATE_LIMITED` |
| `secret-read` | E-103, E-104 | 20 / hour per user per secret document; 60 / hour per user | user | `SECRET_REVEAL_RATE_LIMITED` |
| `secret-write` | E-102 | 30 / hour per user | user | `RATE_LIMITED` |
| `write` | every `POST`/`PATCH`/`PUT`/`DELETE` not listed elsewhere | 600 / min per user | user | `RATE_LIMITED` |
| `read` | every `GET` | 3 000 / min per user | user | `RATE_LIMITED` |
| `search` | E-035, E-069, E-133 | 60 / min per user | user | `RATE_LIMITED` |
| `upload-presign` | E-110 | 120 / hour per user; **10 concurrent `pending` uploads** (`uploads_actor_idx`) | user | `RATE_LIMITED` |
| `bulk-import-export` | E-074…E-077, E-085, E-086 | 20 / hour per user; 1 concurrent import per board | user + board | `RATE_LIMITED` |
| `link-unfurl` | E-118 | 30 / min per user | user | `RATE_LIMITED` |
| `realtime` | E-138 | 10 connections per user per workspace; 5 handshakes / min | user | `RATE_LIMITED` |
| `audit-export` | E-137 | 5 / hour per workspace | workspace | `RATE_LIMITED` |

Three notes. The `search` class is separate because E-133 fans out across every visible board and is
the most expensive read in the product. The `secret-read` bucket is **per secret document as well as
per user**, so enumerating one vault is throttled even by somebody with a generous global budget —
and a throttled attempt **is still audited** (§36.8), because a refusal nobody can see is not a
control. And the `429` from `auth` must not distinguish "no such user" from "wrong password"; both
are `AUTH_INVALID_CREDENTIALS`, same message.

**SSRF is a rate-limit-adjacent control for E-118 `POST /links/resolve`** and canon states it: server-side
fetch only, **private, loopback and link-local ranges blocked** (`LINK_TARGET_BLOCKED`), redirects
followed at most twice and re-checked at each hop, response size capped, short timeout, and the result
cached by normalised URL. Resolve DNS **and check the resolved address**, not just the hostname — a
hostname that resolves to `169.254.169.254` is the whole attack.

### 38.8 Input validation at the boundary

**Schema validation runs before the handler**, on the parsed body, the path parameters and the query
string. A failure is `VALIDATION_FAILED` (400) with `fields: FieldError[]`; the user-facing sentence
is still `error.message` (canon §6.2). Unknown properties are **stripped**, not rejected — a client
that sends a field a newer server added must not break.

**The server-owned fields — stripped from every request body, always.** Sending one is not an error;
it is simply ignored. This is C-09 made concrete.

| Field | Where it really comes from |
| --- | --- |
| `id`, `createdAt`, `updatedAt`, `createdBy`, `updatedBy` | the server |
| `revision`, `version`, `sequence`, `displayId` | the server's counters (§37.1, §37.3) |
| `boardId`, `workspaceId`, `nodeId` on a nested resource | the path |
| `role`, `previewAs` beyond a narrowing, `userId`, `recipientId`, `actor` | the session (C-09, OQ-19, OQ-20) |
| `ip` | the socket (`src/services/audit-service.ts:280-285`) |
| `mentionedUserIds` | parsed server-side from the body text (canon E-120) |
| `lockedBy` | the session (OQ-60) |
| `url`, `thumbnailUrl` on any attachment | minted per response (OQ-75) |
| `canView` and any other permission input | resolved server-side (OQ-18 — `listFiles` takes `canView` from the caller today, `src/services/file-service.ts:105-113`) |
| `isShared`, `isFavorite`, `children`, `blockCount`, `excerpt`, `itemCount`, `openCount` | derived (canon §1.3.1) |

**Validation rules that are business rules, not shape checks** — each has its own reason code:

- `rowIdPrefix` matches `^[A-Z]{1,6}$` → `ROW_ID_PREFIX_INVALID` (`normalizePrefix`,
  `src/lib/row-id.ts:18-20`).
- A select option id of `"__empty__"` → `OPTION_ID_RESERVED` (`src/lib/transition-rules.ts:28`).
- A date-only cell is `YYYY-MM-DD` and **is never parsed through UTC** → `DATE_VALUE_INVALID`
  (C-04; `src/lib/calendar.ts:1-24` — *"A due date is a square on a calendar, not a moment"*). A
  timestamp cell is ISO 8601. Which one applies is decided by the column's `DateConfig.includesTime`,
  never guessed from the string.
- `CellValue.kind` must be a `ColumnType` member → `CELL_VALUE_KIND_INVALID`. It **may legitimately
  disagree with its column's `type`** after a conversion and must not be normalised away
  (canon §2.5).
- `config` must match the branch named by `type` → `COLUMN_TYPE_CONFIG_MISMATCH`.
- `ConditionGroup` nesting and size caps → `CONDITION_TREE_TOO_DEEP` (OQ-38).
- `secretIds` requires `minItems: 1` → `SECRET_SELECTION_EMPTY`. **An empty array must never mean
  "every secret"** — that is the unsafe wire default OQ-66 exists to remove
  (`src/services/devtools-service.ts:430-434`).
- Secret keys: non-empty after trim, and free of whitespace, `=`, `"` and `'` → `SECRET_KEY_INVALID`,
  because the copy-all output is `.env` syntax.
- `GanttZoom` accepts the legacy `"day"` on read **and** on write and coerces it to `"week"`; it never
  rejects it (canon §2.6). A Postgres enum that refuses `'day'` needs a data migration first.
- Body size → `REQUEST_TOO_LARGE` (413). Document block count / byte ceiling → `DOCUMENT_TOO_LARGE`
  (OQ-58). Import rows → `IMPORT_ROW_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` (`IMPORT_MAX_ROWS = 5000`).
- Every `limit` is clamped to a server cap from `GET /config`; an unbounded list is a spec defect
  (canon §6.3).

**Cursors are opaque and must be verified, not merely parsed.** A cursor is a base64 of the sort-key
tuple, and *"a client must never construct or parse one"* (canon §6.3). Sign it: `HMAC(secret, tuple ‖
queryFingerprint)`, where the fingerprint covers the filters the cursor was issued for. An
unverifiable or mismatched cursor is `VALIDATION_FAILED`, never a silently different page. Without the
signature, a cursor is an unvalidated tuple that goes straight into a `WHERE (position, id) > (…)`
comparison.

### 38.9 Parameterised queries

**Every value is bound. No exceptions, no string interpolation, no "it's only an integer".** Two
places in this system genuinely tempt dynamic SQL, and both have a rule:

1. **The audit search filter (E-136).** `matchesSearch` spans six fields including the IP
   (`src/lib/audit.ts:67-79`). The server-side form is a single `@@ websearch_to_tsquery('simple', $1)`
   against `audit_events_search_idx`. The user's text is **the bound parameter**, never concatenated
   into the tsquery.
2. **Sorting and filtering a board by a user-named column.** `ViewSort.columnId` and
   `ViewFilter.columnId` are ids the caller supplies. They are **identifiers, and identifiers cannot
   be bound**. The rule: resolve the id against `board_columns` for this board *first*, and use the
   resolved column's known `type` to pick from a fixed, code-level set of SQL fragments. The caller's
   string never reaches the query — only the branch it selected does. Same for `SortDirection`, which
   is a two-member enum mapped to a literal `ASC` / `DESC` by a lookup, not by interpolation.

**JSONB paths are built with functions, not strings.** `cells -> $1 ->> 'value'` with `$1` bound, or
`jsonb_extract_path_text(cells, $1, 'value')`. Never `cells #>> '{" + columnId + ",value}'` — a JSONB
path literal is a string, and a string built from input is an injection surface whether or not it is
SQL.

**Table and column names are never taken from input.** The dynamic-looking endpoints — E-057 column
conversion, E-084/E-085 import mapping, E-086 export scope — all operate on `cells` JSONB and on rows,
not on schema objects. Nothing in this API issues DDL at request time.

### 38.10 XSS and stored content

**The model: store raw, escape at render, never store HTML.** Two content types matter.

**Comment bodies.** Stored as raw text with mentions encoded as `@[Mai Tran](usr_mai)` and record
references as bare `TASK-042` (`src/lib/mentions.ts:12-16`, `src/lib/row-id.ts:29`). The parser
produces a `BodySegment[]` discriminated union — `text` / `mention` / `record` — which the renderer
maps to elements (`src/types/collab.ts:69-72`). **The body is never HTML and is never rendered as
HTML.** Three server rules follow:

- Store the trimmed body verbatim. Do **not** sanitise it into a different string: the body is the
  thing the author typed, `isEdited` is derived from it changing, and a silent rewrite would set that
  flag for nobody.
- `body_plain` — written in the same statement, used by the search index and the notification preview
  — is `plainBody(body)`, mention tokens flattened to `@Name`. It is plain text by construction.
- **Notification `title` and `body` are pre-rendered plain text** (canon T-35) with the label frozen at
  creation (OQ-79). They are the one place the server produces display strings, and they must be
  produced by concatenating known-safe pieces, never by templating raw user input into markup.

**Document blocks.** `Block` is a discriminated union of 14 types over 9 interfaces
(`src/types/document.ts:4-18`). The payload must match the type or `BLOCK_TYPE_PAYLOAD_MISMATCH`
(400). Three block types carry an attack surface and get an explicit rule:

- `LinkBlock` and `EmbedBlock` URLs: **the scheme must be `http` or `https`**. Reject `javascript:`,
  `data:`, `vbscript:`, `file:` at write time with `LINK_URL_INVALID`. `normalize` in the frontend
  prepends `https://` to a bare host and requires a dot in the hostname
  (`src/services/link-service.ts:38-50`) — the server reproduces that and adds the scheme allow-list,
  because the frontend's version would happily accept `javascript://x.y/…`.
- `ImageBlock` and `AttachmentBlock` carry an `assetId`, never a URL (OQ-75). An `ImageBlock` whose
  source is an arbitrary URL is both an XSS vector and a tracking pixel.
- `CodeBlock` content is text with a `CodeLanguage` tag from a closed 8-member enum. The language
  selects a highlighter; it never selects a renderer.

**Two more surfaces that are easy to miss:**

- **File names in headers.** `file_assets.name` is user input. Encode it into `Content-Disposition`
  with RFC 5987 `filename*=UTF-8''…` and strip CR, LF and `"` before it goes anywhere near a header —
  an unencoded newline in a header is response splitting.
- **Spreadsheet formula injection on export (E-086).** A cell whose text begins with `=`, `+`, `-`,
  `@`, tab or CR is executed as a formula by Excel and Sheets when the exported file is opened.
  `src/lib/csv.ts` is a correct RFC 4180 writer and does **not** guard against this, because it never
  had to — the file was generated in the user's own browser from data they already had. **The moment
  export moves server-side (OQ-42), the exported value must be prefixed with `'` — for `.csv`, `.tsv`
  and `.xlsx` alike.** A board is a place where one user types a value another user exports.

### 38.11 Search permission filtering

**The permission funnel runs before scanning, not after** (canon E-133). The frontend states the
principle and the reason: *"Everything searchable is reachable from the drive tree, so permission is
applied once — at the node — and every result kind inherits it: a record inside a board you cannot
open is never scanned, and a comment on it is never returned."*
(`src/services/search-service.ts:26-32`).

**The shape of the query, mandatory:**

1. Resolve the visible node-id set once: `collectAllowed(tree, node => !node.isTrashed &&
   capabilitiesFor({ role, user, node }).view)` — **subtree-wide pruning**
   (`src/services/search-service.ts:60-67`).
2. Every group's query then carries `… AND <table>.<node column> = ANY($visible)`:
   `nodes.id`, `board_rows.board_id → boards.node_id`, `documents.node_id`,
   `comments.target_node_id`.
3. Rank, group and cap **after** the filter. `SEARCH_GROUP_LIMIT = 5` per group, so one noisy board
   cannot crowd out a kind (`src/config/app.ts:31`, `src/lib/search-index.ts:69-97`).

**Filtering after ranking is a leak even when the results are correct**, because the group counts, the
score distribution and the "in Drive" fallback all become oracles for content the caller cannot see.
Same rule for the snippet: `snippetAround` must only ever run over text from a row that survived
step 2.

**Three related rules.** `role` and `user` are **request parameters on search today** (OQ-20,
`src/services/search-service.ts:45-50`) and must come from the session. E-035 drive quick-find applies
the same funnel with a cheaper matcher (OQ-94). And E-134 My Work and E-135 the dashboard are the same
shape — five readings of one record set, *"so a board they lose access to disappears from all five at
once"* (`src/services/my-work-service.ts:18-25`).

### 38.12 The no-secret-logging rule

**A secret value never leaves the process that decrypted it, except in the body of the response to the
reveal that was permitted, audited and rate-limited.** Not in a log line, not in an error message, not
in an exception's `detail`, not in a stack trace, not in an APM span attribute, not in a metrics label,
not in a database statement log, not in a crash dump, not in a test fixture.

Four concrete controls:

1. **Type the plaintext so it cannot be logged by accident.** The decrypted value is carried in a
   wrapper whose `toString()`, `toJSON()` and inspect hook all return `"[redacted]"`, and it is
   unwrapped exactly once, at the point of serialising the reveal response.
2. **`INTERNAL_ERROR`'s `detail` carries the original message in non-production only** (canon §4.3).
   In production the user gets *"Something went wrong"* and the detail goes to the server log — which
   means the server log is the place a leaked value would land, and is why control 1 exists.
3. **Statement logging must not log parameters** on any connection that touches `secrets`. If
   `log_min_duration_statement` is on, `log_parameter_max_length = 0`.
4. **The `secret_access_events` and `audit_events` rows record the key, never the value.** The
   frontend's fixture detail is the right register: *"Revealed once and cleared after 30 seconds."*
   (`src/services/audit-service.ts:50-54`).

### 38.13 What must never appear in a log line

Applies to application logs, access logs, error trackers, APM spans, metrics labels and audit `detail`
alike. The request id is what ties a line to a user; almost nothing else needs to.

| Never logged | Why | Log instead |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A secret value, plaintext or ciphertext | §38.12 | `secretId`, `key` |
| A KMS data key, wrapped or unwrapped | It is the whole vault | the `dek_version` integer |
| A session token, refresh token, invitation token, or their hashes | A hash in a log is still a lookup key into `user_sessions` / `workspace_invitations` | `sessionId`, `familyId`, `invitationId` |
| A signed URL, or its `X-Amz-Signature` / query string | It is a bearer credential for its whole TTL (§38.5) | `assetId`, `storageKey` |
| A password, in any form, at any stage | — | nothing |
| Cell values, comment bodies, document block content, config file content | Permission-bearing content. A log aggregator has no ACL for a restricted folder | `rowId`, `columnId`, `commentId`, `nodeId`, and counts |
| The **name** of a node the caller was denied | *"A refusal is not a place to describe the access-control graph to somebody outside it"* (`src/services/authz.ts:60-66`, `:150-158`) | `nodeId` and the `PermissionKey` that was missing |
| A user's email address, outside the auth flow's own audit row | It is the login identifier and a personal identifier | `userId` |
| Full `Authorization` / `Cookie` headers, and `Idempotency-Key` | — | the presence of the header |
| Raw request bodies on `POST /auth/login`, `PUT /nodes/{nodeId}/secrets`, `POST /links/resolve` | Credentials, secrets, and a URL that may itself be a capability | the endpoint, the outcome, the reason code |
| A file's bytes, or the sniffed first 4 KB | It is the file | `assetId`, detected type, size |
| `AuditContext` | It is the internal payload the API deliberately never returns (OQ-25) | the `auditEventId` |

**Always safe, and always worth logging:** `requestId`, `userId`, `workspaceId`, the resource id, the
endpoint id (`E-066`), the `ErrorReason`, the HTTP status, the duration, the row counts, and the
`Idempotency-Key`'s **presence**. That set is enough to reconstruct any incident in this system, and
none of it is a credential.

---

### Chapter notes — divergences, decisions and traps

These are places where I followed canon or an existing chapter that I believe needs one correction,
plus the drift I found between chapters. None of it changed what I wrote.

1. **`search_vector` vs `search_tsv` — pick one name.** The full-text column is called
   `search_vector` on `nodes` (part 3, §4.x indexes), `board_rows` (part 4, §4.16) and `documents`
   (part 6), and `search_tsv` on `comments` (part 5) and again in part 2's summary table for `nodes`.
   I used each chapter's own name in §35.2 so no chapter is contradicted, and §35.6 lists them
   together. **Recommendation: `search_vector` everywhere**, and one line in part 5.

2. **`secrets` foreign key column — `node_id` or `secret_document_id`?** Part 6 (the dedicated schema
   chapter) uses `secrets.node_id` and `UNIQUE (node_id, key)`; part 2 §5.5.1 uses
   `secret_document_id` and `UNIQUE (secret_document_id, key)`. They are the same column —
   `secret_documents`' primary key **is** `node_id` — but the two names will not merge cleanly. I
   followed part 6. The same drift affects `secret_rotations` and `secret_access_events`.

3. **`config_versions` — part 2 and part 6 disagree about a unique constraint.** Part 2 §5.5.1 says
   there is deliberately **no** `UNIQUE (node_id, version)` *"because a folded autosave rewrites the
   head at the same number"*; part 6 declares `UNIQUE (node_id, version DESC)`. Both are reconcilable
   and part 6 is right: an autosave fold is an `UPDATE` of the head row, not an `INSERT` at the same
   number, so uniqueness holds and is worth having. I listed the unique index and said why in §35.2.6.

4. **The brief for §35 named `notifications(user_id, read_at, created_at)`, `audit_logs`, `favorites`
   and `row_relations`.** Canon's names are `notifications.recipient_id`, `audit_events` with an `at`
   column, `node_favorites` and `board_row_relations`. §35.3 maps every one of them, and I built the
   canonical names.

5. **`NodeState` cannot be indexed.** The brief asked for `nodes(parent_id, state)`. `NodeState` is
   derived and explicitly never a stored column (canon §2.4), so I replaced it with the four partial
   indexes its four values actually reduce to. If a future chapter is tempted to materialise `state`
   as a column to make that index possible, note that `frozen` depends on an **ancestor**, so the
   column would have to be maintained across a subtree on every archive — which is precisely why it
   is derived.

6. **`ConflictNotice` granularity is per row, not per cell** (§37.2). This produces a notice for two
   users editing *different* columns of the same row. It is what the frontend implements
   (`baseRevisions: Record<rowId, number>`) and I documented it as intended rather than as a defect,
   but it is the kind of thing a reviewer will read as a bug. The message text — *"your edit was
   kept"* — is what makes it defensible.

7. **§37.3's `current` field on the 409 body is a genuine addition** to the error envelope, raised
   under OQ-57 with the four-part block. It is additive and the frontend ignores unknown keys today,
   but if the editor would rather the envelope stay exactly as canon §6.2 declares it, the fallback is
   one extra `GET` after every conflicted document save.

8. **The board-level schema lock in §36.12 and §37.9 is mine.** Canon and part 4 establish a
   `FOR UPDATE` on the *column* row for option creation (part 4, §4.13) and on the *board* row for the
   sequence counter (§4.11.1); I generalised the board-row lock to cover every schema write, so a
   column delete and a column reorder cannot interleave. It reuses a lock those endpoints already
   take for the counter, so it costs nothing new, but it is a decision rather than a citation.

9. **Spreadsheet formula injection on export (§38.10) has no OQ id** and is not mentioned anywhere in
   the frontend, because export is generated client-side today from data the user already has
   (`src/lib/csv.ts`, `src/lib/xlsx.ts`). It becomes a real issue the moment E-086 generates the file
   server-side, which is OQ-42's subject. If the editor wants it tracked, it belongs as a line under
   OQ-42 rather than as a new id.

10. **Rate-limit numbers in §38.7 are RECOMMENDATIONS with no frontend grounding whatsoever.** The
    frontend has exactly two rate-limit-shaped facts: canon says E-103 is *"rate-limited per user"*
    and the error registry has `AUTH_RATE_LIMITED` and `SECRET_REVEAL_RATE_LIMITED`. Everything else
    in that table is a starting point to be tuned against real traffic, and the endpoint **classes**
    are the durable part, not the numbers.

---

## 39. Backend Implementation Order

This section does not rank features by appeal. It reads the dependency graph that already exists in
the frontend — foreign keys that cannot be written, gates that cannot answer, screens that cannot
mount — and turns it into a build order. Everything here is a **RECOMMENDATION** about *sequence*;
every module, table, endpoint and priority band it schedules is settled elsewhere (canon §1, §3;
part 1 §2.3) and is reproduced, not re-decided.

Three constraints produce the order, in descending hardness:

| # | Constraint | The test |
| --- | --- | --- |
| O-1 | **A table cannot be created before the table its foreign keys point at.** | Can you run the `CREATE TABLE` at all? |
| O-2 | **An endpoint cannot be gated before `authorize()` can answer.** Every write re-checks its `PermissionKey` server-side; the frontend gate "is not security" (`src/lib/permissions/evaluate.ts:24-25`). | Can you serve a *correct* response, or only a permissive one? |
| O-3 | **A frontend screen is dark until every endpoint it mounts against exists.** | Does the route render, degrade honestly, or throw? |

O-1 and O-2 are absolute. O-3 is what decides the order among the things O-1 and O-2 leave free, and
it is why `insights` — a P1 module — lands before `files`, `devtools` and `collab`: `/` redirects to
`/dashboard` (`src/app/(workspace)/page.tsx`), so the landing route is the app's first impression.

---

### How to read the graph

| Edge | Means | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `A --> B` (solid) | **A must exist before B.** Either B holds a column referencing a table A owns, or B cannot answer a request correctly without calling into A. | `drive --> boards`: `boards.node_id` is `UNIQUE NOT NULL` referencing `nodes` (canon T-10, OQ-30 position), and `seedFromNode` resolves the node before a board exists at all (`src/services/board-service.ts:83-98`). |
| `A -.-> B` (dashed) | **B ships without A and degrades honestly.** The dashed edge names what stays empty until A lands. | `collab -.-> files`: `comment_attachments` (T-30) is the one file table whose FK target does not exist until `collab` ships, so it waits for Phase 6. |

**Two edges are deliberately not drawn.**

- **Every module writes `audit_events` (T-36).** "Rows are written by the endpoint that performs the
  action, inside its transaction" (canon §3.23; `src/services/audit-service.ts:14-20`). That is a
  *write* dependency on a table that exists from Phase 1, not a build-order dependency, and drawing
  twelve arrows back to `governance` would hide the graph's real shape.
- **Every module emits realtime frames.** Frames are published **after commit** (part 17 §36, T-02),
  unknown frame types are ignored by the client (`src/types/realtime.ts:14`), and
  `REALTIME_ENDPOINT` is `null` today (`src/config/app.ts:65-69`) — so every module ships before its
  frames and gains them later without a client release.

```mermaid
graph TD
    subgraph PH0["Phase 0 — session and tenancy"]
        identity["identity<br/>P0"]
        workspace["workspace<br/>P0"]
    end

    subgraph PH1["Phase 1 — the tree and the gate"]
        drive["drive<br/>P0"]
        governance["governance<br/>P0"]
        rt05["realtime · RT-05 only<br/>P0"]
    end

    subgraph PH2["Phase 2 — the board engine"]
        templates["templates · built-ins<br/>P0"]
        boards["boards<br/>P0"]
        views["views<br/>P0"]
    end

    subgraph PH3["Phase 3 — pages"]
        documents["documents<br/>P0"]
    end

    subgraph PH4["Phase 4 — the landing screen"]
        insights["insights<br/>P1"]
    end

    subgraph PH5["Phase 5 — bytes"]
        files["files<br/>P1"]
    end

    subgraph PH6["Phase 6 — collaboration"]
        collab["collab<br/>P1"]
        rtfull["realtime · RT-01…RT-04, RT-06…RT-11<br/>P1"]
    end

    subgraph PH7["Phase 7 — dev tools"]
        devtools["devtools<br/>P1"]
    end

    subgraph PH8["Phase 8 — bulk, trash, import, export"]
        system["system<br/>P1"]
    end

    subgraph PH9["Phase 9 — finding and linking"]
        search["search<br/>P1"]
        relations["relations<br/>P2"]
        usertpl["templates · user-authored<br/>P2"]
    end

    identity --> workspace
    identity --> governance
    identity --> collab
    identity --> insights

    workspace --> drive
    workspace --> governance
    workspace --> templates
    workspace --> files
    workspace --> rt05

    drive --> governance
    governance -.-> drive
    drive --> boards
    drive --> documents
    drive --> devtools
    drive --> files
    drive --> collab
    drive --> system
    drive --> search

    governance --> boards
    governance --> devtools
    governance --> files
    governance --> rt05
    governance --> search

    templates --> boards
    boards --> views
    boards --> insights
    boards --> files
    boards --> collab
    boards --> system
    boards --> search
    boards --> relations
    boards --> usertpl
    views --> system

    documents --> files
    documents --> system
    devtools --> system

    collab --> search
    collab -.->|T-30 comment_attachments| files
    collab -.->|the mentioned widget| insights
    collab --> rtfull
    boards --> rtfull
```

**The one real cycle is `drive` ⇄ `governance`, and it is a read-time cycle, not a schema cycle.**
`access_rules.node_id` references `nodes` — that is the hard direction, and it is why `nodes` is
created first. The other direction is a *read*: the tree endpoint is pruned by visibility **before**
it is returned (`visibleTree`, `src/lib/permissions/visibility.ts:197-240` — "no surface asks 'may I
show this', because what it was handed is already the answer"). Both live in Phase 1 and ship as one
milestone. Part 1 §2.3 states the same conclusion for the whole P0 band: "the eight P0 entries are
not eight milestones — they are one."

**The one edge whose direction the backend reverses.** In the frontend, `devtools-service.ts` imports
`ENVIRONMENT_OPTIONS` from `src/lib/board-templates.ts:28-37` — the deployment-label list DV-ENV-21
lives beside the board templates that use it. In the backend the owner is `environments` (T-26,
canon OQ-63 position), and a template's Environment column is an ordinary `select` column whose
options are copied verbatim out of the template's JSONB at instantiation (part 17 §36.2 step 5), so
it needs nothing from `devtools`. `environments` is therefore created in **Phase 0** — it has no
dependency beyond `workspaces`, and `POST /workspaces` seeds its three rows in the same transaction
(part 17 §36.1 step 3). Its endpoints (E-106 – E-109) wait for Phase 7, where something finally
reads them.

---

### The phased build order

| Phase | Modules | Depends on | Unblocks (FE screens) | Priority |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **0** | `identity`, `workspace` | — | Sign-in. `WorkspaceGuard` stops refusing (`src/components/workspace/workspace-guard.tsx:10-27`). `WorkspaceSwitcher`, `UserMenu`, `WorkspaceSettingsDialog` → General / Members / Danger zone, `InviteMemberDialog`, `StorageMeter` (reads `0 B`). | **P0** |
| **1** | `drive`, `governance`, `realtime` (RT-05 only) | 0 | `/drive` and every nested route, `AppSidebar` + `TreePanel`, `BreadcrumbNav`, `DriveView` / `DriveGrid` / `DriveList`, `RenameDialog`, `NodeDetail`, `/favorites`, `/archive`, `NodeAccessDialog` + `AccessList`, `PermissionDialog` + `RoleMatrix`, `RolePreviewBanner`, `WorkspaceRestrictedTab`, `/audit`. `useAccessSync` starts working. | **P0** |
| **2** | `templates` (built-ins), `boards`, `views`, `realtime` (RT-06 … RT-10) | 1 | `BoardPage` and every view: `TableGrid`, `KanbanBoard`, `CalendarBoard`, `GanttBoard`. `RowDrawer` + `ActivityTimeline` + `SubtaskPanel`. `ViewTabs`, `ViewConfigBar`, `FilterMenu`, `SortMenu`, `GroupMenu`, `DateMenu`. `ColumnMenu`, `ConvertColumnDialog`, `SelectColumnDialog`, `TransitionRulesEditor`, `ConditionBuilder`, `StepNumberingDialog`, `ApiDuplicateBanner`. | **P0** |
