#### Chapter notes — divergences, decisions and traps

1. **A new open question is proposed as OQ-105.** §39's closing block ("when a URL path resolves to a
   node the caller may not see, does the API tell them *something* is there?") has no canon id.
   Canon §8 ends at OQ-101; part 9 has claimed OQ-102 and part 12 cites it. **OQ-105** was chosen to
   leave OQ-103 and OQ-104 free for parts still in flight. If the editor prefers a different number,
   the only text to change is the heading of that block and the cross-reference from §39.1.2 step 10.

2. **Canon §4.2 and `src/hooks/use-drive-location.ts:56` are in genuine tension and this chapter
   follows canon.** The frontend ships a distinct "You don't have access to this item" screen for a
   path that resolves in the full tree but not the pruned one. A real API serves only the pruned tree,
   so that screen becomes unreachable and `isDenied` becomes dead code. This is a **client-visible
   behaviour change** and should be flagged to product rather than discovered in QA.

3. **§39 reproduces part 1 §2.3's P0/P1/P2 bands verbatim and adds only the phase column.** If those
   bands move, §39's register and the phase table both need the same edit. Three entries in the
   register are finer-grained than §2.3's module rows — `templates` split into built-ins (P0) and
   user-authored (P2), `relations` split into the write side (Phase 2) and the read side (Phase 9),
   and `board_view_preferences` / E-083 called out as the P2 endpoint of a P0 module — but none of
   them contradicts §2.3; they refine it.

4. **Two schedule decisions are mine and are worth a second opinion.**
   (a) `environments` (T-26) is created in **Phase 0**, not with the rest of `devtools`, because part
   17 §36.1 seeds three rows inside `POST /workspaces`. The alternative is a backfill migration in
   Phase 7. (b) **E-135 ships as a zeroed stub in Phase 1** so `/` → `/dashboard` renders
   `OnboardingPanel` rather than an error panel from the first deploy. Both are cheap; both are
   reversible; neither changes a contract.

5. **§39.1.6 and part 12 §24.10 both diagram a QA/QC import, at different altitudes.** §24.10 shows
   the wizard's four steps and the full statement list; §39.1.6 shows the five gates and the
   transaction boundary and defers to §24.10 for the rest. They agree on every fact — the same
   template columns, the same re-plan-under-lock rule, the same create-then-delete-then-insert order,
   the same two frames. If either moves, they must move together. The same applies to §39.1.3 and
   part 9 §18.5, and to §39.1.5 and part 10 §21.2.

6. **§39.1's gate table is a condensation of the governance chapter's `authorize()` pseudocode.** It
   is reproduced here so the seven flows can say "Gate 2" without re-deriving it. If the governance
   chapter renumbers or merges gates, this table is the second place that needs the edit.

7. **One canon statement is quoted with a qualification, and the qualification is part 9's.** Canon
   §3.8 says E-066 is "always `200`… never `409`". §39.1.3 reads that as governing *concurrency*
   only, because canon §4.3 registers `TRANSITION_NOT_ALLOWED` and `OPTION_UNAVAILABLE` as `409`
   under E-066's own module, and part 9 §18.5 reaches the same reading. If canon means "never 409
   under any circumstances", then §39.1.3, part 9 §18.5 and canon §4.3 all need the same correction —
   not just this one.

8. **Two line citations were corrected against the real source and canon still carries the old
   ones.** Canon §2.9 cites the `task` template's "Blocked by" relation column at
   `src/lib/board-templates.ts:188`; it is at **`:192`** (line 188 is `col_due`). And the `qa`
   template referenced throughout §39.1.6 is at `src/lib/board-templates.ts:281-339`. Neither changes
   a decision — only the pointer. Worth a one-character fix in canon so the next writer following the
   citation lands on the relation column.

## 40. Open Questions

Every block below marks a place where **the frontend does not settle a business rule**. The
specification took a position anyway — it had to, or nineteen chapters could not agree — but a
position is not an answer, and the difference is what this section exists to make visible.

The ids are the ones reserved in canon §8. They are stable: cite them, never renumber them. The
eight audit fact sheets each numbered their own questions from `OQ-01`; those local numbers are
dead, and canon's `Raised in` column is the only map between them.

### How to read a block

| Field | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| **Current evidence** | What the frontend and the PRD actually show, cited `path:line`. Nothing inferred. |
| **Unclear** | The precise question a human has to answer. One sentence, answerable yes/no or A/B. |
| **Recommendation** | What this document does, and why. Where canon §8.8 already took a position, this restates it — a chapter may expand a position, never contradict one. |
| **Impact if wrong** | What has to be rewritten if the answer is the other one. Schema, endpoint contract, or frontend change — named. |
| **Blocks** | The phase and module that cannot be *finished* until this is answered. Many questions do not block a start; they block a sign-off. |

The metadata line on each block reads **Severity · Module · Status**. Severity is canon's, unchanged.
`Module` is one of the sixteen in canon C-14. `Status` is one of:

| Status | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Position taken** | Canon §8.8 decided it. Build to that. Confirmation is still owed, but work can proceed. |
| **Position taken here** | No canon position; this document takes one and names it. Same rule: build to it, confirm later. |
| **Answer required** | No safe default exists. Building either way risks a rewrite that is not mechanical. |

### Build phases used in the "Blocks" field

| Phase | Covers | Sections |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **P0 Foundation** | identity, sessions, workspaces, membership, the `nodes` tree, access rules, capabilities | §4 (`users` … `access_rules`), §8, §9–§11, §28 |
| **P1 Boards** | board aggregate, columns, cells, rows, subtasks, relations, views, filters | §13–§19 |
| **P2 Content** | pages and blocks, versions, config documents, secrets, files and uploads | §12, §21–§23 |
| **P3 Collaboration** | comments, mentions, watches, notifications, My Work, search, dashboard | §20, §25–§27 |
| **P4 System** | import/export, trash and archive lifecycle, audit, realtime, quota | §24, §29, §30, §36–§38 |

A question that blocks P0 blocks everything after it. That is why the eleven **blocking** and
**critical** entries in §40.12 are the only list a project manager needs from this section.

### 40.1 Identity, tenancy and plans

#### OQ-01 — There is no authentication, session or token model anywhere in the frontend

**Severity** blocking · **Module** identity · **Status** Position taken (canon §8.8; built out in §8)

**Current evidence** — The signed-in user is a module-level constant:
`CURRENT_USER = { id: "usr_khanh", name: "Khanh Luu", email: "khanhluu95@gmail.com", … }`
(`src/mock/users.ts:3-9`), imported by every store, every service and fourteen hooks. The permission
guard resolves the caller from it rather than from a request:
`contextFor` reads `CURRENT_USER.id` directly (`src/services/authz.ts:44`), and the module's own
header says why — *"A role the client sends is a claim, not a fact… The honest caveat: there is no
server here"* (`src/services/authz.ts:24-32`). There is no login route among the thirteen in the
`(workspace)` group; the Sign out menu item has no handler
(`src/components/layout/header/user-menu.tsx:61-64`); nothing but `nexdrop-recent`,
`nexdrop-comment-draft:<key>` and `nexdrop-theme` is persisted in the browser; `AsyncState` has four
states and none of them is "signed out" (`src/types/async.ts:23-27`); and `src/types/` contains no
credential, session, token or identity-provider type. Two facts do exist and constrain the design:
the seeded audit trail already names a successful sign-in
`system.session.start` with `severity: "info"` and `target: null`
(`src/services/audit-service.ts:238-247`), and the IP on an audit row is explicitly the server's to
stamp — *"A real backend reads it off the socket — the client must never send one"*
(`src/services/audit-service.ts:280-285`). The PRD covers no authentication feature at all
(`PRD_FSD_All_in_One_Workspace_45_Detailed.md`, features 1–45).

**Unclear** — Which authentication mechanism does the product use: email + password owned by this
service, an external identity provider (SSO/OIDC), or both; and is the session a cookie-borne
opaque session or a bearer JWT the client stores?

**Recommendation** — Email + password, Argon2id, with a short-lived access token and a rotating
refresh-token family in `user_sessions` (T-02), both carried in `httpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax`
cookies. Identity, role, IP and clock come from the session and the socket, never from a body
(canon C-09). No SSO in the first release: `SY-POS-45` does not scope it, and adding an OIDC
provider later is a new row in `user_sessions` plus a callback route, not a schema change. The
reason to prefer cookies over a client-stored JWT is `SY-RBC-42`'s explicit requirement that a role
downgrade *"takes effect on open screens"* — a self-contained bearer token cannot be narrowed
mid-flight, so authorisation must be re-resolved server-side on every request against
`workspace_members` and `access_rules` (which §28 does) and the token must be short enough that a
revoked session dies quickly.

**Impact if wrong** — Contained but wide. If the answer is SSO-only, `users.password_hash` and the
whole `/auth/login` + `/auth/refresh` pair (E-001, E-003) are deleted and replaced by an
authorisation-code callback; `user_sessions` survives unchanged, and so does every other table. If
the answer is a client-stored bearer JWT, the cookie handling in §8 is replaced and the
downgrade-on-open-screens requirement has to be met some other way (short TTL plus a deny-list),
which is strictly more machinery. **Nothing in the domain schema depends on the choice**, which is
why this is blocking-but-cheap: it blocks starting, not rewriting.

**Blocks** — **P0 Foundation, in its entirety.** Every endpoint's permission check, every
`created_by`/`updated_by` column, and every audit row is unattributable until a caller identity
exists. §28's permission model is a specification of a check that has nobody to check.

---

#### OQ-02 — Is there a tenant above the workspace, and who owns a workspace?

**Severity** med · **Module** workspace · **Status** Position taken (canon §8.8)

**Current evidence** — `Workspace.slug` is documented as *"URL-safe identifier, unique across the
tenant"* (`src/types/workspace.ts:17`), but no tenant or organisation type exists anywhere in
`src/types/`. `Workspace` has no `createdAt`, no `updatedAt` and no owner field
(`src/types/workspace.ts:6-24`). There is no `workspace.create` permission key — the catalogue has
`workspace.manage` and `workspace.delete` and nothing between them
(`src/types/permission.ts:35-38`). Creation puts the creator in as an admin in the same write:
`members: [{ ...creator, role: "admin", joinedAt }]` (`src/lib/workspace-access.ts:238`), with
the comment that a workspace whose creator is added afterwards *"has a moment where nobody can
administer it"* (`:211-218`). Membership is the only tenancy dimension the code has —
`visibleWorkspaces` filters by it (`src/lib/workspace-access.ts:44-49`) and `memberRoleOf` returns
`null` rather than a default, because *"a default here is a way in"* (`:29-35`).

**Unclear** — Is this deployment single-tenant (one `workspaces` table, globally unique slugs), or
does an organisation sit above the workspace with its own billing, member directory and slug
namespace?

**Recommendation** — Single tenant. `workspaces.slug` is globally unique; add `created_at`,
`updated_at` and `created_by` (`created_by` is the ownership attribute OQ-03 needs). Do not build an
`organizations` table: nothing in the frontend reads one, and the PRD's `WS-ARC-02` describes
"Super Admin khởi tạo Workspace" — creating a workspace, not creating a tenant that contains
workspaces.

**Impact if wrong** — Mechanical but broad. Real multi-tenancy adds `tenant_id` to `workspaces` and
to every workspace-scoped unique index (`workspaces_slug_uniq`, and the workspace-scoped uniqueness
on `environments` and `board_templates`). No FK direction reverses, no endpoint path changes except
that `/workspaces` becomes tenant-scoped. Estimate: one migration, one middleware, no rewrite.

**Blocks** — Nothing outright. It blocks **sign-off on §4 (`workspaces`) and §9 (Workspace APIs)**,
because a later `tenant_id` invalidates the unique indexes those sections declare.

---

#### OQ-03 — Is there a fifth role, "Super Admin"?

**Severity** high · **Module** governance · **Status** Position taken (canon §8.8)

**Current evidence** — The PRD contradicts itself. `WS-ARC-02` has *"Super Admin khởi tạo
Workspace"* and `SY-AUD-41` restricts the audit log to *"role Super Admin"*, while `SY-RBC-42`
specifies *"4 cấp bậc Role chuẩn"* and names Viewer, Member, Manager, Admin. The frontend ships
exactly four: `WORKSPACE_ROLES` is `["viewer", "member", "manager", "admin"]` with the comment that
*"order is the rank"* (`src/types/permission.ts:8-15`); the audit page is gated on
`workspace.audit.view`, which is in the ADMIN addition set (`src/lib/permissions/roles.ts:65-75`);
and `docs/GOVERNANCE.md` §6 lists *"No custom roles. Four roles, as specified"* as a deliberate
non-goal. The one place the code models "more than a role" is ownership, which escalates five keys
without being a role (`OWNER_ESCALATIONS`, `src/lib/permissions/roles.ts:98-108`).

**Unclear** — Does a workspace Admin get to read and export their own workspace's security audit
trail, or is that reserved for an operator role outside the tenant?

**Recommendation** — Four roles. Read "Super Admin" as the workspace's Admin, and model the creator
as an ownership attribute on the workspace row (`workspaces.created_by`, OQ-02), the same shape node
ownership already uses. If a genuine cross-workspace operator is needed, that is platform staff — a
separate authentication realm and a separate console, not a fifth member of `WorkspaceRole`.

**Impact if wrong** — Adding a fifth rank later is a migration over `workspace_members.role` and
over every `access_rules.subject_role` value, plus a re-ordering of `roleRank` that changes the
meaning of every stored rule (a rule granting "manager" means something different once a rank is
inserted above it). It also re-cuts the 39-key matrix. This is the most expensive "additive" change
in the governance model, which is why it is high and not medium.

**Blocks** — **P0 Foundation, §28 (RBAC).** The role enum is a Postgres `ENUM` whose *order* is
load-bearing; it must be right before `workspace_members` takes its first row.

#### OQ-04 — The invitation flow implied by `WorkspaceMember.joinedAt` is unmodelled

**Severity** med · **Module** workspace · **Status** Position taken (canon §8.8; E-013, E-018, E-019)

**Current evidence** — `WorkspaceMember.joinedAt` exists (`src/types/user.ts:24`) and is set at
membership creation (`src/lib/workspace-access.ts:246-256` `withMember`), but nothing produces it
except a direct add. The catalogue describes `workspace.member.manage` as *"Invite people and change
what role they hold"* (`src/lib/permissions/catalog.ts:19`) — an invitation, not an insertion. The
members tab adds a person from the in-memory directory with no email step at all
(`src/store/workspace-store.ts:362-372` `addMember`). There is no `WorkspaceInvitation` type, no
token, no expiry and no accept route among the thirteen frontend routes.

**Unclear** — Is a member invited by email link with an acceptance step, or added directly from a
directory the workspace already has (which is what the mock does)?

**Recommendation** — Email invitation. `workspace_invitations` (T-05) holds
`(id, workspace_id, email, role, token_hash, invited_by, expires_at, accepted_at)`; `POST
/workspaces/{workspaceId}/members` (E-013) returns a `WorkspaceInvitation` rather than a
`WorkspaceMember`, and `POST /invitations/{token}/accept` (E-019) creates the membership and stamps
`joined_at`. Direct-add is kept as a special case only when the invited email already belongs to an
active `users` row *and* the deployment is single-tenant — and even then the row is created through
the same code path so `joined_at` has one writer.

**Impact if wrong** — If invitations are not wanted, `workspace_invitations`, E-018 and E-019 are
dropped and E-013 returns a `WorkspaceMember`. One table, two endpoints. If they are wanted and we
skip them, `workspace.member.manage` cannot be implemented as its own catalogue text describes it.

**Blocks** — **P0 Foundation, §9 (Workspace APIs).** E-013's return type cannot be settled without
the answer, and the frontend's members tab reads the response.

#### OQ-05 — Storage quota: who maintains `usedBytes`, and what happens at 100 %?

**Severity** high · **Module** workspace · **Status** Position taken (canon §8.8)

**Current evidence** — `Workspace.storage` is `{ usedBytes, totalBytes }`
(`src/types/workspace.ts:5-10`) and the sidebar renders a meter against it, but **nothing ever
recomputes it**: `makeWorkspace` sets `storage: { usedBytes: 0, totalBytes: 15 * GIGABYTE }`
(`src/lib/workspace-access.ts:239`) and no upload path writes to it. `validateUpload` checks size,
emptiness and extension only (`src/lib/file-validation.ts:28-57`) — there is no quota branch, and no
upload is ever refused for space. The seeded notification fixtures nonetheless include *"Storage is
at 52% of the team plan"* (`src/mock/collab.ts:230`), so the product intends the meter to mean
something.

**Unclear** — Two questions, and the second is the one nobody has answered: (a) does a trashed item
still count toward the quota during its retention window, and (b) is the refusal at 100 % a hard
block on new uploads or a soft warning?

**Recommendation** — `workspaces.used_bytes BIGINT` maintained transactionally with every
`file_assets` insert and permanent delete, under `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` on the workspace row (canon
§1.4, and §37 for the lock order). Never recomputed by aggregate on read. An upload whose declared
size would exceed `total_bytes` is refused **before the presigned URL is issued** (E-110) with
`QUOTA_EXCEEDED` → `upload_failed` / **507**. Trashed items **do** count until purge — the bytes are
still stored, and telling a user they freed space they have not freed is worse than the alternative
— and `TrashEntry` already carries the information to explain it.

**Impact if wrong** — If trashed items must not count, `used_bytes` is decremented on soft delete
and re-incremented on restore, which makes restore able to fail for quota — a new error path on
E-037 that the frontend's trash UI has no branch for. If the refusal is meant to be soft, E-110 stops
returning 507 and the meter becomes advisory; that is a one-line change and cheap.

**Blocks** — **P2 Content, §21 (Attachments/uploads).** E-110's pre-flight validation cannot be
written without the rule.

#### OQ-06 — Where does `StorageQuota.totalBytes` come from?

**Severity** low · **Module** workspace · **Status** Position taken here

**Current evidence** — `WorkspacePlan` is `"free" | "team" | "enterprise"`
(`src/types/workspace.ts:3`) with **no size attached to it anywhere in `src/`**. The only number is a
literal in the constructor: every workspace, on every plan, is created with
`totalBytes: 15 * GIGABYTE` (`src/lib/workspace-access.ts:209` and `:239`), and `plan` is hard-coded
`"free"` on the same object. So the plan and the quota are unrelated in the shipped code.

**Unclear** — Is `totalBytes` a per-plan constant, or a per-workspace number an operator can raise
for one customer without changing their plan?

**Recommendation** — Static service config: a `Record<WorkspacePlan, number>` in the backend
configuration, plus a nullable `workspaces.storage_limit_bytes` override that wins when set. Canon
§1.2 is explicit that `plans` is **not a table** — three tiers with fixed quotas is service config,
not a row that can drift — and the override column is what makes "no plans table" survive the first
enterprise negotiation. `totalBytes` on the wire is `COALESCE(storage_limit_bytes, planQuota(plan))`.

**Impact if wrong** — If plans need to be data (per-customer pricing, more than three tiers), a
`plans` table appears and `workspaces.plan` becomes an FK. One migration, no endpoint change:
`StorageQuota` is computed either way.

**Blocks** — Nothing. It blocks **sign-off on §9's `GET /workspaces/{workspaceId}/storage`**
(E-017), not its implementation.

### 40.2 Drive tree

#### OQ-07 — Is `isFavorite` per user or a global flag on the node?

**Severity** schema · **Module** drive · **Status** Position taken (canon §8.8; T-07 `node_favorites`)

**Current evidence** — `DriveNodeBase.isFavorite: boolean` is a plain boolean on the node with no
user dimension (`src/types/node.ts:58`), and `toggleFavorite` flips it on the shared tree
(`src/store/workspace-store.ts:180`, declaration; the tree is shared state). But `SmartViewId` includes `"favorites"`
(`src/types/view.ts:15-20`) and the sidebar destination is described as *"Folders, boards and files
you starred"* (`src/config/app.ts`, `SMART_VIEWS`) — second person, per reader. `RecentEntry` next
to it is unambiguously per-user (`src/types/collab.ts:184`).

**Unclear** — Does one person favouriting a folder pin it into everybody's sidebar?

**Recommendation** — Per user. `node_favorites (user_id, node_id, created_at)` with
`PRIMARY KEY (user_id, node_id)`; `isFavorite` on the wire is projected for the requesting user by a
`LEFT JOIN` on the session's id. E-028/E-029 (`PUT`/`DELETE /nodes/{nodeId}/favorite`) carry no user
in path or body (canon P-06, C-09). `isShared` is the sibling case and is likewise derived — true
when any `access_rules` row exists on the node (canon §1.3.1).

**Impact if wrong** — If it is genuinely global, the join table collapses to a boolean column on
`nodes` and the join disappears from the tree read. That direction is trivial. The other direction —
shipping a boolean and discovering it must be per-user — is a migration plus a change to every read
that projects the tree. The per-user reading is the safe one because the failure it prevents (a
shared sidebar that reorders itself when a colleague stars something) is the one users report as a
bug.

**Blocks** — **P0 Foundation, §4 (`node_favorites`) and §11 (Folder/Drive APIs).** The tree read
(E-020) either joins or it does not.

---

#### OQ-08 — Is `isPinned` per user or global?

**Severity** schema · **Module** documents · **Status** Position taken (canon §8.8: "pinning follows the same shape once confirmed")

**Current evidence** — `DocumentNode.isPinned` sits on the node beside `isFavorite`
(`src/types/node.ts:88`), and `WorkspaceDocument` carries its own copy
(`src/types/document.ts:118-133`). The pin action goes through
`documentService.setPinned(nodeId, isPinned)` — no actor argument
(`src/services/document-service.ts`), and `DocumentActionId` lists `pin`/`unpin` as a page-level
menu item, not a personal bookmark (`src/types/document.ts:153-162`). Nothing in the copy says
"your pinned pages". That is the whole difference from OQ-07: favourites read as personal in the
product copy, pins do not.

**Unclear** — Is a pin a property of the page (it sits at the top of the folder for everybody) or of
the reader (it sits at the top of *my* list)?

**Recommendation** — **Global, on the node.** `nodes.is_pinned BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT false`,
written under `document.update`. This deliberately diverges from OQ-07 rather than following it,
because the frontend evidence diverges: the pin has no actor anywhere, and the two properties sit
in different UI registers ("pin this page for the team" vs "star this for me"). Canon §8.8 says
pinning "follows the same shape once confirmed" — that confirmation is exactly what this block asks
for, and until it arrives the node column is the smaller commitment.

**Impact if wrong** — If pins are personal, `nodes.is_pinned` becomes
`node_pins (user_id, node_id)` — the same shape as `node_favorites`, one migration, and E-093's
response is projected per reader instead of shared. Cheap either way; the cost is a wrong default
being visible to a whole team for one release.

**Blocks** — **P2 Content, §12 (Page APIs).** E-093 `PUT /nodes/{nodeId}/document/pin`.

#### OQ-09 — Does renaming re-mint the slug?

**Severity** blocking · **Module** drive · **Status** Position taken (canon §8.8)

**Current evidence** — **The frontend does both, in two places, for the same logical action.**
`renameNode` re-slugs and de-duplicates against siblings
(`src/store/workspace-store.ts:498`, and the uniqueness guard the comment at `:472-480` explains). `applyDocumentSummary`
deliberately does not, and says why: *"the slug is the routing key and is minted once, at creation:
renaming a page the user is standing on must not break its URL"*
(`src/store/workspace-store.ts:883-885`). So renaming from the tree changes the URL and renaming from the
page header does not.

**Unclear** — Is the slug the routing key (mint once, never re-mint) or a derived display value
(re-mint on every rename)?

**Recommendation** — **Mint once at creation. Never re-mint on rename.** E-025 `PATCH /nodes/{nodeId}`
changes `name` and leaves `slug` alone. Re-uniquification happens only on **move** (OQ-10), against
the new sibling set. The frontend needs one change: remove the re-slug from `renameNode`. If human-
readable URLs must track the name, the escape hatch is a `nodes.slug_history` table and a 301, which
is additive and can land later.

**Impact if wrong** — If slugs must track names, every existing link, bookmark and pasted URL to a
renamed item breaks on the day of the rename, and — worse — a slug collision inside a sibling set
makes the *losing* sibling unreachable, which is precisely the hazard the store's own comment at
`workspace-store.ts:472-480` warns about. If we mint once and the product wanted tracking, the cost
is cosmetic: URLs carry a stale word.

**Blocks** — **P0 Foundation, §11 (Folder APIs) and every route in §12/§13** that addresses content
by path. E-021 `GET /nodes/resolve?path=` is unimplementable until the rule is fixed.

---

#### OQ-10 — Move does not re-uniquify the slug against its new siblings

**Severity** blocking · **Module** drive · **Status** Position taken (canon §8.8)

**Current evidence** — `moveNode` relocates a node by rewriting `parentId` and re-writing the tree;
it does not touch `slug` (`src/store/workspace-store.ts:183`, delegating to `moveNode` in
`src/lib/tree.ts:170-197`, which validates `same-parent` / `into-self` / `into-descendant` /
`invalid-target` and nothing else). Uniqueness is enforced only at creation and at rename
(`uniqueSlug(slugify(name), taken)`, `src/lib/workspace-access.ts` and
`src/store/workspace-store.ts:489-498`). Two folders each holding `notes` therefore collide the
moment one is moved into the other's parent.

**Unclear** — On move, does the moved node keep its slug (and the collision is refused), or does the
server re-uniquify it (`notes` → `notes-2`) and the URL changes?

**Recommendation** — **Re-uniquify on move, silently, against the new siblings.** `UNIQUE
(parent_id, slug) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL` is the constraint (canon §1.3.1 — it must hold *across
kinds*, and it must exclude trashed rows so a restore never collides). E-026 returns the node with
its possibly-new slug, and `MoveNodeResponse` carries it so the client re-routes rather than
404-ing. Refusing the move instead would make "move" fail for a reason the user cannot see or fix
from the drag they just performed.

**Impact if wrong** — If moves must refuse rather than rename, `MoveRejection` grows a fifth member
(`slug-conflict`), which is a wire-enum change the frontend switch at `src/lib/tree.ts:170-197`
must learn. If we refuse and the product wanted renaming, every move into a populated folder is a
coin flip. Note this interacts with OQ-09: mint-once-plus-re-uniquify-on-move is one coherent rule;
mint-once-and-never-touch-it is not, because it cannot satisfy the unique index.

**Blocks** — **P0 Foundation, §11 (Folder APIs).** E-026 and the `nodes` unique index are the same
decision.

#### OQ-11 — Is a derived `NodeState` vocabulary wanted, and is the precedence right?

**Severity** low · **Module** drive · **Status** Position taken (canon §2.4, §8.8)

**Current evidence** — The frontend has no such enum. It carries `isArchived` and `isTrashed` as
separate booleans (`src/types/node.ts:56-70`) and resolves "frozen by an archived ancestor"
separately, in `inheritedArchiveOf` (`src/lib/archive.ts:19-45`), which deliberately does **not**
read the node's own flag: *"a surface must keep offering Restore on the thing you are standing on"*
(`src/lib/permissions/evaluate.ts:58-62`). The permission evaluator applies the three narrowing
layers in a fixed order — trashed first (`if (node?.isTrashed) return key === "node.delete"`), then
frozen, then locked (`src/lib/permissions/evaluate.ts:79-85`).

**Unclear** — Should the API expose a single derived `state` field, and is `trashed > frozen >
archived > active` the precedence the product wants?

**Recommendation** — Yes, additive. `state: NodeState` is computed on read, never stored, and
`isArchived` / `isTrashed` stay on the wire unchanged because the frontend reads them. The
precedence is transcribed from `evaluate.ts:79-85`, so it cannot disagree with the permission check
that actually refuses writes.

**Impact if wrong** — Zero schema impact — it is a projection. If the vocabulary is unwanted, delete
one field from the node response; nothing reads it today.

**Blocks** — Nothing.

---

#### OQ-12 — Does duplicating a container duplicate its descendants' *content*, and what happens to secrets?

**Severity** high · **Module** drive · **Status** Answer required

**Current evidence** — The frontend duplicates **structure only**. `cloneNode` copies the node,
resets `isFavorite` and `isShared`, and recurses into `children`
(`src/lib/tree.ts:203-217`) — it never touches board rows, document blocks, config content or
secrets. Content duplication is a *separate, single-node* call made afterwards by the page that
initiated it: `duplicateNode(node.id)` then `documentService.duplicate(document.nodeId, clone.id,
clone.name)` (`src/hooks/use-document-actions.ts:90-99`). There is no equivalent call for boards,
and no traversal that would issue one per descendant. So duplicating a project today produces a tree
of empty shells, and nothing in the code says that is intended.

**Unclear** — Three sub-questions, and all three need an answer: (a) does duplicating a folder or
project copy the *content* of every descendant board, page, config and file, (b) does it copy a
descendant secret document's **values**, and (c) does it copy `access_rules` written on descendants?

**Recommendation** — (a) **Yes**, deep-copy content: a duplicate that produces empty boards is not a
duplicate, and the frontend's per-node content call is a limitation of a mock that cannot traverse,
not a design. (b) **No — never copy secret values.** Copy the `secret_documents` container and the
`secrets` rows' `key`, `environment_id`, `note` and `position`, and leave `value_encrypted` NULL,
marking each entry as needing a value. Copying ciphertext duplicates the blast radius of one leak
and produces two rows that a rotation cannot keep in step. Write one `audit_events` row per copied
secret container at `warn`. (c) **No**, do not copy access rules: `cloneNode` already resets
`isShared` (`src/lib/tree.ts:209`), and a copy that silently carries a grant is a share nobody
performed. The copy inherits from its new parent.

**Impact if wrong** — If content must not be copied, E-027 becomes a structure-only clone and is
cheap. If secrets must be copied with values, the encryption design (OQ-65) grows a re-wrap step and
the audit story changes materially. If access rules must be copied, E-027 gains a transaction over
`access_rules` and a second permission check (`node.share`) — which the endpoint currently does not
require.

**Blocks** — **P0 Foundation, §11 (E-027 `POST /nodes/{nodeId}/duplicate`)**, and P2 for the secret
branch. A deep duplicate is also the single largest transaction in the drive module (§36), so its
scope has to be known before §36 can bound it.

---

#### OQ-13 — Does the tree endpoint serve the whole workspace, or lazy children beyond a depth?

**Severity** med · **Module** drive · **Status** Position taken here

**Current evidence** — The client holds the entire tree in memory and every helper walks it:
`getFullTree()` returns all nodes for the active workspace (`src/store/workspace-store.ts`),
`flattenTree` recurses without bound (`src/lib/tree.ts:221-223`), `collectAllowed` prunes whole
subtrees on a predicate (`src/lib/tree.ts:297-320`), and the sidebar renders from the same array.
Search resolves visibility once over that array before scanning anything
(`src/services/search-service.ts:64-70`). There is no page size, no depth parameter and no lazy
loader anywhere in `src/store/workspace-store.ts`.

**Unclear** — At what workspace size does the whole-tree read stop being acceptable, and is lazy
loading required in v1?

**Recommendation** — Serve the whole tree in v1 (E-020), pruned by visibility server-side, with a
hard server cap (`AppConfigResponse.treeMaxNodes`) that returns `409` rather than a truncated tree —
a silently truncated tree is a tree with missing folders. The escape hatch is already shaped: E-023
`GET /nodes/{nodeId}/children` exists, so lazy expansion is a client change plus a `hasChildren`
boolean on the node, not a new endpoint. Do not build it speculatively.

**Impact if wrong** — If lazy loading is required from day one, `DriveNode.children` stops being
"always the full set" and every frontend helper that walks the tree (`resolvePath`, `collectAllowed`,
`effectiveAccess`, breadcrumbs) needs a "not loaded yet" state. That is a substantial frontend
change, not a backend one — which is the argument for deciding it before the frontend is adapted.

**Blocks** — Nothing to start. It blocks **sign-off on §11 (E-020)** and on §35's index plan for
`nodes_parent_idx`.

#### OQ-14 — Trash retention window, purge job, and whether `purgeAt` is returned

**Severity** high · **Module** system · **Status** Position taken (canon §8.8)

**Current evidence** — `TRASH_RETENTION_DAYS = 30` exists with the comment *"How long Trash holds a
deleted item before **the backend sweeps it** (SY-TRH-38)"* (`src/config/app.ts:42`). `TrashEntry`
carries `deletedAt` and `deletedBy` but **no `purgeAt`** (`src/types/system.ts:171-180`), and the UI
computes `daysLeft` client-side against the frozen clock (`src/hooks/use-trash.ts:35`). Nothing
sweeps: `trashByWorkspace` is an in-memory map that only ever grows
(`src/store/workspace-store.ts:341-344`).

**Unclear** — Is 30 days the retention window for every entity, is the window per-plan, and does the
purge cascade into the deleted subtree's content (board rows, document versions, stored objects)?

**Recommendation** — 30 days, workspace-wide, one number served from `GET /config` (E-139) so the
client cannot disagree with the sweeper. A nightly job purges `nodes` with
`deleted_at < now() - interval '30 days'`, and the purge is a **cascade**: the node's side table,
its rows and their activity, its versions, its `file_assets` rows and the objects behind them, and
`workspaces.used_bytes` decremented in the same transaction. `TrashEntry.purgeAt` is returned, so
"deleted in 12 days" is the server's statement rather than the client's arithmetic.

**Impact if wrong** — A shorter window loses work. A longer one is additive. Not purging at all is
the real failure: `used_bytes` (OQ-05) counts bytes nobody can reach, and the product advertises an
expiry that never happens — a retention-compliance gap, not a cosmetic one.

**Blocks** — **P4 System, §36–§38 (the sweeper transaction and the quota counter).** Also blocks
sign-off on E-036, which returns `purgeAt`.

#### OQ-15 — Rows are deleted permanently while nodes get a 30-day trash — is that intended?

**Severity** med · **Module** boards · **Status** Position taken here

**Current evidence** — Row deletion is permanent and the mock says so at the call site: *"Permanent,
and said so at the call site: records have no trash of their own"*
(`src/services/board-service.ts:1049`), and `bulkDelete` also purges the deleted rows' activity
history (`:1066`). Nodes, by contrast, go through `TrashEntry` with a 30-day window
(`src/types/system.ts:162-180`, `src/config/app.ts:42`). The audit seed contains a real example of
the hazard — a bulk action that removed twelve records in one call
(`src/services/audit-service.ts:78-85`). Meanwhile canon §1.4 puts `deleted_at` on `board_rows`
alongside `nodes` and `comments`.

**Unclear** — Should a deleted record be recoverable, and if so by whom — the user (a records bin in
the UI) or only an operator (a soft delete with no UI)?

**Recommendation** — Keep the product decision — records have no trash, and no UI offers one — but
make the deletion **operationally** recoverable: `board_rows.deleted_at` + `deleted_by`, filtered
out of every read, swept by the same job as the trash on the same 30-day window. Row activity is
retained for the same period rather than purged immediately, so "what was in TASK-042" is answerable
for as long as the row is. This costs one predicate on every row read (`WHERE deleted_at IS NULL`,
which goes in the index predicate — §35) and buys back an accidental twelve-record bulk delete.

**Impact if wrong** — If records must be user-recoverable, `TrashEntry` grows a `row` variant, E-036
returns two shapes, and the trash UI grows a second list — a real feature, not a flag. If hard
deletes are genuinely required (a data-erasure obligation), the sweeper becomes an immediate
`DELETE` and the `deleted_at` column is dropped; that direction is one migration.

**Blocks** — **P1 Boards, §15 (Row APIs).** E-065 and E-076's delete semantics, and every row-read
predicate in §35.

### 40.3 Governance, permissions and audit

#### OQ-16 — 40+ write operations carry no permission check in the mock — is the matrix the intended policy?

**Severity** critical · **Module** governance · **Status** Position taken (canon §8.8)

**Current evidence** — Nine of `board-service`'s thirty-one operations call `requirePermission`; the
other twenty-two do not. `importRows` checks `board.import`, `createColumn`/`duplicateColumn` check
`board.column.create`, `updateColumn`/`reorderColumn`/`convertColumn` check `board.column.update`,
`deleteColumn` checks `board.column.delete`, `reorderView` checks `board.view.manage` — and
`createRow`, `updateCells`, `deleteRow`, `setRowParent`, `duplicateRow`, all four bulk operations,
`createSelectOption`, `createView`, `updateView` and `deleteView` check nothing at all
(`src/services/board-service.ts:1383-1415`, and the per-operation bodies). Every one of them **is**
gated in the UI. `src/services/authz.ts:16-33` states the intent plainly: the guard exists so that a
call must get past it *"whether it came from the app's own UI, from a stale tab whose role was
downgraded a minute ago, or from a console"*, and `src/lib/permissions/evaluate.ts:24-25` says
*"None of this is security. It decides what the UI offers; the backend decides what actually
happens, and must re-check every one of these keys."*

**Unclear** — Is the 39-key matrix in `src/lib/permissions/roles.ts:20-96` the intended
authorisation policy in full, or is it a UI affordance list that the real policy will differ from?

**Recommendation** — Treat the matrix as the policy, and gate **every** write with the catalogue key
the endpoint's **Perm** column in canon §3 names. The gaps are gaps in the mock, not in the design —
the UI already gates all of them, and the two files above say so. Canon P-09 makes the Perm column
normative for exactly this reason.

**Impact if wrong** — If the real policy differs from the matrix, the divergence is not a code change
but a product decision replayed across 140 endpoints, and every frontend `can(...)` call becomes a
lie in a different direction. There is no cheap direction here: the matrix is either authoritative or
the whole permission layer is decorative.

**Blocks** — **P0 Foundation, §28 (RBAC), and the sign-off of every write endpoint in §9–§27.**

---

#### OQ-17 — `bulkMove` gates neither board and does not verify the target is a board

**Severity** critical · **Module** boards · **Status** Position taken (canon §3.9, E-077)

**Current evidence** — `bulkMove` reads the source board, reads a target by node id and writes rows
into it with **no `requirePermission` on either side** (`src/services/board-service.ts:1100-1160`).
It is the only operation in the codebase that writes into two aggregates at once, and
`BulkMoveResult.droppedColumns` shows it also reshapes data on the way
(`src/types/system.ts:45-50`). Nothing checks that `targetNodeId` addresses a board rather than a
folder.

**Unclear** — Which permission does a cross-board move require: `row.move` on both, or `row.delete`
on the source plus `row.create` on the target?

**Recommendation** — `row.delete` on the source **and** `row.create` on the target, checked
independently, because that is what the operation actually is: the record ceases to exist on one
board and comes into existence on another with a new `displayId` from the target's counter
(`src/services/board-service.ts:1137`). `row.move` is the *within-board* re-parent key (E-067) and
must not be overloaded. The target is resolved through `nodes` and refused with
`BULK_TARGET_NOT_A_BOARD` when its `kind` is not `board`, and with `BULK_TARGET_BOARD_SAME` when it
is the source. One transaction over both boards (canon §3.9).

**Impact if wrong** — If the intended key is `row.move` on both, a Member who may reorder records
but not delete them gains the ability to empty a board into another one — which is a delete wearing
a move's clothes. Changing the check later is one line; changing it after a leak is an incident.

**Blocks** — **P1 Boards, §15 (E-077)** and §36's two-aggregate transaction.

#### OQ-18 — `listFiles` takes `canView` from the caller

**Severity** critical · **Module** files · **Status** Position taken (canon §8.8, E-113)

**Current evidence** — `fileService.listFiles({ folderId, canView, signal })` takes the **answer** to the permission
question as an input: `if (!canView) throw permissionDenied(...)`
(`src/services/file-service.ts:105-118`). The caller decides whether the caller may read the folder.
This is the same class of defect as OQ-19 and OQ-20 and the same fix applies. Canon C-09 states the
rule the frontend's own guard already articulates: identity, role and visibility come from the
session (`src/services/authz.ts:24-32`).

**Unclear** — Nothing about the policy; only whether any client-supplied visibility hint should
survive into the API as an optimisation.

**Recommendation** — No. E-113 `GET /folders/{nodeId}/files` resolves visibility server-side from
the session against the node's access chain and never accepts a predicate, a role or a user id.
Client-side filtering stays in the client as a rendering convenience.

**Impact if wrong** — There is no "wrong" direction here — a caller-supplied visibility filter is
not a policy option. The block exists so the reviewer can see that the mock's shape was noticed and
deliberately not carried forward.

**Blocks** — **P2 Content, §21 (E-113).**

#### OQ-19 — `userId` is a request parameter on watches, notifications and My Work

**Severity** critical · **Module** collab · **Status** Position taken (canon P-06, C-09)

**Current evidence** — `watchService.list(userId)`, `watchService.setWatching(...)`,
`notificationService.list(userId)`, `notificationService.markRead(userId, ids)`,
`notificationService.markAllRead(userId)` and `myWorkService`'s `MyWorkInput.userId` all take the
subject as an argument (`src/services/watch-service.ts:49,65`,
`src/services/notification-service.ts:28,36,57`, `src/services/my-work-service.ts:48`). Every call
site passes `CURRENT_USER.id` (`src/store/watch-store.ts:58,82`,
`src/store/notification-store.ts:64,84,102`).

**Unclear** — Nothing about the policy; only whether an operator surface ever needs to read another
user's inbox.

**Recommendation** — Session-scoped collections live under `/me` and take no user parameter in path
or body: `/me/watches` (E-126–E-128), `/me/notifications` (E-129–E-132), `/me/work` (E-134). Mark-read
(E-130) **ignores ids outside the caller's own inbox rather than refusing** — the frontend already
sends whatever it has loaded, and a 403 there would be a worse contract than a no-op. If an
operator ever needs another user's inbox, that is a new, separately-audited endpoint, not a
parameter on this one.

**Impact if wrong** — None in this direction. If an admin inbox view is later required, `/me/...`
stays and `/workspaces/{id}/users/{userId}/notifications` is added under `workspace.member.manage`
with an audit row.

**Blocks** — **P3 Collaboration, §25 (Notifications) and §26.**

#### OQ-20 — `role` and `user` are request parameters on search

**Severity** critical · **Module** search · **Status** Position taken (canon C-09, E-133)

**Current evidence** — `SearchInput` is `{ query, role, user, limitPerGroup? }`
(`src/services/search-service.ts:45-50`), and the permission funnel is computed from those two
supplied values: `capabilitiesFor({ role, user, node })` inside `collectAllowed`
(`src/services/search-service.ts:64-70`). A caller who claims `role: "admin"` gets an admin's search
results.

**Unclear** — Nothing about the policy. The related real question is whether the funnel can be
pushed into SQL rather than run as a pre-pass.

**Recommendation** — Resolve role and identity from the session. Keep the funnel-before-scan
ordering the frontend already has — visibility is resolved once at the node and every result kind
inherits it, so *"a record inside a board you cannot open is never scanned, and a comment on it is
never returned"* (`src/services/search-service.ts:26-31`) — but express it as a visible-node-id set
computed in the query, so the scan is `target_node_id = ANY($visible) AND search_tsv @@ …` rather
than a post-filter (§27, §38).

**Impact if wrong** — None in this direction.

**Blocks** — **P3 Collaboration, §27 (E-133).**

#### OQ-21 — How does the role-preview narrowing (`previewAs`) reach a real API?

**Severity** critical · **Module** governance · **Status** Position taken (canon §8.8)

**Current evidence** — Preview is client state: `permissionStore.previewRole: WorkspaceRole | null`,
*"It can only ever narrow what is on screen"* (`src/store/permission-store.ts:23-31`), applied by
`clamp(real, preview) = roleRank(preview) < roleRank(real) ? preview : real`
(`src/hooks/use-permissions.ts:49-57`). `docs/GOVERNANCE.md:358-359` says it *"is not a session
switch… it does not re-authenticate, and a reload clears it"*. But three service operations already
take a `role` argument that comes from that clamped value —
`revealSecret({ nodeId, secretId, role, action })` and
`copySecrets({ nodeId, secretIds, role })` (`src/services/devtools-service.ts:333-336`, `:424-427`)
— so a narrowing meant for the UI is already crossing a service boundary.

**Unclear** — Does preview exist server-side at all, and if so how does the server prove that the
previewed role is a narrowing rather than an escalation?

**Recommendation** — Preview is a **request-scoped narrowing header**, never a session mutation:
`X-Preview-Role: member`. The server computes `effective = min(real, preview)` by `roleRank` and
uses it for the whole request. A `previewAs` that outranks the caller's real role is refused with
`PREVIEW_ROLE_ESCALATES` → `validation` / **400** rather than silently clamped, because a client
sending an escalation is either broken or probing and both deserve a visible answer. Preview never
appears in a request body (a body role is a claim, canon C-09), never widens, and is recorded in the
audit `context` of any write made under it so the log can explain a surprising refusal.

**Impact if wrong** — If preview must be purely cosmetic, the header is dropped and the three
service signatures lose their `role` argument — cheap. If it is meant to be a genuine session
switch ("act as"), that is a different feature with its own audit obligations and it must not be
built on this mechanism.

**Blocks** — **P0 Foundation, §28 (RBAC)** and the devtools reveal path in §23.

#### OQ-22 — "Deepest wins" (code) vs "union of permissions" (PRD `SY-INH-43`)

**Severity** blocking · **Module** governance · **Status** Position taken (canon §8.8)

**Current evidence** — The PRD says both. `SY-INH-43`'s body describes an **Override Permission**
isolating a child — a deeper rule *reducing* access — while its edge case says *"Xung đột quyền giữa
Group và User: Áp dụng mức quyền cao hơn (Union of permissions)"*. The frontend resolves it by
scope: **depth** decides between nodes — `matchIn` walks the chain root-to-node and keeps the last
match, *"Root → node, so the last match is always the most specific one"*
(`src/lib/permissions/inheritance.ts:40-42`, loop at `:60-76`) — and **specificity** decides between
subjects at one node: a rule naming the person beats one naming their role
(`const rule = direct ?? viaRole`, `src/lib/permissions/inheritance.ts:73`, with the comment at
`:49-53`). `docs/GOVERNANCE.md` §3 states it as *"The deepest rule wins, not the strongest. A
project-level grant of Manager is taken back down to Member inside one folder."* The union rule
appears nowhere in the code.

**Unclear** — When a project grants Manager and a folder inside it grants Member, does the person
hold Manager or Member in that folder?

**Recommendation** — Member. Deepest node wins; at one node a user-scoped rule beats a role-scoped
rule; the workspace role is the floor. Read the PRD's "union" as applying only to two rules of the
**same subject kind at the same node**, where taking the higher is unambiguous and harmless — which
is the only reading under which Override Permission is expressible at all.

**Impact if wrong** — A true union makes every Override Permission a no-op, and "cô lập bảo mật" —
the stated purpose of the override — becomes impossible to build. In the other direction, a user who
is Manager via their role and Member via a personal rule is under-privileged. The algorithm sits at
the centre of §28 and of the `access_rules` chain query in §35; changing it later changes the
meaning of every stored rule, not just the code.

**Blocks** — **P0 Foundation, §28 (RBAC)** and §11's tree pruning.

#### OQ-23 — Who may reveal a secret — Admin only (FE) or Admin/Manager (PRD `DV-SEC-23`)?

**Severity** blocking · **Module** devtools · **Status** Position taken (canon §8.8)

**Current evidence** — `DV-SEC-23` says *"Người dùng có quyền (Role Admin/Manager) bấm nút Reveal"*
and its edge case refuses Member/Viewer. `SY-RBC-42` gives Admin *"Toàn quyền Workspace… Audit Log,
Trash, Cấu hình hệ thống"* and lists neither secrets nor audit under Manager. The frontend chose
Admin-only: `secret.reveal` and `secret.rotate` are in the ADMIN addition set
(`src/lib/permissions/roles.ts:65-75`), and the refusal reads *"Revealing {key} needs the Admin
role"* (`src/services/devtools-service.ts:344-348`). `docs/GOVERNANCE.md` §2 agrees.

**Unclear** — Does a Manager hold `secret.reveal`?

**Recommendation** — Admin only, expressed as the permission key `secret.reveal` rather than a role
literal, so moving it to Manager later is one row in `roles.ts` and one row in the matrix — not a
code change. Keep the conservative reading until product confirms: the expensive direction is
granting it.

**Impact if wrong** — If Manager is entitled, every Manager is refused today and the audit log fills
with false denials (which are recorded — `src/services/devtools-service.ts:341-343`), so the mistake
is at least *visible*. If Admin-only was intended and Manager is granted, production credentials
reach every project lead and nothing in the log distinguishes an intended read from a leak.

**Blocks** — **P2 Content, §23 (Secret Documents)** — E-101 through E-105.

#### OQ-24 — `comment.delete` is a Member key with no ownership scope — whose comments?

**Severity** high · **Module** collab · **Status** Position taken (canon §8.8)

**Current evidence** — `comment.delete` is granted at Member (`src/lib/permissions/roles.ts:28`) and
the catalogue text does not scope it. The comment service has **no delete operation at all** —
`commentService` exports `list`, `countFor`, `listMentioning`, `scan`, `add`, `edit`, `attach`,
`reset` (`src/services/comment-service.ts:257`) — so nothing in the code demonstrates the intended
scope. `edit` does model ownership: it refuses a non-author with *"You can only edit your own
comments"* (`src/services/comment-service.ts:174-178`).

**Unclear** — May a Member delete anyone's comment, or only their own?

**Recommendation** — Own comment at `member`; anyone else's at `manager`. This mirrors the
ownership axis the codebase already uses for edit and the `OWNER_ESCALATIONS` pattern
(`src/lib/permissions/roles.ts:98-108`) — the key names the action, ownership decides the scope.
Deletion is a **tombstone** (`deleted_at`, `deleted_by`), never a row removal, so replies do not
orphan (OQ-80).

**Impact if wrong** — If Members may delete anything, a single Member can erase a thread and the
tombstone is the only trace. If only Managers may delete anything at all, authors cannot retract
their own comment — which the edit path shows the product does care about. Changing the scope later
is one predicate, but the deleted rows do not come back.

**Blocks** — **P3 Collaboration, §20 (E-122).**

#### OQ-25 — Which actions must emit an audit row? The seed advertises 19; two emitters exist

**Severity** high · **Module** governance · **Status** Answer required

**Current evidence** — `auditService.record` is called from exactly three sites: the secret path
(`pushAudit`, both allowed and denied — `src/services/devtools-service.ts:373-395`) and the access
rule writer in the permission store (`src/store/permission-store.ts:71-78`). The seeded log,
however, advertises nineteen distinct `action` strings across all nine `AuditModule` values —
`system.session.start`, `row.bulk.delete`, `secret.reveal`, `node.access.change` and others
(`src/services/audit-service.ts:200-250`). So the vocabulary is designed and the emission is not.
`SY-AUD-41` requires an actor and an IP on every record, and the service exposes `record` and `list`
and nothing else *"so no screen can grow an Edit button that quietly works"*
(`src/services/audit-service.ts:14-20`).

**Unclear** — Is the audit log a **security** log (privileged and destructive actions only) or an
**activity** log (every write)?

**Recommendation** — A security log. Audit: every key held only by Manager or Admin; every
**denial** of any key; every secret reveal/copy/rotate (allowed and denied); every access-rule and
access-mode write; every membership and role change; every permanent delete and trash-empty; every
export; session start and end; and the privileged reads of OQ-26. Do **not** audit ordinary
`row.update` / `comment.create` traffic — the row activity stream (T-14) already covers it, and
over-auditing costs six index inserts per event inside the caller's transaction (§35, §36) before it
costs readability. The seeded nineteen action strings are the starting vocabulary and must be used
verbatim so the shipped fixture and the real log agree.

**Impact if wrong** — Under-auditing is a compliance gap discovered during an incident, when the
missing rows cannot be reconstructed. Over-auditing makes the log unreadable and makes every write
pay for it. There is no cheap correction in the first direction, which is why this is high.

**Blocks** — **P4 System, §29 (Audit Logs) and §4 (`audit_events`)**, and it touches the transaction shape of every
write in §36.

#### OQ-26 — Which privileged *reads* must themselves be audited?

**Severity** med · **Module** governance · **Status** Position taken (canon §3.5, §3.23)

**Current evidence** — The frontend audits exactly one read: a secret reveal, and it audits the
denial too (`src/services/devtools-service.ts:373-395`). The admin recovery console — which lists
every restricted node in the workspace regardless of grants — is a plain read with no audit at all
(`restrictedNodesOf`, `src/lib/permissions/visibility.ts:279-291`, surfaced by
`src/components/workspace/workspace-restricted-tab.tsx`). The audit log itself is read without a
record.

**Unclear** — Which reads are privileged enough that reading them is itself an event?

**Recommendation** — Three, at `warn`: the secret reveal/copy (already), E-046
`GET /workspaces/{workspaceId}/restricted-nodes` (the deliberate access bypass), and E-137
`GET /workspaces/{workspaceId}/audit/export` (exfiltration of the log itself). Reading the audit
*page* (E-136) is not audited — it is the surface an auditor uses, and auditing it makes the log
grow by looking at it.

**Impact if wrong** — If more reads must be audited, adding one is a line inside the endpoint's
existing transaction. If these must not be, three rows too many appear at `warn`. Genuinely cheap in
both directions — it is medium because it is a compliance question someone must sign, not a
technical one.

**Blocks** — Sign-off on **§28 (E-046)** and **§4 (`audit_events`)**.

#### OQ-27 — Audit retention period and export

**Severity** high · **Module** governance · **Status** Answer required

**Current evidence** — There is no retention rule anywhere. The log is an in-memory array that
*"only ever grows at the head"* (`src/services/audit-service.ts:265`), `AUDIT_PAGE_SIZE = 40`
(`src/config/app.ts:57`) is the only bound, and `AuditQuery` has no `from`/`to`
(`src/types/audit.ts:42-48`). No export exists in the frontend at all — `AuditPage` is
`{ events, total, bySeverity }` and the page renders filters and a reload
(`src/hooks/use-audit-log.ts`).

**Unclear** — How long are audit events retained, and is a CSV export required in v1?

**Recommendation** — **12 months**, then partition-drop by month (`audit_events` is monthly-
partitioned on `at` in §35, which makes retention a `DETACH PARTITION` rather than a delete storm).
Twelve months is the shortest window that survives an annual review cycle, and it is a number
somebody in compliance has to actually approve — hence "answer required" rather than "position
taken". Ship E-137 as a CSV stream gated on `workspace.audit.view`, and audit the export itself at
`warn` (OQ-26).

**Impact if wrong** — A shorter retention destroys evidence that a regulator may ask for. A longer
one is storage, and with monthly partitions it is cheap. Getting the *partitioning* wrong is the
expensive part: switching to partitions after the table is large is an offline rewrite, so the
decision has to be made before the first row lands, even if the number is later changed.

**Blocks** — **P4 System, §4 (`audit_events` partitioning) and §35.** The partition scheme has to be
in the first migration.

#### OQ-28 — Audit list has a limit but no cursor and no date range

**Severity** med · **Module** governance · **Status** Position taken (canon §6.3)

**Current evidence** — `auditService.list` slices `matched.slice(0, query.limit ?? AUDIT_PAGE_SIZE)`
— no offset, no cursor (`src/services/audit-service.ts`). `AuditQuery` offers `module`, `severity`,
`actorId`, `search`, `limit` (`src/types/audit.ts:42-48`). `AuditPage.total` is documented as
*"matches before the limit was applied"* (`src/types/audit.ts:52`), so more rows are known to exist
with no way to reach them.

**Unclear** — Nothing contentious; only confirmation that `total` and `bySeverity` are facets over
the **whole filtered set** rather than the page.

**Recommendation** — Keyset cursor on `(at DESC, id DESC)`, plus `from`/`to` as ISO 8601 query
parameters, `limit` capped at 200. `total` and `bySeverity` stay facets over the full match set —
that is how the header renders them today (`src/types/audit.ts:50-55`). Purely additive to the
frontend: the existing fields keep working.

**Impact if wrong** — If `total` was meant to be the page count, the header reads "40 of 40" forever
and the facets become meaningless. Cheap to correct.

**Blocks** — Sign-off on **E-136**; nothing to start.

#### OQ-29 — `ExportOutcome.omittedColumns` implies column-level permissions that exist nowhere

**Severity** high · **Module** system · **Status** Position taken here

**Current evidence** — The frontend does implement a withholding rule, and it is **not** an ACL: a
regex over the column *name*. `SENSITIVE_NAMES = /secret|token|password|credential|api[\s_-]?key|
private[\s_-]?key/i` and `isSensitiveColumn` tests the name
(`src/lib/board-export.ts:40-51`); `selectExportColumns` drops those columns unless
`canViewSensitive` (`:63-75`); and `canViewSensitive` is `can("secret.reveal")`
(`src/components/board/board-page.tsx:82`). The dialog then tells the user *"…are left out — your
role cannot read those columns"* (`src/components/board/export/export-dialog.tsx:129-136`). The file
comments call this out itself: *"Column-level ACLs are a backend concern; until they exist this name
test is the honest stand-in"* (`src/lib/board-export.ts:41-47`). Nothing in `src/types/` models a
per-column ACL — `BoardColumn.hidden` is a schema flag and `SavedView.hiddenColumnIds` is a view
flag, neither is a permission, and `AccessRule` is per node.

**Unclear** — Is the name heuristic the intended rule, is it meant to become a real per-column
permission, or should it be dropped?

**Recommendation** — Reproduce the shipped rule **server-side, verbatim**, including the regex and
the `secret.reveal` gate, and return the withheld column names in `ExportOutcome.omittedColumns`.
Do **not** build a column-level ACL: nothing else in the model has one, and inventing it is exactly
the speculative generality ground rule 8 forbids. Note the rule honestly in §24 as a heuristic, not
a control — a column named "Prod credentials" is caught and one named "PW" is not.

**Impact if wrong** — If real per-column permissions are intended, this is a genuine data-leak
surface with its own design: a `column_access_rules` table, a resolution order against node access,
and a change to every board read — not just export. That is a feature, and it must be scoped as one.
If the heuristic is meant to be dropped, deleting it is one function.

**Blocks** — **P4 System, §24 (Export).** E-086's response cannot be specified without it.

---

### 40.4 Boards — records, schema, views, import and export

#### OQ-30 — Board and document carry an id *and* a `nodeId`; config and secret carry only a `nodeId`

**Severity** schema · **Module** boards · **Status** Position taken (canon §8.8)

**Current evidence** — `Board` has both `id` and `nodeId` (`src/types/board.ts:412` and `:416`), and so
does `WorkspaceDocument` (`src/types/document.ts:118-119`). `ConfigDocument` and `SecretDocument`
have **no** separate id — they are keyed by `nodeId` alone (`src/types/devtools.ts:40`, `:85`). Both
ids are genuinely used as foreign keys in different places: `BoardRow.boardId`
(`src/types/board.ts:239`) and `EmbedBlock.boardNodeId`. `Board.name` duplicates the node's name, and
`WorkspaceDocument` duplicates `title`, `icon`, `isPinned`, `isLocked` and `isArchived` from the node.

**Unclear** — Should the two ids be collapsed into one, and which side owns the duplicated lifecycle
fields?

**Recommendation** — Keep both ids: the frontend relies on both, and collapsing them would touch
every board route. `node_id` is `UNIQUE NOT NULL` on `boards` and on `documents`. The **node owns**
`name`, `is_pinned`, `is_locked`, `is_archived`, `deleted_at` — they are stored once and **projected**
into the board/document response, never stored twice. Canon P-04 makes this the routing rule too:
content is entered through its node (`GET /nodes/{nodeId}/board`) and then addressed by its own id
(`/boards/{boardId}/...`).

**Impact if wrong** — Storing the lifecycle fields on both sides guarantees drift, and the frontend
reads both copies (`DocumentNode.isLocked` in the tree, `WorkspaceDocument.isLocked` on the page).
If the ids were meant to be one, the change is a migration plus every `/boards/{boardId}` path
becoming `/nodes/{nodeId}` — a full re-cut of §13–§19.

**Blocks** — **P1 Boards, §4 (`boards`, `documents`) and §13.**

---

#### OQ-31 — `BoardKind` and `BoardViewType` are different vocabularies

**Severity** med · **Module** drive · **Status** Position taken (canon §8.8)

**Current evidence** — `BoardNode.boardKind` is `"kanban" | "table" | "timeline" | "doc"`
(`src/types/node.ts:38`); `SavedView.type` is `"table" | "kanban" | "calendar" | "gantt"`
(`src/types/board.ts:270`). `"doc"` has no view counterpart and `"timeline"` is presumably `"gantt"`
under an older name. A board has many saved views, so one `boardKind` cannot be "the view type".

**Unclear** — Is `boardKind` the default view a board opens on, or only the icon the sidebar draws?

**Recommendation** — A **presentation hint on the tree node**. Stored as sent, not validated against
`BoardViewType`, not used to pick a view. The authoritative view list is `Board.views`, and the view
a board opens on is the first in `position` order.

**Impact if wrong** — If it was meant to be the default view, boards open on the wrong one. One
column, one line of read logic — cheap to change, which is why it is medium and not schema-blocking.

**Blocks** — Sign-off on **§4 (`nodes.board_kind`)**.

---

#### OQ-32 — Does a date cell hold a day key or an instant when `includesTime` is true?

**Severity** critical · **Module** boards · **Status** Position taken (canon §8.8, C-04)

**Current evidence** — One field serves both cases:
`{ kind: "date"; iso: string | null; text?: string }` (`src/types/board.ts:223`). `Condition.value`
and `ViewFilter.value` are both documented as `YYYY-MM-DD` for date columns
(`src/types/board.ts:41-43`, `:296-300`). Everything downstream reads through `dayKey`, which slices
the first ten characters of a UTC ISO string (`src/lib/board-dates.ts:6-10`) — the dashboard
(`src/lib/dashboard.ts:104-118`), My Work (`isSameCalendarDay` / `isBeforeDay`,
`src/lib/my-work.ts:151-163`), the Gantt (`dayIndex`, `src/lib/board-dates.ts:18-20`). And
`src/lib/calendar.ts:1-16` exists entirely to prevent the classic bug: *"A due date is a square on a
calendar, not a moment… pick the 27th, save it, reload it as the 26th — happens the instant that
square is turned into a timestamp in one zone and read back in another."*

**Unclear** — When `DateConfig.includesTime` is true, is `iso` a full instant, and if so is the
day-key comparison still the right one for filters and deadline buckets?

**Recommendation** — **Store the string exactly as the frontend sends it** inside the `cells` JSONB:
`YYYY-MM-DD` when `includesTime` is false, a full ISO 8601 instant when it is true. Never normalise
one into the other, never widen a date through UTC. For indexing, expose **two** generated columns on
`board_rows` — `due_date DATE` and `due_at TIMESTAMPTZ` — and index those (canon §1.3.2). All
filtering and all deadline bucketing compare on the day key. `DATE_VALUE_INVALID` rejects a value
that does not match its column's `includesTime`.

**Impact if wrong** — This is the highest-risk item in the whole data model. Parsing a date-only
value through a timezone shifts every due date by a day for half the world, silently, and the wrong
value is then the stored value — there is nothing to recover from. The frontend built an entire
day-key layer specifically to avoid it, and a backend that re-introduces the conversion undoes that
work invisibly.

**Blocks** — **P1 Boards, §4 (`board_rows` generated columns), §15 (E-066), §19.1 (filters)** and
**P3 (§27 My Work, dashboard)**.

---

#### OQ-33 — What bounds the subtask hierarchy — depth, cross-board parents, cycles, archive cascade?

**Severity** high · **Module** boards · **Status** Position taken (canon §8.8)

**Current evidence** — The type comment is explicit: *"Nothing here caps the depth: a subtask may
itself be a parent, and the hierarchy helpers walk as far as the data goes"*
(`src/types/board.ts:255-262`), and `src/lib/board-hierarchy.ts:5-16` repeats it — *"no nested
arrays, no second copy of a record, and no depth limit"*. Cycles are guarded **defensively at read
time**, not rejected at write time: `descendantIdsOf` carries a `seen` set *"Guarded so a cyclic
write cannot hang a render"* (`src/lib/board-hierarchy.ts:79-95`) and `ancestorIdsOf` does the same
(`:98-110`). At write time, `setRowParent` refuses self-parenting and refuses a parent that is
already a descendant (`src/services/board-service.ts:384-392`), and it looks the parent up inside the
**same board record** (`record.rows.get(parentRowId)`, `:387`), so a cross-board parent is
structurally impossible today. Deleting a parent lifts its children rather than cascading (canon
§3.8, E-065).

**Unclear** — Is there a maximum nesting depth, and is a cross-board parent ever wanted?

**Recommendation** — (a) parent and child on the **same board**, refused with
`ROW_PARENT_CROSS_BOARD`; (b) **depth cap 5**, refused with `ROW_PARENT_TOO_DEEP`; (c) cycles
rejected at write time by a recursive CTE over `parent_row_id`, under the board's advisory lock
(§37) because a cycle is a property of a set of rows and two concurrent legal moves can produce one;
(d) archiving a parent does **not** cascade — children are full records with their own lifecycle
(`src/types/board.ts:257-259`); (e) deleting a parent **lifts** its children to top level and returns
them in `DeleteRowResponse` so the client reconciles.

**Impact if wrong** — A cycle makes every hierarchy walk on the server unbounded (the client is
guarded; SQL is not). A cross-board parent breaks `SubtaskDisplay: "nested"`, which renders within
one board's row set (`src/types/board.ts:378`). If the depth cap is unwanted it can be raised
without a migration; if it is wanted and absent, a pathological import can build a 500-deep chain.

**Blocks** — **P1 Boards, §16 (Subtask APIs), E-067** and §37's lock plan.

---

#### OQ-34 — How are rows ordered with no sort applied, and is manual reordering required?

**Severity** schema · **Module** boards · **Status** Position taken (canon §8.8)

**Current evidence** — `BoardRow` has no `position` or `rank` field (`src/types/board.ts:236-266`).
`sequence` exists but is *"the numeric part of the display id; monotonic per board, never reused"*
(`src/types/board.ts:242`) — an identity, not an order. `SavedView.sorts` is multi-level and may be
empty (`src/types/board.ts:342`). Insertion already carries meaning: a new row goes after
`afterRowId`, and a subtask is filed after its parent's last descendant
(`src/services/board-service.ts:320-341`). `row.move` is a permission key and `BulkActionId` has
`"move"`, but `BulkMoveResult` shows `move` means **move to another board**
(`src/types/system.ts:45-50`), not reorder. `docs/BOARD.md` §5.7 names this outstanding:
*"`rowOrder` is currently the array the server sent. Manual reordering and concurrent inserts need
an explicit order key (fractional index / LexoRank) and `PATCH /rows/:id/position`."*

**Unclear** — May a user drag records into an order, and does Kanban card position within a column
persist?

**Recommendation** — `board_rows.position NUMERIC NOT NULL`, a fractional index, defaulted on insert
(midpoint between neighbours, or `max + 1` at the end). Default order is `(position, id)`, which is
also the row-pagination sort key (OQ-36). `PATCH /boards/{boardId}/rows/{rowId}/position` (E-073) is
specified and reserved even though no frontend surface calls it yet. Kanban card position within a
column follows the view's sort and is not separately stored.

**Impact if wrong** — Without an order key, two concurrent inserts race for the same slot and the
board's order differs per client — which then makes `SY-BLK-34`'s shift-click range selection select
*different records for different people*. Adding the column later is a full-table backfill and a
change to the row read contract. It costs one column now.

**Blocks** — **P1 Boards, §4 (`board_rows`), §15 (E-061, E-062, E-073)** and §35's
`board_rows_position_idx`.

#### OQ-35 — `BoardRow` has `createdBy` but no `updatedBy`

**Severity** low · **Module** boards · **Status** Position taken here

**Current evidence** — `BoardRow` carries `createdAt`, `updatedAt`, `createdBy` and no `updatedBy`
(`src/types/board.ts:245-247`). The information exists elsewhere: `ActivityEntry.actor` records who
made each change (`src/types/board.ts:500`).

**Unclear** — Should the last editor be a column on the row, or only reconstructible from activity?

**Recommendation** — Add `board_rows.updated_by UUID REFERENCES users(id)` and return `updatedBy`.
It is one column, it is already implied by the activity stream, and every list that renders "updated
2h ago" eventually wants "by whom" without a join against a table that may have been pruned
(OQ-52).

**Impact if wrong** — Purely additive in both directions. If it is unwanted, one column goes unread.

**Blocks** — Nothing.

#### OQ-36 — Row pagination: `nextCursor` exists and is always `null`; filtering is client-side

**Severity** critical · **Module** boards · **Status** Position taken (canon §8.8, §6.3)

**Current evidence** — `BoardSnapshot.nextCursor` is typed `string | null` with the comment *"Null
when the whole record set arrived in one page"* (`src/types/board.ts:433`) and the service returns
`null` unconditionally, saying *"The whole record set arrives in one page today"*
(`src/services/board-service.ts:236-241`). The store has no cursor state and no fetch-on-scroll;
`use-virtual-rows.ts` virtualises a fully-loaded array. **Every view filters, sorts and groups
client-side over `rowsById`** (`src/store/board-store.ts`, and the whole of `src/lib/board-filter.ts`
/ `board-sort.ts` / `board-group.ts`). The only row-count ceiling anywhere is `IMPORT_MAX_ROWS =
5_000` (`src/config/app.ts:48`), and it bounds one import, not a board.

**Unclear** — Does the server take over filtering, sorting and grouping, or does the client keep
them and simply fetch every page?

**Recommendation** — Return a **real** `nextCursor` on `(position, id)` (E-047, E-061) and have the
client fetch pages **eagerly until the set is complete**, keeping client-side filtering exactly as
it is. Cap a board at a documented row count served from `GET /config`, and refuse a create past it
with `BOARD_ROW_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` → `conflict` rather than truncating a read. Server-side query is a
separate, later feature (§19.1 specifies the filter semantics precisely enough to move them, when
someone asks).

**Impact if wrong** — Server-side pagination **without** server-side filtering is the single
highest-risk mismatch in the audit: the UI would render "12 of 5000 matches" where the 5000 is a
page, and every count, every group header and every bulk-select range would be silently wrong. In
the other direction, eager paging of a 10 000-row board is slow but correct, and correctness is the
one that cannot be patched later.

**Blocks** — **P1 Boards, §13 (E-047), §15 (E-061)**, and it is a precondition for OQ-42's
board-scope export.

---

#### OQ-37 — `ConditionOperator` is documented as a superset of `FilterOperator` and is not

**Severity** low · **Module** boards · **Status** Position taken (canon §2.5)

**Current evidence** — `src/types/board.ts:21-23` claims `ConditionOperator` is *"deliberately a
superset of `FilterOperator`"*. It is not: `FilterOperator` uniquely has `onOrBefore` and `onOrAfter`
(`src/types/board.ts:284-294`); `ConditionOperator` uniquely has `isAnyOf`, `isNoneOf` and `on`
(`src/types/board.ts:25-36`). Eight operators are shared.

**Unclear** — Were they meant to be one vocabulary?

**Recommendation** — Ship **two** Postgres enums, exactly as the code has them, and flag the comment
as stale to the product owner. Unifying them silently would either drop `onOrBefore`/`onOrAfter`
from view filters or add set operators to a UI with no control for them.

**Impact if wrong** — If they were meant to be one, we ship two enums where one would do — cosmetic.
If we unify them wrongly, every saved view holding `onOrBefore` breaks on read.

**Blocks** — Nothing.

---

#### OQ-38 — How deep may a `ConditionGroup` nest, and how large may a column `config` be?

**Severity** med · **Module** boards · **Status** Position taken here

**Current evidence** — `ConditionGroup.groups: readonly ConditionGroup[]` is recursive with no
stated bound (`src/types/board.ts:63`), and the tree is stored inside
`SelectConfig.options[].availability`, i.e. inside a column's `config` JSONB. Evaluation recurses
without a depth guard (`src/lib/conditions.ts`). The UI offers no control for nesting past one
level.

**Unclear** — What are the caps, and are they product limits or safety limits?

**Recommendation** — Safety limits, enforced at the validation boundary and served from
`GET /config` so the client can pre-check: **depth 3**, **50 conditions per group**, and a
**256 KB** ceiling on the whole `board_columns.config` document. Past any of them,
`CONDITION_TREE_TOO_DEEP` → `validation` / **400**.

**Impact if wrong** — Without a cap, a hand-crafted payload blows the evaluator's stack on both
client and server, and a column config can grow past a sane row size. Caps that turn out to be too
low are raised in config, with no migration.

**Blocks** — Sign-off on **§14 (Column APIs)** and §18's rule evaluation.

---

#### OQ-39 — How is a column type conversion requested? `ColumnPatch` has no `type` and no `position`

**Severity** med · **Module** boards · **Status** Position taken (canon §3.7)

**Current evidence** — `ColumnPatch` is `{ name?, width?, hidden?, config?: Partial<...> }` —
**no `type`, no `position`** (`src/types/board.ts:446-451`). `ConversionPreview` exists for a
conversion flow (`src/types/board.ts:453-460`), the service has a `convertColumn` operation gated on
`board.column.update` (`src/services/board-service.ts:1402`), and the catalogue describes the key as
*"Rename, resize, hide and convert columns"* (`src/lib/permissions/catalog.ts`).

**Unclear** — Nothing about intent; only confirmation that conversion and reorder stay off the
patch.

**Recommendation** — Three endpoints, not one overloaded patch: `PATCH
/boards/{boardId}/columns/{columnId}` for name/width/hidden and a **discriminated** config patch
(`{ type: "select"; config: Partial<SelectConfig> } | …`, never a union-indexed `Partial`);
`POST .../convert` with `?dryRun=true` returning `ConversionPreview` without writing; and
`POST /boards/{boardId}/columns/reorder`. `COLUMN_TYPE_CONFIG_MISMATCH` rejects a `select` config
sent against a `date` column.

**Impact if wrong** — A single loose PATCH invites exactly that mismatch, and conversion is where
the `CellValue.text` preservation rule lives (`src/types/board.ts:214-218`) — it must be its own
audited operation with its own dry run.

**Blocks** — **P1 Boards, §14 (E-053, E-056, E-057).**
